steps: Heat the oven to 220 C (425 F). Cut the sweet potato into thick wedges and roast for 25 minutes, turning once, until soft inside and browned at the edges.
Squeeze over the lemon and sprinkle with chili and salt.

name: Karanga, roasted peanuts with lemon and chili
inspiredBy: East African karanga, the spiced roasted peanuts sold in paper cones
about: Roasted peanuts tossed with a squeeze of lemon, a pinch of chili and salt. They are salty, crunchy and satisfying. Peanuts bring **vitamin E, magnesium and protein**.
steps: Toss the warm peanuts with the lemon juice, chili and salt.
Eat right away while they are still crunchy.

name: Ndizi choma, roasted plantain with lemon and chili
inspiredBy: Swahili coast ndizi choma, roasted plantain
about: Plantain roasted until the edges caramelize, with lemon and a pinch of chili. It is sweet, smoky and filling, and the kind of thing sold on the roadside in Tanzania. Plantain brings **potassium and fibre**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C (425 F). Peel the plantain and cut it into thick coins or long wedges.
Roast on a tray for 25 minutes, turning once, until soft inside and browned at the edges. Squeeze over the lemon and sprinkle with the chili and salt.

name: Maziwa moto, warm spiced milk with cardamom and ginger
inspiredBy: Swahili and Somali spiced milk, drunk hot in the evening
about: Milk warmed with cardamom and a little fresh ginger until it smells like a Mombasa kitchen. It is soothing and a little sweet on its own. The milk brings **calcium and protein**.
steps: Warm the milk in a small pot with the cardamom and the sliced ginger until it steams, about 5 minutes.
Strain into a mug and sip it hot.

name: Kasha with mushrooms and a fried egg
inspiredBy: Ukrainian and Polish buckwheat with mushrooms (hrechka z hrybamy, kasza gryczana z grzybami)
about: Toasty buckwheat kasha folded through browned mushrooms and onion, with a fried egg on top and a crunchy dill pickle on the side. It is the breakfast of a thousand Ukrainian and Polish kitchens. The egg and mushrooms bring **protein, choline and B vitamins**, and the buckwheat adds magnesium.
steps: Tip the kasha into a small pot with twice its volume of boiling water and a pinch of salt. Cover and simmer very gently until the water is absorbed, about 12 minutes, then take it off the heat and keep the lid on.

While it cooks, cover the dried porcini with a few spoonfuls of hot water and leave them for 10 minutes. Warm half the rapeseed oil in a wide pan over medium-high heat. Cook the onion for 3 minutes, then add the fresh mushrooms in a single layer. Leave them alone for a few minutes so they brown, then add the chopped porcini and their soaking liquid and keep going until it has cooked off, about 8 minutes. Season with salt and pepper.
Fluff the kasha with a fork and fold it into the mushrooms with half the dill.
Push the kasha to one side, add the rest of the rapeseed oil and fry the egg until the white is set and the yolk is still runny, about 3 minutes.

Toast the sunflower seeds in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until golden. Drizzle the kasha with the sunflower oil, which gives it that nutty, toasted-seed flavour. Serve with the egg on top, scattered with the seeds and the rest of the dill, with the pickle on the side for a sharp, crunchy bite.
tip: Cook a double batch of kasha the night before. It warms through in the pan in two minutes, which makes this about a 15-minute breakfast.
ingredients: dried porcini (soaked in hot water for 10 minutes, then chopped, with the soaking liquid kept)

name: Kefir with soaked buckwheat, apple and raspberries
inspiredBy: Ukrainian and Polish kefir with soaked buckwheat (hrechka z kefirom, kasza gryczana z kefirem)
about: Toasted buckwheat groats soaked overnight in cold kefir until they turn tender and nutty, then topped with grated apple, raspberries, toasted sunflower seeds and a sprinkle of poppy seeds. It is a classic cool, sour-sweet breakfast across Ukraine and Poland. The kefir and poppy seeds bring **calcium**, and the sunflower seeds add **vitamin E**.
steps: The night before, rinse the buckwheat in a sieve and stir it into the kefir in a jar or bowl with a pinch of cinnamon. Cover and refrigerate for at least 10 hours, until the groats are tender with a little nutty chew.
In the morning, toast the sunflower seeds in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until golden and fragrant.
Grate the apple straight into the bowl and stir it through.
Top with the raspberries, the warm sunflower seeds and a sprinkle of poppy seeds.
tip: Use pear or whatever berries are in season.

name: Baked tvorog and oat syrniki with raspberries
inspiredBy: Ukrainian syrnyky and Polish placuszki z twarogu, baked and made with oats
about: Little golden tvorog cakes, bound with oats instead of flour and baked instead of fried, served with a spoonful of sour cream and crushed raspberries. It is a slow Saturday morning breakfast that makes the next morning's too. The tvorog and oats give you **protein, calcium and slow carbohydrate**.
steps: Heat the oven to 200 C and line a tray with parchment. Whizz the oats in a blender for a few seconds, until they look like a coarse flour.

Mash the tvorog with the egg, grated apple, cinnamon, lemon juice and salt until mostly smooth, then stir in the ground oats. Let the dough rest for 10 minutes so the oats swell and it firms up. If it is too soft to shape, spoon it onto the tray in rounds.
With wet hands, shape it into 8 small, thick rounds and set them on the tray. Brush the tops with half of the oil.
Bake for 12 minutes, flip them, brush with the rest of the oil and bake another 8 minutes, until golden and set.
While they bake, toast the sunflower seeds in a dry pan for 2 minutes. Crush half the raspberries with a fork to make a quick sauce and keep the rest whole.

Serve 4 syrniki per person with the raspberries, a spoonful of sour cream and a scatter of sunflower and poppy seeds. Keep the second portion in the fridge and warm it in the oven or a dry pan on Sunday morning.
tip: If the dough feels soft, chill it for 20 minutes before shaping. Frozen raspberries are fine.
ingredients: farmer's cheese. If you use cottage cheese, drain it in a sieve for 10 minutes first
rapeseed oil, for the tray and the tops

name: Open rye sandwiches with pickled herring, onion and dill
inspiredBy: Polish and Baltic herring on rye (śledź na chlebie)
about: Dark rye topped with pickled herring, thin onion and dill, with sauerkraut and a dill pickle on the side. It is the plate you would be served at a Polish or Baltic lunch table. The herring brings **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**, and the rye keeps you full.
steps: Slice the onion very thin and rinse it under cold water for a minute to take off the sharpest bite. Drain the herring, pat it dry and cut it into bite-size pieces.
Lay the herring on the rye and scatter the onion rings on top.
Finish with dill and a grind of black pepper. Serve the sauerkraut and pickle alongside for crunch and extra tang.
tip: If pickled herring is too salty for you, rinse the pieces for a minute and pat them dry. Rollmops work too, and a spoonful of sour cream is a lovely addition.

name: Ukrainian borscht with white beans and beef, with rye bread
inspiredBy: Ukrainian borscht with beans, as cooked in Kyiv and Chernihiv homes
about: A ruby-red Ukrainian borscht with beets, cabbage, carrot and white beans, built on a little beef and finished with garlic, dill and a spoonful of sour cream, with dark rye alongside. Frying the beets with tomato paste and vinegar first keeps their colour. It makes two portions and it is even better tomorrow, with **iron, folate and potassium** in every bowl, and half a boiled egg adds choline.
steps: Put the beef in a large pot with the bay leaf, allspice and a pinch of salt. Cover with cold water by about 3 cm, bring to a boil, skim off any foam and simmer gently, partly covered, for 40 minutes.

While the beef simmers, boil the egg for 9 minutes, cool it under cold water, then peel and halve it. Warm the oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Cook the onion until soft and golden, about 6 minutes. Add the carrot and beets, the tomato paste and the vinegar and cook, stirring, until they have softened and the pan smells sweet and sharp, about 10 minutes.
Add the cabbage to the beef pot and simmer for 10 minutes.

Stir in the beet mixture and the beans and simmer 10 minutes more, until the cabbage is soft and the beef is falling apart. Taste, and add salt or a splash of vinegar until it is pleasantly sweet and sour.
Stir in the garlic and half the dill. Ladle into bowls with half an egg each, a spoonful of sour cream and the rest of the dill, and serve with the rye.
Cool the second portion and pack it for tomorrow's lunch. Reheat it gently, since boiling hard dulls the colour.
tip: In a pressure cooker, simmer the beef for 15 minutes, then add everything else and cook 5 more.
ingredients: from a tin, drained and rinsed
half a hard-boiled egg per bowl, so one egg for two portions

name: Georgian lobio, red bean stew with walnuts and herbs, with warm cheese and lavash
inspiredBy: Georgian lobio, with canned beans and lavash for shoti and mchadi
about: Soft red kidney beans in a golden onion and garlic base, scented with khmeli-suneli and thickened with a paste of ground walnuts, cilantro and vinegar. Georgians eat it with a slice of soft sulguni cheese and flatbread. The beans, walnuts and cheese bring **iron, folate, calcium and plant omega-3**.
steps: Warm the oil in a pot over medium heat. Cook the onion until deeply golden, about 10 minutes, stirring now and then.
Add the garlic and khmeli-suneli and stir for a minute, until it smells fragrant.
Tip in the beans with a good splash of water and simmer for 10 minutes. Mash about a quarter of the beans against the side of the pot so the stew turns creamy.
Mix the walnuts with half the cilantro, the vinegar and a ladle of the bean liquid to make a rough paste. Stir it in and simmer 3 more minutes. Season with salt and pepper.
Lay tonight's cheese slices over the hot lobio for the last 2 minutes, lid on, until soft. Keep the rest of the cheese to warm over tomorrow's portion.
Finish the lobio with the rest of the cilantro and the pomegranate seeds. Serve with warm lavash.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. It firms up in the fridge, so loosen it with a splash of water when you warm it.
tip: Georgians eat lobio with pickled vegetables too, and with a spoonful of adjika for heat. Sulguni is salty, so taste before you add more salt to the pot.

name: Gołąbki, Polish cabbage rolls with barley and pork in tomato sauce
inspiredBy: Polish gołąbki, with barley as in the old village version
about: Tender cabbage leaves rolled around lean pork, barley and onion, then braised in a tomato and dill sauce until sweet and soft. Barley, kasza jęczmienna, is the old village filling, with rice a later arrival. The cabbage and tomato bring **vitamin C and K**, and the barley adds slow fibre.
steps: Simmer the barley in salted water until just tender, about 30 minutes, then drain, keeping a few spoonfuls of the cooking water. While it cooks, cut out the core of the cabbage and put the whole head in a big pot of boiling water for a few minutes, peeling off the outer leaves as they soften.
Warm half the oil in a pan and cook the onion and carrot until soft, about 6 minutes. Cool for a few minutes.
Mix the pork, egg, barley, onion mixture, garlic, half the dill, the paprika, marjoram, salt, pepper and 3 tablespoons of the barley's cooking water with your hands, so the filling stays moist.
Shave down the thick rib on each cabbage leaf. Put a spoonful of filling at the base, fold in the sides and roll up tightly.

Shred the remaining cabbage into a wide oven dish or pot. Whisk the tomato paste with about 2 cups of hot water (for two portions) and the rest of the oil, season it with a pinch of salt, and pour about half over the cabbage. Set the rolls on top, seam side down, and pour over the rest.
Cover and bake at 180 C for 45 minutes, then uncover for the last 15 so the sauce thickens, until the cabbage is soft. Stir in the lemon juice and the rest of the dill.
Serve the rolls with plenty of sauce. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Roll the cabbage on Tuesday night while the lobio simmers, then keep the rolls covered in the fridge and bake them on Wednesday. Freezing the whole cabbage head overnight and thawing it also makes the leaves peel off soft with no blanching.
ingredients: one small green cabbage, about 4 big outer leaves per portion, the rest shredded for the pot
one egg for two portions, to bind the filling

name: Chicken with kasha and mushrooms, with mizeria
inspiredBy: Polish and Ukrainian chicken with kasha and mushrooms, with Polish mizeria made lighter with kefir
about: Browned chicken thighs cooked on a bed of toasted kasha and mushrooms with plenty of dill, and a cool, tangy cucumber mizeria on the side. The kasha soaks up all the juices, so it is one pan with no rice or potatoes. The chicken and mushrooms bring **protein, niacin and B vitamins**, and the buckwheat adds magnesium.
steps: Season the chicken with half the salt, the pepper and the paprika. Warm the oil in a wide pan with a lid over medium-high heat and brown the thighs for about 4 minutes a side. Set them on a plate.

Meanwhile, cover the dried porcini with a few spoonfuls of hot water. In the same pan, cook the onion and fresh mushrooms until the mushrooms are browned, about 6 minutes, then add the chopped porcini and keep the soaking liquid. Add the garlic for the last minute.

Beat the egg in a bowl, stir in the kasha until every grain is coated, then push the mushrooms aside and toast it in the clear space for 2 minutes, stirring, until the grains separate and smell nutty. This is the old trick for fluffy, crumbly kasha. Pour in the porcini soaking liquid and enough hot water to make about 1¼ cups (300 ml) in all for both portions, roughly twice the volume of the kasha. Nestle the chicken on top, cover and simmer gently for 15 minutes without stirring, until the water is absorbed and the chicken is cooked through with no pink.
Scatter over half the dill and leave the pan covered, off the heat, for 5 minutes.
For the mizeria, toss the cucumber with a pinch of salt and let it sit for 10 minutes, then squeeze out the water. Stir in the kefir, lemon juice and the rest of the dill.
Serve the chicken and kasha with the mizeria on the side. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, and dress its cucumber just before eating so it stays crisp.
tip: Do not stir once it is covered, or the grains go sticky. Slice and salt the cucumber for the second portion only on the day.
ingredients: one egg for two portions, to keep the kasha fluffy
dried porcini (soaked in hot water for 10 minutes, then chopped, with the soaking liquid kept)

name: Balkan white bean and sweet pepper stew with beef
inspiredBy: Serbian pasulj and Bosnian grah, with smoked paprika in place of smoked meat, and sweet pepper and spinach added
about: A thick Balkan-style white bean stew with sweet red pepper, carrot and tender beef, scented with smoked paprika and bay, and finished with a splash of vinegar and dill. It is honest, filling cold-weather food that you eat with rye bread and a pickle. The beans, spinach and peppers bring **iron, folate and vitamin C**.
steps: Warm the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat and brown the beef for 5 minutes. Take it out.
Lower the heat, add the onion, carrot and red pepper and cook until soft and sweet, about 8 minutes. Stir in the garlic and tomato paste for a minute.
Take the pot off the heat for a moment, stir in both paprikas and then return it to the heat. This keeps the paprika sweet instead of bitter.

Return the beef with the bay leaf, salt, pepper and enough water to just cover. Simmer, partly covered, for 40 minutes, then add the beans and simmer 20 minutes more, until the beef is tender and the stew is thick. Mash a few beans against the pot to thicken it.
Stir in the spinach, vinegar and dill and cook for 2 minutes, until the spinach wilts. Serve with rye bread and sliced pickle.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. It tastes even better after a night in the fridge.
tip: A pressure cooker does the beef in 25 minutes. With dried beans (soaked overnight) the broth gets thicker, so use about a third of a cup of dry beans per portion.
ingredients: from a tin, drained and rinsed

name: Satsivi, Georgian chicken in walnut sauce, with cucumber and herb salad
inspiredBy: Georgian satsivi, with chicken thighs and a lighter sauce
about: Poached chicken under a rich, silky sauce of ground walnuts, garlic, onion and warm spices, traditionally served at room temperature at feasts. The sauce is thickened only by walnuts, with a splash of vinegar for sparkle. The chicken and walnuts bring **protein, plant omega-3 and magnesium**, and it gets better as it sits.
steps: Put the chicken in a pot with the halved onion, the bay leaf, a pinch of salt and enough water to cover. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook for 25 minutes, until cooked through. Leave it in the broth for 10 minutes, then lift it out.
Warm the oil in a small pan and cook the chopped onion until golden, about 8 minutes. Stir in the khmeli-suneli, coriander, cinnamon, turmeric and clove for a minute, until fragrant.

Grind the walnuts and garlic in a food processor to a fine paste. Add the onion and spices, then slowly blend in about a cup of the warm broth (for two portions) until the sauce is the thickness of heavy cream. Stir in most of the vinegar and season.
Warm the sauce in a small pot for 5 minutes. Do not let it boil, or it can split and turn bitter.
Slice or shred the chicken, spoon over the sauce and leave it for 20 minutes so the flavours settle. Garnish with the pomegranate seeds and half the cilantro.
Toss the cucumber with the rest of the cilantro, a pinch of salt and a splash of vinegar. Serve alongside the chicken, with lavash for scooping.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow. It is best at room temperature, and the sauce thickens in the fridge, so loosen it with a spoonful of water.
tip: Georgian cooks often add a pinch of dried marigold petals (Imeretian saffron) and a little blue fenugreek (utskho suneli). If you can find them at a Georgian or Eastern European shop, they are worth a try.
ingredients: half in two pieces for the pot, the rest finely chopped

name: Baked trout with dill potatoes and sauerkraut salad
inspiredBy: Baltic and Carpathian baked trout with dill potatoes
about: A plump trout fillet baked with garlic and lemon, served with hot potatoes tossed in butter and dill, with a glass of cold kefir alongside, and a crunchy sauerkraut and carrot salad. It is the simple supper of the Carpathians and the Baltics. The trout brings **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**, and the sauerkraut adds a tangy crunch.
steps: Heat the oven to 200 C. Put the potatoes in a pot of cold salted water with a few dill stems, bring to a boil and cook until tender, about 15 minutes.
While they cook, make the salad. Squeeze the sauerkraut dry (rinse it first if it is very sour) and mix with the carrot and onion. Drizzle with the sunflower oil and a grind of pepper.

Set the trout skin-side down on a piece of parchment on a tray. Scatter over the garlic, lemon juice, a pinch of salt and half the butter in small pieces. Bake for 12 to 15 minutes, until the flesh turns opaque and flakes with a fork.
Drain the potatoes and toss them with the rest of the butter and most of the dill. Serve the cold kefir in a glass alongside, or pour some over, the way Polish cooks eat new potatoes with dill.
Serve the trout on the potatoes with the sauerkraut salad and the rest of the dill.
tip: Salmon or mackerel fillets work the same way. A whole gutted trout takes about 25 minutes.
ingredients: scrubbed, halved or quartered so the pieces match
cold, to serve with the potatoes
chopped, plus a few stems for the pot
unrefined sunflower oil, to drizzle on the salad

name: Spinach pkhali with pomegranate and lavash
inspiredBy: Georgian spinach pkhali
about: Georgian spinach and walnut pâté, bright with garlic, cilantro and a little vinegar, shaped into small balls and topped with ruby pomegranate seeds. Scoop it up with warm flatbread. The spinach and walnuts bring **folate, iron and vitamin K**.
steps: Drop the spinach into boiling water for 1 minute, then cool it under cold water and squeeze out as much water as you can with your hands. Chop it finely.
Pound or blitz the walnuts with the garlic and salt to a thick paste.
Mix the spinach with the walnut paste, cilantro, vinegar and khmeli-suneli. Taste for salt and a little more vinegar.
Shape into 4 small balls, top with the pomegranate seeds and serve with warm lavash.
tip: Make it a day ahead if you like: the flavours settle, and it keeps 3 days in the fridge. Beets, cabbage and green beans make good pkhali too.

name: Apple with toasted sunflower seeds
about: Crisp apple wedges with a handful of warm, toasted sunflower seeds, the semechki that Ukrainians crack and munch all year round. The seeds bring **vitamin E and magnesium**.
steps: Toast the sunflower seeds in a dry pan for 2 to 3 minutes, until golden and fragrant. Eat them with the apple wedges.

name: Smoked sprats on rye with dill pickle and lemon
inspiredBy: Baltic and Ukrainian smoked sprats on rye (shproty na chornomu khlibi)
about: Smoked sprats from the tin laid on a slice of dark rye with sliced dill pickle, fresh dill and a squeeze of lemon, the classic Baltic and Ukrainian zakuska. Sprats are eaten whole, bones and all, so they bring **omega-3 and calcium**.
steps: Lay the sprats on the rye. Top with the pickle slices and dill, squeeze over the lemon and finish with black pepper.

name: Tvorog with dill and cucumber on rye
inspiredBy: Polish twarożek with dill and cucumber on rye (twarożek z koperkiem i ogórkiem)
about: Fresh tvorog mixed with chopped dill and cucumber and spread on dark rye, a Polish twaróg sandwich that makes a good afternoon snack. The tvorog brings **protein, calcium and B12**.
steps: Mix the tvorog with the cucumber, dill, salt and pepper. Spread it on the rye.

name: Kefir with raspberries
about: A glass of cold kefir with crushed raspberries and a pinch of cinnamon, a classic Slavic afternoon drink. The kefir brings **calcium and B12**.
steps: Pour the kefir into a glass or bowl, crush half the raspberries into it and top with the rest, with a pinch of cinnamon.

name: Baked apple with walnuts and honey
inspiredBy: Polish and Ukrainian baked apples (pieczone jabłka)
about: A soft baked apple filled with chopped walnuts and cinnamon, a cosy Polish and Ukrainian winter treat. The apple adds fibre and the walnuts bring **plant omega-3**.
steps: Heat the oven to 190 C. Core the apple, leaving the bottom intact, and stand it in a small dish.
Mix the walnuts with the cinnamon and spoon them into the apple. Add a splash of water to the dish.
Bake for 25 minutes, until the apple is soft and the skin starts to wrinkle.

name: Chicken liver pâté on rye with pickle
inspiredBy: Polish and Ukrainian chicken liver pâté (pasta z wątróbki, pechinkovyi pashtet)
about: Chicken livers cooked with plenty of onion until just done, mashed into a rough pâté and piled on dark rye with a slice of dill pickle. It is a Polish and Ukrainian classic that tastes like home. A little liver goes a long way: it brings **iron, B12, folate and choline** in one small snack.
steps: Melt the butter with the rapeseed oil in a small pan over medium heat and cook the onion until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the liver and marjoram and cook, stirring, until the liver is browned outside and just cooked through with no pink inside, about 5 minutes. Season with salt and pepper.
Mash with a fork, or pulse a few times, to a rough pâté. Spread it on the rye and top with the pickle.
tip: Once a week is plenty of liver.

name: Tvorog with apple and poppy seeds
inspiredBy: Polish and Ukrainian twaróg and poppy seed sweets (twaróg z makiem)
about: Fresh tvorog with grated apple, a pinch of cinnamon and a spoonful of poppy seeds, a Polish and Ukrainian sweet snack that tastes like a cheesecake. The tvorog brings **protein and calcium** and the poppy seeds add a little extra **calcium**.
steps: Spoon the tvorog into a bowl and grate the apple over it. Stir in the cinnamon and let it sit for 5 minutes so the apple softens.
Sprinkle over the poppy seeds and eat right away.

name: Baked apple with poppy seeds and cinnamon
inspiredBy: Polish and Ukrainian baked apples with poppy seeds (pieczone jabłka z makiem)
about: A soft baked apple filled with poppy seeds and cinnamon, a Polish and Ukrainian winter treat that tastes a bit like makowiec. The apple adds fibre and the poppy seeds add a little **calcium**.
steps: Heat the oven to 180 C. Core the apple, leaving the bottom intact, and stand it in a small dish.
Mix the poppy seeds with the cinnamon and spoon them into the apple. Add a splash of water to the dish.
Bake for 25 minutes, until the apple is soft and the skin starts to wrinkle.

name: Sauerkraut and carrot slaw
inspiredBy: Polish sauerkraut surówka (surówka z kapusty kiszonej)
about: A crisp, sharp Polish surówka of sauerkraut and grated carrot with a little sunflower oil. It cuts through a rich meal as well as it makes a snack. The sauerkraut brings **fibre and vitamin C**, and the carrot adds vitamin A.
steps: Squeeze the sauerkraut dry (rinse it first if it is very sour) and put it in a bowl.
Add the carrot and onion, then dress with the sunflower oil and a grind of pepper. Toss and eat right away, or chill it for 20 minutes.

name: Arepas with huevos pericos and black beans
inspiredBy: Colombian and Venezuelan arepas with huevos pericos, the everyday scramble of eggs, tomato and scallion
about: Golden corn arepas with a soft scramble of eggs, tomato, scallion and wilted spinach, warm black beans and a squeeze of lime. Arepas are made from precooked corn flour, so they are naturally gluten-free and cook in a dry pan. The eggs, beans and spinach bring **protein, choline, iron and folate**, and the lime keeps it bright.
steps: Use black beans from your Sunday pot (see the plan notes), or canned beans at about three times the dry weight, drained and rinsed. Warm them with a splash of water.

Stir the masarepa with a pinch of the salt and enough warm water to make a soft dough, a bit firmer than play dough. Let it rest for 5 minutes, then shape it into two discs (one at the Light size) about 1.5 cm thick, pinching any cracks closed.

Cook the arepas in a dry nonstick or cast-iron pan over medium heat until they have a golden crust and sound hollow when tapped, about 7 minutes a side. Or brown them for 4 minutes a side and finish them in a 200°C (400°F) oven for 8 minutes.
While they cook, warm the oil in a second pan and soften the scallion for 2 minutes. Add the tomato and cook for about 4 minutes, until it turns jammy, then stir in the spinach until it wilts.
Beat the eggs with the rest of the salt, pour them in and stir gently until just set and still glossy, about 2 minutes. Stir in half the cilantro.
Split the arepas and fill them with the eggs, or serve them alongside. Add the beans, a squeeze of lime and the rest of the cilantro.
tip: Cook the arepas the night before and re-crisp them in a dry pan or toaster for 3 minutes, and breakfast takes 10. At the Light size, make one arepa. Check the label on the masarepa: it should say precooked corn, nothing else (buy a gluten-free line if you are celiac).
ingredients: precooked cornmeal for arepas, not masa harina

name: Tapioca crepes with queijo coalho, a fried egg and linhaça mango yogurt
inspiredBy: Brazilian tapioca, the cassava-starch crepe sold at breakfast stands in the northeast, with a fried egg and iogurte com linhaça (yogurt with ground flaxseed) on the side
about: A lacy, chewy crepe made from cassava starch, folded around golden queijo coalho that goes soft and spotty in the pan, with a fried egg alongside. Cool yogurt with mango and a spoon of ground flaxseed makes it a proper breakfast. It is **gluten-free by nature**, and the egg, cheese and yogurt bring protein, choline and calcium.
steps: Stir the tapioca starch and salt with just enough water to make it feel like damp sand that holds together when squeezed. Leave it for 10 minutes, then rub it through a sieve so it turns into fine, fluffy crumbs.
Heat a nonstick pan over medium heat. Scatter the crumbs in an even round about 18 cm wide, with no oil. After about a minute they fuse into a pale, lacy crepe.
Lay the coalho on one half, press lightly and let it soften for 1 to 2 minutes, until the cheese is spotty and the crepe is just set. Fold the crepe over and slide it onto a plate.
Fry the egg in the same pan, without oil, until the white is set and the yolk is still soft, about 2 minutes. Tuck it next to the crepe, or inside it, as many Brazilians do.
Stir the ground flaxseed into the yogurt, toss the mango with the lime juice and spoon it over the yogurt.
tip: Brazilian shops sell tapioca already hydrated (goma), which skips the first step. Or hydrate and sieve the starch the night before; it keeps in a sealed tub in the fridge, and breakfast takes 8 minutes. If you are celiac, buy the starch from a gluten-free line. Queijo coalho is sold at Brazilian shops, and halloumi grills the same way.
ingredients: ground flaxseed, stirred into the yogurt

name: Quinoa con leche with banana and cinnamon
inspiredBy: Peruvian quinua con leche, the warm breakfast quinoa simmered in milk with cinnamon and clove
about: Quinoa simmered slowly in milk with cinnamon and clove until creamy, sweetened with mashed banana and topped with a few slices. It is the kind of breakfast Lima sells in a cup on cold mornings. Quinoa and milk together bring **complete protein, magnesium and calcium**.
steps: Rinse the quinoa in a fine sieve under cold running water for a minute, until the water runs clear. This washes off the bitter coating.
Put the quinoa, milk, cinnamon, clove and salt in a pot (enough for both bowls) and bring it to a gentle simmer. A cinnamon stick, if you have one, is even better.
Cook uncovered on low heat for about 20 minutes, stirring now and then, until the grains have popped open and the porridge is creamy. Add a splash of milk or water if it gets too thick.
Mash half the banana into the pot for sweetness.
Spoon one portion into a bowl and slice half of the remaining banana on top.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow. It sets firm in the fridge, so loosen it with a splash of milk when you reheat it, and slice the last of the banana on top.
tip: Cook it on Wednesday evening while dinner is on, then reheat one bowl on Thursday and the other on Friday, about 3 minutes each. Stir in a spoon of raisins or a little honey if you like it sweeter.
ingredients: half mashed in, the rest sliced on top

name: Rice and black beans with garlicky couve, orange and grilled queijo coalho
inspiredBy: the Brazilian everyday plate of arroz e feijão with couve refogada, laranja and queijo coalho grelhado
about: Rice and black beans with thin ribbons of garlicky couve (kale or collards), sweet orange slices and squares of golden grilled queijo coalho. It is the Brazilian lunch plate found in every kitchen, and the orange is there to cut through the beans. The beans, greens and cheese bring **iron, folate and calcium**, and the orange helps you absorb the iron.
steps: Use a few spoons of leftover rice, or cook it fresh: rinse it and simmer it covered in twice its volume of water for about 15 minutes, then let it rest off the heat for 5. Use the beans from your Sunday pot (see the plan notes), or canned beans at about three times the dry weight, drained and rinsed, and warm them with a splash of water.
Soften the onion in half the oil for about 6 minutes, until soft and golden, then stir it through the beans.

In the same pan, warm the rest of the oil with the garlic for 30 seconds. Add the couve and toss over high heat for 2 to 3 minutes, until bright green and still a little crisp. Season with salt and the lime juice.
Slice the coalho into thick squares and cook in a dry nonstick pan over medium heat for 1 to 2 minutes a side, until golden and spotty.
Pile the rice and beans on a plate. Add the couve, cheese and orange.
tip: Queijo coalho is sold at Brazilian shops; halloumi grills the same way.
ingredients: cook it fresh, see the steps
couve: collard greens or kale, about half a bunch, stems out, rolled and sliced into thin ribbons

name: Caldo tlalpeño with chicken, chickpeas and chipotle
inspiredBy: Mexico City caldo tlalpeño, the smoky chicken and chickpea soup
about: A brothy, smoky Mexico City soup of shredded chicken, chickpeas and carrot in a tomato and chipotle broth, finished with avocado, cilantro and lime. The sauce is fried first, which is what gives it that sweet, deep red base. Chicken and chickpeas bring **protein, iron and folate**.
steps: Blend the tomato, chipotle, garlic, half the onion, the cumin and oregano with a splash of water until smooth.
Warm the oil in a pot, add the sauce and fry it for 5 minutes, stirring, until it darkens and thickens.

Add the chicken thigh, the carrot, the cilantro stems (chop the leaves for the end), the salt and enough water to cover by 3 cm. Simmer for 15 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through. Lift it out and shred it.
Add the chickpeas to the pot and simmer for 5 minutes. Return the chicken.
Ladle into a bowl and top with the rest of the onion, finely chopped, plus the avocado, cilantro and a squeeze of lime.
tip: Check the label on the canned chipotles and on any boxed broth you use. Half a chipotle gives a gentle heat; add a whole one if you like it hot.

name: Causa with sardines, egg and avocado
inspiredBy: causa limeña, the cold layered potato terrine from Lima, here with canned sardines and avocado in the middle
about: A cool, lime-bright layer of golden mashed potato spiked with ají amarillo, filled with mashed sardines and creamy avocado, and finished with sliced egg, tomato and cilantro. It is a Lima lunch staple and a lunchbox hero because it is served cold. The sardines bring **omega-3, calcium and vitamin B12**, and the potato brings potassium.
steps: Lower the egg into a pot of boiling water with the potato chunks. Boil for 10 minutes, then lift the egg into cold water. Keep the potatoes going until very tender, about 15 minutes in all. Drain them, and let them steam dry in the pot for a minute.
Mash the warm potatoes until smooth with the ají amarillo paste, most of the lime juice, the oil and a pinch of salt. You want a smooth, bright yellow dough. Chill it for 10 minutes.
Mash the sardines (bones and all, they melt in) with the avocado, the rest of the lime juice, the sliced scallion and a pinch of salt.
Press half the potato into a flat layer on a plate, spread the sardine and avocado filling over it and top with the rest of the potato, smoothing the surface.
Garnish with the sliced egg, tomato wedges and cilantro. Eat it cold or at room temperature.
tip: Boil the potatoes the night before and lunch is a 10 minute assembly. Canned tuna or chicken are the classic fillings, and both work here. Buy sardines in oil or water, not in a sauce, and check the label on the ají paste.
ingredients: canned in oil, drained, with the bones

name: Beef in hogao with black beans and baked maduros
inspiredBy: Colombian hogao, the tomato and scallion sofrito, over lean beef, with black beans in place of red, ripe plantain and avocado from the bandeja paisa plate
about: Lean ground beef simmered in hogao, the Colombian tomato and scallion base, with spinach wilted in, next to warm black beans, sweet caramelized baked plantain and a few slices of avocado. The sweet plantain with the savoury, tangy beef is the classic Colombian pairing. The beef, beans and spinach bring **iron, zinc and vitamin B12**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Peel the plantain and slice it on a long diagonal into thick pieces. Toss with a third of the oil and a pinch of salt and roast for 20 to 25 minutes, turning once, until soft and caramelized at the edges.
For the hogao, warm half the remaining oil in a pan and soften the scallion and garlic for 2 minutes. Add the tomato and cumin and cook for 8 minutes, until it turns jammy. Scoop out a third.

Use black beans from your Sunday pot (frozen, if you stashed a tub), or canned beans at about three times the dry weight, drained and rinsed. Warm them in a small pot with the scooped-out hogao and a splash of water.
Brown the beef in a pan with the rest of the oil for about 5 minutes, breaking it up. Stir in the rest of the hogao and the salt, and simmer for 5 minutes, then fold in the spinach until it wilts.
Serve the beef with the beans, maduros and avocado, with the cilantro and lime juice over everything.
tip: The plantain should be properly ripe, with a mostly black skin, for real sweetness.

name: Peruvian quinoa soup with beef and vegetables
inspiredBy: Peruvian sopa de quinua, the everyday Andean quinoa soup, with lean ground beef and greens for a fuller meal
about: A bright, herby soup of lean beef, potato, carrot and quinoa, finished with kale, peas, a fistful of cilantro and lime. It is an Andean home classic on cold evenings and it reheats beautifully. The quinoa and beef bring **protein, iron and zinc**, and the lime helps you absorb the iron.
steps: Warm the oil in a wide pot over medium heat. Cook the onion, garlic, ají amarillo paste and cumin until the onion is soft and sweet, about 5 minutes.
Add the beef and stir for 4 minutes, breaking it up, until it loses its raw colour. Add the carrot, potato, oregano and salt, then pour in enough water to cover everything by 3 cm.
Bring to a boil, lower the heat and simmer for 12 minutes. Rinse the quinoa in a sieve, stir it in and simmer for 12 minutes more, until the grains look translucent and have popped their tails.
Stir in the peas and kale for the last 3 minutes. Switch off the heat and stir in the cilantro and lime juice.
Eat one portion now. Pack the second for tomorrow's lunch, and loosen it with a splash of water when you reheat it, because the quinoa keeps drinking.
tip: Rinse the quinoa well, and skip bulk bins if you are celiac, since cross-contact is common there. If you use boxed broth in place of water, check the label for wheat.

name: Roasted salmon in ají amarillo glaze with crisp potatoes and salsa criolla
inspiredBy: Peruvian flavours: the ají amarillo of every Lima kitchen, and the lime-and-onion salsa criolla that goes with fish
about: Salmon roasted with a fruity, gently hot ají amarillo and garlic glaze, next to crisp-edged potatoes and roasted red pepper with a sharp onion salsa. The glaze caramelizes while the fish stays tender. Salmon brings **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the potatoes and red pepper with half the oil and a pinch of the salt on a tray. Roast for 25 minutes, turning once, until the potatoes are crisp and golden at the edges.

Meanwhile make the salsa criolla. Soak the sliced onion in cold water for 2 minutes to soften its bite, drain, then toss with half the lime juice, half the cilantro and a pinch of salt. Leave it to sit.
Stir the ají amarillo paste with the grated garlic, the rest of the lime juice and a spoon of the oil. Pat the salmon dry, season it with salt and spread the glaze over the top.
Push the vegetables over, put the salmon on the tray skin-side down and roast for 10 to 12 minutes, until it just flakes and the glaze has darkened at the edges.
Serve the salmon with the potatoes and pepper, drizzle with the last of the oil, and spoon the salsa criolla on top with the rest of the cilantro.
tip: Ají amarillo paste is sold at Latin grocers and online; check the label, since a few brands add fillers.
ingredients: half for the glaze, half for the salsa
sliced very thin, red onion if you have it

name: Beef picadillo tacos with carrot, peas and cabbage slaw
inspiredBy: Mexican picadillo, the home-style ground beef with tomato, carrot and peas, served in corn tortillas
about: Lean ground beef simmered with tomato, onion, carrot and peas and a little ancho and cumin, spooned into warm corn tortillas with crunchy lime cabbage and a little grated queijo coalho. Picadillo is an everyday Mexican supper and it is on the table in about 35 minutes. The beef brings **iron, zinc and vitamin B12**, and the carrots bring vitamin A.
steps: Toast the ancho in a dry pan for 20 seconds each side, then soak it in hot water for 10 minutes, until soft. Blend it with the tomato, garlic, cumin and oregano until smooth.
Warm the oil in a wide pan and soften the onion and carrot for 5 minutes. Add the beef and brown it for about 5 minutes, breaking it up.
Pour in the blended sauce and the salt and simmer for 10 minutes, until thick and clinging. Stir in the peas for the last 3 minutes.
Toss the cabbage with half the lime juice and a pinch of salt. Warm the tortillas in a dry pan.
Fill the tortillas with the picadillo and top with the grated coalho (queso fresco or cotija if you have it), the cilantro and the rest of the lime juice. Serve the slaw alongside.
tip: Queso fresco is the Mexican choice if you can find it. Check the tortillas say 100% corn, nothing else, and check the label on the ancho powder if you use it. Picadillo keeps 3 days and is good over rice or in a baked potato.
ingredients: stemmed and seeded, toasted and ground, or 1 tsp ancho powder

name: Galinhada with chicken, corn and peas
inspiredBy: Brazilian galinhada from Goiás, the one-pot chicken and rice coloured with urucum, with a little chicken liver the way many home cooks add giblets
about: Chicken thighs and a little chicken liver cooked with rice in one pot with tomato, sweet pepper and golden urucum, with corn and peas scattered on top and spinach folded through at the end. It is Brazilian Sunday comfort food on a Thursday, and it is even better the next day. The liver is a small amount with a big payoff: it brings **iron, vitamin B12 and folate**.
steps: Toss the chicken with the lime juice, half the salt and the pepper. Warm the oil in a wide heavy pot over medium-high heat and brown the chicken for about 3 minutes a side. Set it aside.

In the same pot, cook the onion, red pepper and garlic with the colorau for 5 minutes, until soft. Add the tomato and the raw chopped liver and cook for 4 minutes more, stirring, until the tomato is jammy and the liver melts in.
Stir in the rinsed rice for a minute so every grain gets coated. Return the chicken and pour in hot water, about twice the volume of the rice. Add the rest of the salt.
Bring to a simmer, cover and cook on low for 15 minutes. Scatter the corn and peas on top, cover again and cook for 5 minutes more. Switch off the heat and leave it covered for 10 minutes.
Fluff with a fork and fold in the spinach, scallion and cilantro, so the spinach wilts in the steam. Eat one portion now and pack the second for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: The liver disappears into the rice and just adds depth; leave it out if you prefer. Colorau is sold at Brazilian and Latin shops. Check the label, because some brands cut it with wheat flour; plain sweet paprika plus a pinch of turmeric is a safe stand-in.
ingredients: chicken liver, trimmed and chopped small
or sweet paprika with a pinch of turmeric

name: Salmon moqueca capixaba-style with peppers, tomato and mashed cassava
inspiredBy: moqueca capixaba from Espírito Santo, the coconut-free moqueca cooked with tomato, peppers, cilantro and urucum, with salmon and a mash of cassava where the coast would serve pirão
about: Salmon gently stewed with ripe tomato, sweet pepper, onion, cilantro and golden urucum, spooned over a soft mash of cassava that soaks up the juices, with quick garlicky kale (couve) on the side. The capixaba style skips the coconut and lets the tomato and lime do the work. Salmon brings **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**, and the kale brings calcium.
steps: Put the cassava in a pot of salted water, bring it to a boil and cook for about 20 minutes, until a knife slides in with no resistance.

Meanwhile, rub the salmon with half the lime juice and a pinch of salt. Layer the onion, pepper and tomato in a wide pan with the garlic, half the oil, the colorau and a pinch of salt. Cover and cook over medium heat for 10 minutes, until the vegetables are soft and have made a juicy sauce.
Nestle the salmon into the vegetables, cover and simmer gently for 8 minutes, until the fish flakes. Do not stir, or the fish will break up.
Drain the cassava, keeping a splash of its water. Mash it with a spoon of the oil, the rest of the lime juice, a pinch of salt and enough cooking water to make it creamy.
Warm the rest of the oil in a pan with a pinch of salt and toss the kale over high heat for 2 to 3 minutes, until bright green and still a little crisp.
Spoon the mash into a bowl, lay the fish and stew over it, and scatter with the cilantro. Serve the garlicky kale alongside.
tip: Frozen peeled cassava is sold at most Latin and Caribbean shops and saves the peeling. Any firm fish works, and shrimp is classic. Check the label on the colorau.
ingredients: skinless fillet, or pull the skin off
peeled, cut in chunks, woody core removed
couve: stems out, sliced into thin ribbons

name: Pork tamales in red chile salsa with lime cabbage slaw
inspiredBy: Mexican tamales rojos de puerco, with olive oil in the masa in place of lard
about: Soft, tender masa wrapped around shredded pork in a deep guajillo and ancho salsa, steamed in corn husks until the masa pulls away clean. It is the weekend project: put on some music and fold a batch. The masa is corn, so it is **naturally gluten-free**, and the pork brings protein and thiamin.
steps: Soak about eight dried corn husks (they are a wrapper, not on the list) in a big bowl of hot water for 30 minutes, weighed down with a plate, until soft and pliable.
Simmer the pork in a pot of salted water with a quarter of the onion and garlic for 40 minutes, until it shreds easily. Lift it out, shred it, and keep about 2 cups of the broth.

Toast the guajillo and ancho in a dry pan for 20 seconds each side, then soak in hot water for 10 minutes. Blend with the tomato, most of the remaining onion (keep a thin slice for the slaw), the rest of the garlic, cumin, oregano and a pinch of salt. Simmer the salsa in a pan for 8 minutes, until thick and darker, then stir in the pork and let it cool.

Mix the masa harina and the rest of the salt with warm broth, a splash at a time, until it comes together. Then beat in the oil for 3 minutes, until the dough is soft and spreadable like thick hummus.
Spread a few spoons of masa over the lower two thirds of a husk, add a spoonful of pork, fold in the sides and fold the narrow end up. Stand the tamales upright, folded side down, in a steamer.
Steam, covered, for 60 to 70 minutes, topping up the water now and then, until the masa pulls away cleanly from the husk. Rest for 10 minutes.

Toss the cabbage with the lime juice, a pinch of salt and a little of the onion, sliced thin, and serve with the tamales. Keep the second portion for tomorrow's lunch and reheat it in a steamer or microwave, still in its husk.
tip: Dried corn husks are sold at Latin grocers and in many supermarkets' Mexican aisle. No husks? Use parchment squares tied with kitchen string. Traditional masa is whipped lard; oil gives a denser, still tender tamale. Tamales freeze for 3 months. Check the label on the masa harina (buy a gluten-free line if you are celiac).

name: Ajiaco with chicken, corn and potatoes
inspiredBy: Colombian ajiaco santafereño from Bogotá, with the three kinds of potato simplified and yogurt standing in for cream
about: A thick, golden Bogotá soup of chicken, corn and potatoes, perfumed with guascas and finished with creamy avocado, fresh cilantro and a spoon of cool yogurt. Some of the potatoes melt into the broth to thicken it, and the rest stay in tender chunks. Potatoes and corn bring **potassium, vitamin C and B6**.
steps: Warm the oil in a pot over medium heat and soften the scallion and garlic for 2 minutes. Add the chicken, the salt and enough water to cover everything by 3 cm.
Bring to a simmer and cook for 15 minutes. Add the sliced potatoes, which will dissolve into the broth, and simmer for 15 minutes more.
Add the potato chunks, the corn and the guascas and simmer for another 15 minutes, until the chunks are tender and the broth is thick and golden.
Lift the chicken out, shred it and return it to the pot for a minute.
Ladle into a bowl. Top with the avocado, cilantro and a spoon of the yogurt.
tip: Guascas is sold dried at Colombian shops; leave it out if you cannot find it. Yellow potatoes plus some russets give the classic texture. A few capers and a spoon of cream on top is how Bogotá serves it. Check the label on any boxed broth.
ingredients: half peeled and sliced thin, half in chunks
in place of cream, about ¼ cup
dried; or a pinch of dried oregano

name: Mango with lime and chile
about: Juicy mango cubes with a squeeze of lime and a pinch of chile, the way Mexican street stalls sell it. It is sweet, sharp and a little hot. The mango brings **vitamin C and vitamin A**.
steps: Cube the mango and toss it with the lime juice, a pinch of cayenne and a tiny pinch of salt.
tip: Check the label on the chile powder if you use a blend instead of pure cayenne.

name: Orange with lime and chile
about: Juicy orange segments with a squeeze of lime and a pinch of chile, the way Mexican fruit stalls serve it. It is cold, sweet and a little hot. Oranges bring **vitamin C and folate**.
steps: Peel the orange and cut it into rounds or segments, then squeeze the lime over and dust with cayenne and a tiny pinch of salt.
tip: Check the label on the chile powder if you use a blend instead of pure cayenne.

name: Chía fresca with orange and lime
inspiredBy: Mexican chía fresca, the chia agua fresca sold at street stalls, sweetened only with orange
about: Chia seeds soaked in water with fresh orange and lime juice until they plump up and turn jelly-like. It is cool, tangy and lightly sweet. Chia brings **omega-3, calcium and magnesium** in a very Mexican way.
steps: Stir the chia into a tall glass of cold water (about 250 ml) and leave it for 10 minutes, stirring once or twice, until it plumps up.
Stir in the orange juice and lime juice, add ice, and drink it right away.

name: Banana yogurt with flaxseed and cinnamon
inspiredBy: Brazilian iogurte com banana e linhaça, the everyday snack bowl
about: Thick yogurt topped with sliced banana, a spoon of ground flaxseed and a dusting of cinnamon, a very Brazilian way to snack. It is creamy, sweet and a little nutty. The yogurt brings **protein and calcium**, and the flaxseed brings omega-3.
steps: Slice the banana into the yogurt, then sprinkle with the ground flaxseed and cinnamon.

name: Grilled queijo coalho with orange
inspiredBy: queijo coalho na brasa, the grilled cheese sold on skewers on Brazilian beaches
about: Squares of queijo coalho seared until golden and squeaky, with juicy orange segments to cut through the salt. It is the Brazilian beach snack, done in a pan. The cheese brings **calcium and protein**, and the orange brings vitamin C.
steps: Cut the coalho into thick squares and sear them in a dry nonstick pan over medium heat for 1 to 2 minutes a side, until golden and spotty.
Peel the orange, split it into segments and eat them with the warm cheese.
tip: Halloumi works the same way.

name: Black bean dip with carrot and red pepper sticks
inspiredBy: Mexican frijoles negros mashed with lime and cumin, served like a dip
about: Creamy mashed black beans with lime, garlic, cumin and a little olive oil, scooped up with crunchy carrot and red pepper sticks. It is savoury, tangy and filling. Black beans bring **fibre, iron and folate**.
steps: Use beans from your Sunday pot (see the plan notes), or canned beans at about three times the dry weight, drained and rinsed.
Mash them with a fork or blitz with the lime juice, grated garlic, cumin, oil and salt, adding a splash of water for a creamy texture. Stir in the cilantro.
Serve with the carrot and red pepper for dipping.
tip: Make a double batch on Sunday; it keeps 4 days.

name: Guacamole with red pepper strips and baked tortilla wedges
inspiredBy: Mexican guacamole, scooped with crisp baked tortilla and raw red pepper
about: Chunky avocado mashed with lime, onion, cilantro and a little tomato, scooped up with crisp baked corn tortilla wedges and sweet red pepper strips. It is creamy, fresh and very filling. Avocado brings **vitamin E, potassium and healthy fat**, and the red pepper brings vitamin C.
steps: Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Spread the tortilla wedges on a tray and bake for about 8 minutes, until crisp.
Mash the avocado roughly with the lime juice and salt, then fold in the tomato, onion and cilantro, all finely chopped.
Scoop with the warm wedges and the red pepper strips.
tip: Check the tortillas say 100% corn, nothing else.

name: Roasted chickpeas with lime and chile
about: Chickpeas roasted until crunchy and tossed with lime, cumin and a pinch of cayenne. They are salty, tangy and very moreish, the kind of snack you can carry in your pocket. Chickpeas bring **protein, fibre and folate**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Pat the chickpeas very dry with a towel, then toss them with the oil, cumin and salt.
Spread them on a tray and roast for 25 minutes, shaking the tray halfway, until crunchy and deep golden.
Toss with the lime juice and cayenne while hot.
tip: Roast a double batch if you like, and re-crisp the second half in a hot oven for 5 minutes before you eat it.
ingredients: canned, drained, rinsed and dried well

name: Chicken anticuchos with ají amarillo
inspiredBy: Peruvian anticuchos, the street-corner skewers usually made with beef heart, here with chicken thigh
about: Chicken thigh cubes marinated in ají amarillo, garlic, cumin and lime, threaded on skewers and grilled until charred at the edges. They are smoky, juicy and mildly hot. The chicken brings **protein and niacin**.
steps: Stir the ají amarillo paste with the grated garlic, cumin, lime juice, oil and salt. Toss the chicken in it and leave for at least 20 minutes, or all day in the fridge.
Thread the chicken on skewers (soak wooden ones in water first).
Grill or broil about 10 cm from the heat for 8 to 10 minutes, turning once or twice, until charred in spots and cooked through.
tip: Marinate in the morning and it takes 10 minutes at snack time. Check the label on the ají paste.

name: Hard-boiled eggs with lime and chile
inspiredBy: Mexican huevos duros with lime, salt and chile, the bar and street-stall snack
about: Hard-boiled eggs sprinkled with lime juice, a pinch of salt and chile, a simple Mexican snack. They are creamy, sharp and a little hot. The eggs bring **protein and choline**.
steps: Lower the eggs into boiling water and cook for 10 minutes. Cool them in cold water, then peel.
Halve the eggs and sprinkle with the lime juice, salt and cayenne.
tip: Boil a few extra on Sunday; they keep 5 days in the shell. Check the label on the chile powder if it is a blend.

name: Black bean and corn cup with lime
inspiredBy: Mexican ensalada de frijol y elote, the bean and corn salad
about: Black beans and sweet corn tossed with tomato, onion, cilantro, lime and a little olive oil in a cup. It is cool, savoury and bright, and easy to carry. Beans and corn together bring **fibre, iron and folate**.
steps: Use beans from your Sunday pot (see the plan notes), or canned beans at about three times the dry weight, drained and rinsed.
Toss the beans with the corn, tomato, onion, cilantro, lime juice, oil and salt.
Let it sit for 10 minutes so the flavours settle, then eat it cold.
tip: It keeps 2 days in the fridge, so make a double batch.

name: Sardines with lime, tomato and onion
inspiredBy: Mexican sardinas a la mexicana, made here as a no-cook salpicón with lime, tomato and onion
about: Canned sardines, with their soft bones, dressed with lime, diced tomato, onion and cilantro. It takes five minutes and tastes bright and briny. Sardines bring **omega-3, calcium and vitamin B12**.
steps: Mix the tomato, onion, cilantro, lime juice, salt and a pinch of cayenne in a small bowl.
Break the sardines into big chunks, spoon the tomato mixture over and eat right away.
tip: Add a sliced serrano for more heat. Buy sardines in oil or water, not in a sauce.

name: Gulf foul with lemon, cumin and khubz
inspiredBy: Saudi and Emirati foul, the fava bean breakfast every Gulf family knows, with a boiled egg
about: Warm fava beans mashed with garlic, cumin and lemon, then piled with fresh tomato, onion, parsley and a little green chili, with a spoon of tahini, a boiled egg and hot whole-wheat khubz for scooping. A proper Gulf breakfast that keeps you going until lunch. The fava beans bring **folate, iron and fibre**, and the tahini adds calcium.
steps: Lower the egg into a pot of boiling water and cook it for 8 minutes, then cool it under cold water and peel. Do this first so it is ready when the beans are.
Warm half the oil in a small pan, add the garlic and cumin for 20 seconds, then tip in the fava beans with a few spoonfuls of their liquid and the salt.
Warm over medium heat for 5 minutes, then mash about half of the beans with a fork so it is chunky and creamy.
Warm the khubz in a dry pan or the toaster until it is soft with a few toasty spots.
Spoon the foul into a shallow bowl and top it with the tomato, onion, parsley and green chili.
Squeeze over the lemon, drizzle with the rest of the oil and the tahini, and serve with the halved egg and the khubz.
tip: Fresh chopped mint is a common addition. Foul keeps well, so a double batch of the beans makes a second breakfast quick.
ingredients: with a little of the canning liquid

name: Balaleet-inspired saffron vermicelli with a cardamom omelette
inspiredBy: Emirati balaleet, the sweet-savoury vermicelli with a thin omelette on top, made here with whole wheat pasta and much less sugar
about: Thin strands of whole wheat pasta fried in a little ghee, then simmered with saffron, cardamom and a chopped date for just enough sweetness, and topped with a soft, lightly spiced omelette and toasted almonds. It's the sweet and salty breakfast of the Emirates and Qatar. The two eggs bring **protein and choline**, and the almonds add vitamin E.
steps: Steep the saffron in 2 tablespoons of hot water. Melt the ghee in a small pan and stir-fry the broken pasta for 2 to 3 minutes until it smells toasty and turns a shade darker.

Add about a third of a cup (80 ml) of hot water, the chopped date, half the cardamom and half the salt. Simmer, stirring now and then, adding a splash more water only if the pasta is still hard, until it is tender and has soaked up nearly all the liquid, about 8 minutes. Stir in most of the saffron water and let it finish drying.

Beat the eggs with the rest of the cardamom, a teaspoon of the saffron water and the rest of the salt. Warm the oil in a non-stick pan and pour in the eggs, tilting the pan so they spread thin. Cook until just set, about 2 minutes, then fold or roll the omelette.
Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden. Pile the vermicelli on a plate, lay the omelette over it and scatter with the almonds. Serve with the orange segments on the side.
tip: Rose water is traditional if you have a bottle: a few drops in the saffron water. A little date syrup (dibs) or honey over the omelette is a common finish. On a weekday, cook the vermicelli the night before. It reheats in a minute with a splash of water while the omelette cooks.
ingredients: thin spaghetti, snapped into short pieces
a small date, pitted and finely chopped

name: Eggs with tomato and green chili, with cucumber and khubz
inspiredBy: Gulf beid wa tamatem, the everyday tomato and egg skillet
about: Eggs set gently into a juicy skillet of tomato, onion, garlic and green chili, with crunchy cucumber and warm khubz. Quick and homey, and very Gulf. The eggs bring **protein and choline**, and cooked tomato is a good source of lycopene.
steps: Warm the oil in a small skillet and soften the onion with the garlic and green chili until golden at the edges, about 4 minutes. Stir in the turmeric and black pepper for a few seconds.
Add the tomato and the salt. Cook over medium heat, mashing the tomato with your spoon, until it has collapsed into a thick, jammy sauce, about 7 minutes.

Make two wells in the sauce and crack the eggs into them. Cover and cook gently for 3 to 4 minutes, until the whites are set and the yolks are still soft. If you prefer them scrambled, stir the eggs in instead.
Scatter with the cilantro. Serve straight from the pan with the cucumber and warm khubz.
tip: The tomato base keeps for three days in the fridge, so cook a double batch on Wednesday and reheat it on Saturday morning.

name: Gulf lentil soup with lemon and khubz
inspiredBy: Shorbat adas, the red lentil soup of Gulf kitchens, brightened with lemon
about: A smooth, golden red lentil soup with carrot, onion and cumin, finished with lots of lemon and fresh herbs. A crisp cucumber and khubz on the side make it a full lunch. The lentils bring **iron, folate and plenty of fibre**, and the lemon helps your body use that iron.
steps: Warm the oil in a pot and soften the onion and carrot for 5 minutes. Add the garlic, cumin and turmeric and stir for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the lentils, the salt and about 2½ cups (600 ml) of water. Bring to a boil, then simmer gently for 20 minutes, until the lentils have fallen apart and the carrot is tender.
Blend with a stick blender until smooth, or leave it a little rustic. Add a splash of water if it is thicker than you like.
Stir in the lemon juice, taste and add more salt or lemon if it needs it.
Ladle into a bowl and scatter with the cilantro and parsley. Serve with the khubz, the cucumber and an extra squeeze of lemon.
tip: Make it Sunday evening. It keeps three days and thickens as it sits, so loosen it with a splash of water. Double it and freeze a portion if you like. A pinch of chili flakes on top is common.

name: Spiced chickpeas (nakhi) with labneh, radish and khubz
inspiredBy: the Gulf street-side boiled chickpeas, nakhi, here served over labneh with a fresh salad
about: Warm chickpeas tossed with garlic, cumin and lemon, spooned over thick labneh with crunchy radish, cucumber, mint and parsley, and eaten with khubz. It comes together in 15 minutes and tastes fresh and tangy. Chickpeas and labneh together give you **protein, fibre and calcium** in one plate.
steps: Warm half the olive oil in a small pan, add the garlic and cumin and stir for 20 seconds, until it smells toasty.
Add the chickpeas with a splash of water and the salt. Warm them through for 4 to 5 minutes, crushing a few with the back of the spoon, then take off the heat and stir in the lemon juice.
Spread the labneh across a plate and spoon the warm chickpeas over it. Drizzle with the rest of the olive oil.
Toss the radish, cucumber, mint and parsley together and pile them on top. Dust with the sumac.
Warm the khubz and tear it up to scoop everything.
tip: A teaspoon of toasted sesame seeds over the top is a nice touch. Warm the chickpeas gently so they stay soft.

name: Gulf-style chicken shawarma plate with garlic labneh sauce and salata
inspiredBy: Gulf chicken shawarma, pan-seared at home with baharat instead of on a spit
about: Chicken marinated in labneh, garlic, lemon and baharat, seared until browned, with a cool garlic-labneh sauce, a crisp cucumber and tomato salata, quick-pickled radish and carrot and warm khubz. It tastes like a shawarma shop but sits on a plate. The chicken brings **protein and niacin**, and the carrot, herbs and tomato add vitamins A and C.
steps: Mix half the labneh with half the garlic, half the lemon juice, the baharat, half the oil and a pinch of the salt. Toss the chicken strips in it and leave for 15 minutes, or up to a day in the fridge.
Toss the radish and grated carrot with a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of salt and leave them to pickle while the chicken marinates.
For the sauce, whisk the rest of the labneh with the remaining garlic, a squeeze of lemon and a splash of water until it pours like thick cream.
Warm the remaining oil in a heavy pan over high heat and sear the chicken in a single layer, turning once, until browned at the edges and cooked through, about 6 minutes.
Toss the cucumber, tomato and parsley with the last of the lemon juice and a pinch of salt.
Warm the khubz. Pile the chicken, salata and pickled radish and carrot on a plate or into the bread and spoon the garlic sauce over.
tip: Roll everything into the khubz for a handheld wrap, or use chicken breast if you prefer it leaner.
ingredients: for the marinade and the sauce

name: Chicken machboos with brown basmati, almonds and raisins
inspiredBy: Kuwaiti, Emirati and Bahraini chicken machboos, made with brown basmati and less oil
about: Chicken browned with onion and tomato, then simmered with baharat, saffron and sour dried loomi into a fragrant pot of brown basmati rice, finished with toasted almonds and sweet raisins. A Friday lunch favourite in homes across the Gulf. The brown rice and almonds add **fibre and vitamin E**, and tomorrow's lunch is already made.
steps: Soak the rinsed rice in cold water for 20 minutes if you have time, then drain. Steep the saffron in 2 tablespoons of hot water. Pierce the loomi a few times with a knife.
Melt the ghee with the oil in a wide, heavy pot and fry the onion over medium heat until deep golden, about 10 minutes. Stir in the garlic, baharat and tomato paste for a minute.
Add the chicken and brown it for 5 minutes, turning, then add the tomato and the salt. Cook until the tomato breaks down and the pot smells rich, about 6 minutes.
Pour in enough hot water to cover the chicken by a finger, add the loomi, then bring to a boil, cover and simmer for 15 minutes.

Add the rice, pressing it just under the liquid, and top up with hot water if needed so it is covered by about 1 cm. Simmer, covered, over low heat for 30 to 35 minutes, until the rice is tender and the water is gone. Drizzle over the saffron water and rest, covered, for 10 minutes.
While the rice rests, toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, then scatter them over the rice with the raisins.
Fluff gently and serve, nudging the loomi aside or squeezing it over your plate. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Dried black limes (loomi) are sold whole at Middle Eastern grocers. Add a cinnamon stick and a few cardamom pods with the water for a more traditional pot, and a handful of chopped cilantro on top.
ingredients: 1 whole for the pot of 2 servings, pierced

name: Grilled kanaad (Spanish mackerel) with dakkous and khubz
inspiredBy: Gulf samak mashwi with dakkous, the garlicky tomato and chili sauce served beside grilled fish across the Emirates, Qatar and Bahrain
about: A thick steak of kanaad, the Spanish mackerel the Gulf loves, rubbed with turmeric and grilled, with a punchy dakkous of crushed tomato, garlic, green chili, cumin and lemon, and a crunchy cucumber and carrot salad. It gives you **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**, the carrot adds vitamin A and the sauce adds vitamin C.
steps: Pat the fish dry and rub it with the turmeric and half the salt. Leave it on the counter while you make the sauce.

For the dakkous, warm half the vegetable oil in a small pan and cook the garlic and green chili for 30 seconds. Add the tomato, cumin and a pinch of salt and cook, crushing the tomato with a spoon, until thick and saucy, about 8 minutes. Off the heat, stir in half the lemon juice and the parsley.

Heat a heavy pan or a grill until very hot. Brush the fish with the rest of the vegetable oil and cook for 5 to 6 minutes on each side, until the skin is crisp and the flesh just flakes at the thickest part.
Toss the cucumber and carrot with the rest of the lemon juice, the olive oil and a pinch of salt.
Warm the khubz. Serve the fish with a generous spoonful of dakkous on top, the salad alongside and the bread for mopping.
tip: Frozen Spanish mackerel from an Asian or Middle Eastern market is the usual source. King mackerel, Atlantic mackerel or hammour also work if you want a milder fish. Dakkous is great on rice and eggs too, so a double batch will not go to waste.

name: Lamb saloona with eggplant and pumpkin
inspiredBy: Emirati saloona, the everyday tomato and vegetable stew eaten with rice or bread, made with extra vegetables, less meat and no potato
about: Tender lamb simmered with tomato, onion, eggplant and sweet pumpkin in a turmeric and baharat sauce with a whole chili and a tang of loomi, thick enough to scoop with khubz. An everyday Emirati stew. The pumpkin and eggplant bring **vitamin A, potassium and fibre**, and the lamb adds iron and zinc.
steps: Warm the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat. Brown the lamb in batches, about 5 minutes, then lift it out.
Soften the onion in the same pot for 6 minutes, then stir in the garlic, turmeric, half the baharat and the tomato paste until fragrant.
Return the lamb with the tomato, the loomi, the whole green chili, the salt and 2 cups of water. Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer gently for 40 minutes, until the lamb is nearly tender.
Add the eggplant and pumpkin and simmer for 20 to 25 minutes, until everything is soft and the sauce has thickened. Add a splash of water if it gets dry.
Stir in the rest of the baharat, taste and adjust the salt. Fish out the chili and loomi, or leave them in for the table.
Serve with warm khubz. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with its bread wrapped separately.
tip: Saloona is even better the next day. Chicken, fish or just vegetables with chickpeas all make good saloona too.
ingredients: in large cubes, butternut or kabocha squash works
1 whole for the pot of 2 servings, pierced

name: Beef and okra marag with chickpeas and a little brown basmati
inspiredBy: Kuwaiti and Emirati marag bamia, the tomato and okra stew eaten over rice
about: Beef and okra simmered in a bright, garlicky tomato broth with crushed coriander, a good squeeze of lemon and chickpeas, ladled over a small portion of brown basmati. Homely and tangy, and not slimy when the okra is cooked whole and gently. The okra and chickpeas bring **folate, fibre and vitamin K**, and it makes tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Warm the oil in a heavy pot and brown the beef in batches, about 5 minutes. Lift it out, then soften the onion in the same pot for 6 minutes.
Add the garlic, coriander and tomato paste, then the tomato. Cook for 6 minutes, until the tomato starts to break down.
Return the beef with the salt and 2 cups of water. Cover and simmer for about 1 hour and 15 minutes, until the beef is nearly tender.
Add the chickpeas and the whole okra. Simmer gently, without stirring too much, for 15 minutes, until the okra is soft but holds its shape. Stir in the lemon juice.
Meanwhile, cook the rice in plenty of boiling salted water for about 35 to 40 minutes until tender, then drain.
Serve the marag over the rice with the cilantro scattered on top. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Frozen whole okra works well and is easy to find. Trimming the cap without cutting into the pod, and adding lemon or tomato, keeps it from turning slimy.

name: Roasted sardines with cumin sweet potatoes and a cucumber and radish salata
inspiredBy: Omani and Gulf grilled sardines with garlic and coriander, with a crisp salata in the style of salata Arabiya
about: Fresh sardines marinated in garlic, lemon, cumin and cilantro, then roasted until the skin crackles, with cumin-roasted sweet potato wedges and a crisp salata of cucumber, radish, onion, parsley and lemon. Quick and bright. Sardines give you **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**, and the sweet potato gives you vitamin A.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the sweet potato wedges with half the vegetable oil, half the cumin and a pinch of salt on a baking tray and roast for 20 minutes.
Mash the garlic with a pinch of salt and mix it with the cilantro, the rest of the cumin, half the lemon juice and the rest of the vegetable oil. Rub it over the sardines inside and out.
Turn the wedges and push them to one side. Lay the sardines on the tray and roast for 8 to 10 minutes, until the skin is blistered and the flesh flakes easily.
Toss the cucumber, radish, onion and parsley with the rest of the lemon juice, the olive oil, the sumac and a pinch of salt.
Serve the sardines and sweet potatoes with the salata on the side and a lemon wedge if you like.
tip: Frozen sardines work well once thawed. Open the window or use the exhaust fan, since sardines are fragrant. Mackerel can stand in for the sardines.

name: Lamb harees with ghee and cinnamon, laban and cucumber
inspiredBy: Emirati, Qatari and Saudi harees, the slow wheat and meat porridge of Ramadan and celebrations
about: Cracked wheat and tender lamb cooked slowly with onion and cardamom until they melt into a thick, silky porridge, finished with a spoon of melted ghee and a dusting of cinnamon. Cold laban and a cucumber, mint and parsley salad cut the richness. The cracked wheat brings **fibre, magnesium and B vitamins**, and the laban adds calcium. It makes two portions, so Sunday's lunch is done.
steps: Rinse the cracked wheat and cover it with plenty of cold water. Leave it to soak while the lamb cooks, at least an hour.

Put the lamb, the onion, the cardamom and the salt in a heavy pot with about 5 cups of water. Bring to a boil, skim off any foam, then cover and simmer for 1 and a half hours, until the lamb is very tender.

Lift out the onion and discard it. Drain the wheat and add it to the pot with the black pepper. Simmer, covered, over the lowest heat for 1 hour, stirring from time to time and adding hot water whenever it looks dry, until the wheat is very soft and has broken down.

Take the pot off the heat and beat the porridge hard with a wooden spoon or a masher for 5 to 10 minutes, until the lamb shreds into the wheat and it turns smooth and stretchy. Add a little hot water if it is too stiff; it should fall from a spoon in a thick ribbon.
Melt the ghee in a small pan until it just starts to smell nutty.
Spoon the harees into shallow bowls and make a small well in the middle. Pour the hot ghee into the well and dust with the cinnamon.

Toss the cucumber with the mint, parsley and lemon juice and serve it alongside with a glass of cold laban. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch; loosen it with a splash of water when you reheat it.
tip: A drizzle of date syrup (dibs) is a real Saudi finish. Whole wheat berries soaked overnight make a more traditional, silkier harees, but they need about 2 more hours. A pressure cooker does the wheat and lamb together in about 50 minutes. Chicken works well in place of the lamb, and some families add a pinch of sugar with the ghee.

name: Shrimp with tamarind and tomato over brown basmati, with carrot salad
inspiredBy: Kuwaiti and Bahraini robyan, the shrimp cooked in a tangy tamarind and chili sauce and served over rice
about: Plump shrimp cooked in a sour-spicy sauce of tamarind, tomato, chili and coriander, spooned over fragrant brown basmati with a crunchy carrot salad. Quick, bright and very Gulf. The shrimp give you lean **protein, selenium and iodine**, the carrot brings vitamin A and the tomato vitamin C.
steps: Cook the rice in plenty of boiling salted water for about 30 minutes, until tender, then drain and keep covered.
Whisk the tamarind into 3 tablespoons of warm water until smooth.
Warm the oil in a wide pan and soften the onion for 6 minutes. Add the garlic, coriander and dried chili for 30 seconds.
Add the tomato and the salt and cook until it has broken down into a sauce, about 7 minutes. Stir in the tamarind.
Add the shrimp and cook, stirring, for 3 to 4 minutes, until they are pink and curled. Take off the heat and fold in most of the cilantro.
Toss the carrot with the lemon juice and a pinch of salt. Spoon the shrimp over the rice and serve with the carrot salad and the rest of the cilantro.
tip: Start the rice first and the rest comes together while it cooks. Fresh lime is an easy swap for the lemon.

name: Dates with cold laban and cardamom
inspiredBy: Tamr w laban, dates with laban, a classic Gulf pairing
about: A couple of soft dates with a large glass of cold, lightly salted laban and a pinch of cardamom, the way many Gulf families break a fast or end an afternoon. Dates give quick energy and the laban brings **calcium and protein**.
steps: Stir the cardamom into the cold laban and drink it with the dates on the side.
tip: Khalas, sukkari or ajwa are the traditional dates and are worth looking for at a Middle Eastern grocer. Medjool works fine if that is what you can find.

name: Cold cucumber and mint laban
about: Cold laban with grated cucumber, mint and a pinch of salt, a thin, sippable salad that Gulf families have with hot meals and on hot afternoons. Cooling and tangy, and the laban brings **calcium and protein**.
steps: Stir the cucumber, mint and salt into the cold laban.
Chill it for 10 minutes if you have time, then drink it or eat it with a spoon.

name: Warm saffron and cardamom milk with a date and almonds
inspiredBy: the saffron and cardamom milk of Gulf evenings, with the sugar swapped for a date
about: Milk warmed with cardamom and a thread of saffron, with a date and a few almonds on the side instead of sugar. Soothing and fragrant. The milk adds **calcium** and the almonds add vitamin E.
steps: Warm the milk with the cardamom and saffron until steaming, about 3 minutes, and let it sit for a minute so the saffron blooms.
Pour into a glass and sip it with the date and almonds.

name: Orange and pistachios
about: Juicy orange segments with a small handful of pistachios, a fresh and crunchy pairing. The orange brings **vitamin C** and the pistachios add vitamin E and B6.
steps: Peel the orange and eat it with the pistachios.
ingredients: unsalted, in the shell or shelled

name: Pomegranate seeds with pistachios and mint
about: Ruby pomegranate seeds with chopped pistachios and torn mint, a juicy and crunchy bowl. Sweet, tart and refreshing. Pomegranate brings **vitamin C and potassium** and the pistachios add vitamin E.
steps: Scatter the pomegranate seeds in a bowl with the pistachios and mint and eat.

name: Roasted chickpeas with lemon and cumin
about: Chickpeas roasted until crisp with cumin, paprika and a squeeze of lemon, a crunchy snack to nibble on. They are salty, tangy and satisfying. Chickpeas bring **protein, fibre and folate**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F).
Toss the dry chickpeas with the oil, cumin, paprika and salt and spread on a tray.
Roast for 25 to 30 minutes, shaking the tray halfway, until golden and crisp. Squeeze the lemon over them and eat them warm.
ingredients: drained, rinsed and patted very dry

name: Dates stuffed with almonds
about: A date split open and tucked with an almond and a pinch of cardamom, with a few more almonds on the side, chewy and crunchy together. A small, sweet snack for the afternoon. The almonds bring **vitamin E and magnesium**.
steps: Split the dates and remove the pits.
Tuck one or two almonds into each date, dust with the cardamom and press closed. Eat the rest of the almonds alongside.
tip: Khalas, sukkari or ajwa dates are traditional. Medjool works fine too.

name: Dates with pistachios and cardamom
