about: Chopped dates pressed with crushed pistachios and a pinch of cardamom, rolled into small bites. They are sweet and a little green. The pistachios bring **vitamin B6 and vitamin E**.
steps: Mash the dates with the cardamom and half the pistachios until sticky.
Roll into two small balls, then roll them in the remaining pistachios.

name: Almonds, pistachios and raisins
about: A small bowl of toasted almonds, pistachios and sweet raisins, the kind of mix that sits out for guests all over the Gulf. Salty-sweet and crunchy. The nuts bring **vitamin E and magnesium**.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan for 2 minutes, then toss with the pistachios and raisins in a bowl.

name: Khubz with tahini and date
about: A warm piece of whole-wheat khubz spread with tahini and topped with chopped date, the same sweet-and-nutty pairing as tahini with date syrup. Chewy and gently sweet. The tahini adds **calcium and copper**.
steps: Warm the khubz in a dry pan for a minute.
Spread with the tahini, scatter over the chopped date and fold in half.

name: Nasi lemak-inspired plate with sardine sambal, egg and peanuts
inspiredBy: Malaysian nasi lemak, with brown rice, only a little coconut milk and tinned sardines in sambal (sambal sardin)
about: Gingery pandan and coconut rice with a hot, tangy sardine sambal, a boiled egg, crunchy peanuts and cool cucumber, the classic Malaysian breakfast plate. The sardines come with their soft bones, so this plate brings **calcium, omega-3 and vitamin D**.
steps: Lower the egg into a small pot of simmering water for 8 minutes, until the white is set and the yolk is just firm. Cool it under cold water, then peel and halve it.

While the egg cooks, put the rice in another small pot with the coconut milk, the pandan, the ginger, a splash of water and the salt. Cover and warm over low heat for 5 minutes, until it's hot and the grains look glossy. Fish out the pandan and ginger.
Soften the shallot and garlic in the oil in a small pan, about 4 minutes. Stir in the sambal oelek for a minute, until the oil turns red and it smells sweet and sharp.
Add the sardines with their sauce and the tamarind, break them up with a spoon and simmer for 3 minutes, until thick and jammy.
Pile the coconut rice on a plate with the sambal, egg, cucumber and peanuts. Eat everything together.
tip: Boil the eggs and make the sardine sambal the night before, and the plate takes 5 minutes. The sambal keeps 3 days in the fridge, so a double batch covers both nasi lemak mornings. Skip the pandan if you can't find it.
ingredients: full-fat, just enough to scent the rice
a knotted pandan leaf, fresh or frozen
tinned in tomato sauce, bones and all

name: Tapsilog-inspired garlic rice with beef tapa, fried egg and atchara
inspiredBy: Filipino tapsilog (tapa, sinangag, itlog), with lean beef, brown rice and a quick carrot atchara
about: Thin slices of beef cured in soy, calamansi and garlic and seared hot, with garlicky fried brown rice, a fried egg and a quick sweet-sour carrot pickle. It's the Filipino all-day breakfast, and the beef and egg bring **iron, zinc and choline**, while the atchara keeps it bright instead of heavy.
steps: Toss the beef with the soy sauce, calamansi, half the garlic, half the palm sugar and the pepper. Leave it to cure while you make the atchara, or overnight in the fridge.

For the atchara, toss the carrot and ginger with the vinegar, the rest of the palm sugar and a pinch of the salt. Squeeze it with your hands for a minute, then leave it for 15 minutes to turn tangy and a little sweet.

Heat a little of the oil in a wide pan and fry the rest of the garlic until pale gold, about 1 minute. Add the cold rice, breaking up any clumps, and stir-fry for 4 minutes, until hot with a few crisp grains. Season with the rest of the salt and tip it into a bowl.
Wipe the pan, heat it hard with a little more oil and sear the beef for 1 to 2 minutes per side, until browned and sticky at the edges. Pile it on the rice.
Fry the egg in the remaining oil until the edges are crisp and the yolk is still runny. Serve with a spoonful of atchara.
tip: Do steps 1 and 2 the night before and breakfast is 12 minutes. Green papaya is the traditional atchara, so use it in place of the carrot if you have it. A small dish of vinegar with chopped chili and garlic is how most Filipino tables finish it.
ingredients: lean round steak, sliced about 3 mm thick against the grain
minced, half for the beef and half for the rice
half for the beef, half for the atchara

name: Bubur ayam, Indonesian chicken rice porridge with fried shallot
inspiredBy: Indonesian bubur ayam, made with brown rice, mustard greens (sawi) and the chicken liver (ati) that tops the Jakarta version
about: A silky, turmeric-yellow rice porridge with shredded ginger chicken, a little tender chicken liver, mustard greens, crushed peanuts and crisp fried shallots, finished with sweet soy, sambal and a squeeze of lime. It's warm, gentle and the way a lot of Indonesia starts the day. The little bit of liver brings **vitamin A, B12 and iron**.
steps: Fry the shallot rings in the oil over medium heat until golden and crisp, about 4 minutes. Lift them out onto a paper towel and keep the flavoured oil in the pot.

Add the garlic, ginger and turmeric to the oil for 30 seconds. Add the rice, the chicken thigh and about 4 times as much water as rice by volume. Bring to a boil, then simmer gently, stirring now and then, for 25 minutes.
Add the liver and simmer for 5 minutes more. Mash about a third of the rice against the side of the pot, so the porridge turns thick and creamy.
Lift out the chicken and liver, shred the chicken with two forks and chop the liver. Stir the mustard greens into the porridge for 1 minute, until bright, then season with the salt and white pepper.
Ladle into a bowl and top with the chicken, liver, fried shallot and peanuts. Drizzle over the kecap manis, add the sambal and squeeze the lime over.
tip: On weekdays, simmer the porridge with the chicken the night before, then reheat it in the morning with a splash of water and add the liver, greens and toppings fresh (about 10 minutes). A pressure cooker does the whole porridge in 15 minutes. Leave the liver out and use 150 g of chicken if you prefer.

name: Gado-gado with tofu, egg, lontong and peanut sauce
inspiredBy: Indonesian gado-gado, with pan-fried tofu and a lontong-style pressed rice cake made from the batch rice
about: Blanched long beans and bean sprouts with a slice of pressed rice, golden tofu, a boiled egg and crisp cucumber, all under a warm, garlicky peanut sauce with sambal, sweet soy and tamarind. The tofu is calcium-set, so this one lunch brings **lots of calcium and protein**.
steps: Pack the cold rice firmly into a small container lined with plastic wrap, or roll it tightly in the wrap, and chill it while you cook. Slice it into thick squares to serve.

Lower the egg into a pot of boiling water for 8 minutes, then lift it out into cold water. In the same water, blanch the long beans for 3 minutes and the sprouts for 20 seconds. Drain well and let them cool a little.
Pan-fry the tofu cubes in the oil over medium-high heat for 3 to 4 minutes per side, until golden and crisp at the edges.

Blitz the peanuts with the garlic, salt, sambal, kecap manis, tamarind, palm sugar and about 4 tablespoons of hot water in a mini chopper, until it pours like thick cream. Add a splash more water if it's too thick.
Arrange the vegetables, the rice slices, tofu, cucumber and the halved egg on a plate and spoon the sauce over.
tip: The sauce keeps 4 days in a jar in the fridge, thinned with a splash of water. Swap the tofu for tempeh if you like, or add a handful of blanched spinach for more greens.
ingredients: long beans, cut into 4 cm pieces
cold rice from your batch, pressed into a lontong-style block
calcium-set, check the label, cut into cubes

name: Chicken adobo with garlic, bay leaf and wilted mustard greens
inspiredBy: Filipino adobo, braised in cane vinegar, soy sauce and garlic, with mustasa (mustard greens) wilted in at the end
about: Chicken thighs braised in vinegar, soy sauce, garlic, bay leaf and black pepper until the sauce is sticky and tangy, with mustard greens wilted in at the end and fresh tomato wedges to cut the richness. Adobo tastes better the next day, so tomorrow's lunch is done. The chicken and greens bring **protein, vitamin K and calcium**.
steps: Put the chicken thighs, soy sauce, vinegar, garlic, bay leaf, pepper and about ½ cup (125 ml) of water per serving in a wide pot. Marinate for 15 minutes if you have the time.
Bring to a boil, then simmer without stirring for 5 minutes, so the sharp smell of the vinegar cooks off. Cover and simmer gently for 20 minutes, until the chicken is tender.
Lift the chicken out. Boil the sauce hard, uncovered, for 5 to 6 minutes, until it has reduced to a glossy glaze.

Heat the oil in a wide pan with the shallot and brown the chicken for 2 to 3 minutes per side, then pour the sauce back over it. Add the mustard greens and cook for 2 minutes, until just wilted and still bright green.
Serve over rice with the tomato wedges. Pack the second portion, with its rice and a little of the sauce, for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Add a thinly sliced chili to the sauce for heat. Some cooks add a splash of coconut milk at the end (adobo sa gata). To freeze, do it before the greens go in.
ingredients: mustasa (mustard greens), cut into 5 cm pieces

name: Tumis tempeh, tofu and kangkong with chili and kecap manis
inspiredBy: Indonesian orek tempe and tumis kangkung, a sticky, sweet and hot stir-fry
about: Browned tempeh and tofu cubes with plenty of water spinach, stir-fried with shallot, garlic, galangal and plenty of fresh chili, then glazed with sweet soy. Tempeh is a **complete plant protein with iron**, and the calcium-set tofu adds **a lot of calcium**. The leftovers are just as good the next day.
steps: Fry the tempeh cubes in the oil in a wide non-stick pan over medium-high heat for 5 minutes, stirring now and then, until golden. Add the tofu and fry for 3 minutes more. Lift them out.
In the same pan, stir-fry the shallot, garlic, chili and galangal for 2 minutes, until it smells wonderful.
Add the kangkong stems with 2 tablespoons of water for 1 minute, then the leaves for 1 minute more, until bright green and just wilted.
Add the tomato and kecap manis, return the tempeh and tofu to the pan and toss over high heat for 2 minutes, until glossy and sticky. Add the salt.
Serve over rice. Pack the second portion, with its rice, for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: The leftover won't be crisp, but it's just as good in a rice bowl with cucumber. Make it milder by seeding the chili. No water spinach? Use spinach, added at the very end.
ingredients: water spinach, cut into 6 cm lengths

name: Sinigang with mackerel, kangkong and okra
inspiredBy: Filipino sinigang sa sampalok, the sour tamarind soup, made with mackerel (as with hasa-hasa) in place of the usual bangus
about: A bright, sour tamarind broth with tender mackerel, tomato, okra and a big handful of water spinach (kangkong), with a long chili for gentle heat. It's one of the Philippines' great comfort soups, and the mackerel brings **omega-3**, while the greens add folate and vitamin K.
steps: Bring about 2 cups (500 ml) of water per serving to a boil with the shallot, tomato and ginger. Simmer for 8 minutes, until the tomato has softened into the broth.
Stir in the tamarind paste until it dissolves, then the fish sauce. Add the okra and the whole chili and simmer for 3 minutes.
Lay the mackerel in the broth and simmer very gently for 5 minutes, until it's just opaque and flakes. Try not to stir it, or it will break up.
Add the kangkong, stems first, and the leaves for the last 30 seconds, until just wilted. Taste: it should be sour first, then salty. Add more tamarind or fish sauce if it needs it.
Ladle into a deep bowl and eat with the rice on the side.
tip: Bangus (milkfish), salmon belly or a firm white fish all work too, but mackerel is very rich in omega-3. Fish like this doesn't keep well, so it's cooked fresh and doesn't make a leftover lunch.
ingredients: water spinach, cut into 6 cm lengths

name: Pancit bihon with pork, tofu and mustard greens
inspiredBy: Filipino pancit bihon guisado, with tokwa (tofu), extra vegetables and a lighter hand with the noodles
about: Thin rice vermicelli stir-fried with lean pork, golden tofu, long beans, mustard greens, carrot and garlic in a light soy, fish sauce and calamansi sauce. It's the Filipino party noodle turned into a quick lunch, and the calcium-set tofu and mustard greens bring **calcium and protein**.
steps: Soak the vermicelli in hot water for 5 to 6 minutes, until it's pliable but still has some bite. Drain it, keeping about ⅓ cup (80 ml) of the soaking water. Toss the pork with half the soy sauce.
Heat half the oil in a wide pan or wok over high heat and fry the tofu for 4 minutes, turning, until golden. Lift it out.

Add the rest of the oil, then the shallot and garlic for 1 minute, then the pork for 3 minutes, until no longer pink. Add the carrot and long beans and stir-fry for 3 minutes, then the mustard greens for 1 minute.
Add the noodles, the tofu, the rest of the soy sauce, the fish sauce and the reserved soaking water. Toss with tongs for 2 to 3 minutes, until the noodles have soaked up the liquid and are tender.
Finish with pepper and the calamansi, and put extra calamansi on the table.
tip: Cut everything before you start, since stir-frying goes fast. Chicken breast works in place of the pork.
ingredients: sitaw (long beans), cut into 4 cm lengths

name: Pinakbet with pork, squash, okra and long beans
inspiredBy: Tagalog-style pinakbet, with shrimp paste (belacan) in place of the softer bagoong alamang
about: A one-pot Filipino vegetable stew of squash, okra, long beans and tomato, built on lean pork and a spoon of salty shrimp paste. The vegetables steam in their own juices, so it tastes deeply of vegetable, and it covers **lots of fibre, vitamin A and potassium**. It reheats beautifully for lunch.
steps: Soften the shallot, garlic and ginger in the oil in a wide pot over medium heat, about 3 minutes. Add the pork and brown it for 4 minutes.
Stir in the shrimp paste for 1 minute, until it smells fragrant, then add the tomato and cook for 3 minutes, until it breaks down into a sauce.
Add the squash and about ¼ cup (60 ml) of water per serving, cover and simmer for 8 minutes.
Lay the beans on top, cover and cook for 8 minutes. Add the okra for the last 5 minutes. Give the pot a shake now and then instead of stirring, so the vegetables stay whole.
Season with pepper, but taste first: the shrimp paste is the salt here. Serve with rice, and pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Eggplant (talong) and bitter melon (ampalaya) are the classic extras: add a few chunks of eggplant with the beans, and salt a few slices of bitter melon for 10 minutes, squeeze them and add them too. A wedge of calamansi on top is nice.
ingredients: lean pork shoulder, cut into 2 cm cubes
shrimp paste, standing in for bagoong
kalabasa, seeded, cut into 3 cm chunks

name: Lighter beef rendang with garlicky kangkong
inspiredBy: Minangkabau rendang, cooked to the saucier kalio stage with much less coconut milk, served with a quick kangkong stir-fry
about: Lean beef chuck simmered slowly in coconut milk, lemongrass, galangal, chili and tamarind until the sauce cooks down to a thick, dark gravy that clings to the beef, with a quick garlicky stir-fry of water spinach on the side. It uses a fraction of the usual coconut milk, so it's rich and spicy but low in saturated fat, and **high in iron and zinc**. Rendang gets better overnight, so tomorrow's lunch is done.
steps: Blitz the shallot, 6 g of the garlic, galangal, lemongrass, chili, turmeric, coriander, cumin, clove and cinnamon with 2 tablespoons of water into a thick paste.

Spoon the thick cream from the top of the coconut milk into a heavy pot over medium heat and fry the paste for 4 minutes, until it smells wonderful and the oil starts to separate. Add the beef and stir to coat.
Pour in the rest of the coconut milk, the tamarind and about ½ cup (125 ml) of water per serving. Simmer, partly covered, for 75 to 90 minutes, stirring now and then, until the beef is very tender.

Uncover, turn the heat up and cook for 15 to 20 minutes more, stirring often, until the sauce is thick and dark, clings to the beef and a little oil shows at the edges. Stir in the palm sugar and most of the salt.
While it reduces, fry the rest of the garlic in the oil for 30 seconds, then toss in the kangkong with a splash of water and the last pinch of salt for 2 minutes, until just wilted.
Serve the rendang with the rice and the kangkong. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: For a weeknight, cook it in a pressure cooker: 25 minutes on high, then reduce uncovered for 15 minutes. Or do the paste and the long simmer the day before and finish the reduction while the rice reheats.
ingredients: lean beef chuck (or shin), trimmed and cut into 3 cm cubes
peeled, 6 g for the paste and 3 g for the kangkong
water spinach, cut into 6 cm lengths

name: Laksa-inspired noodle soup with shrimp, tofu and bean sprouts
inspiredBy: Malaysian curry laksa, with a fresh paste, a little coconut milk, a shrimp-shell stock and plenty of sprouts and herbs
about: A fragrant, gently spicy coconut broth built on a fresh paste of lemongrass, galangal, chili, shallot and shrimp paste, with a stock made from the shrimp shells, ladled over rice vermicelli, shrimp, golden tofu, mustard greens and crunchy bean sprouts. It's the weekend project, and the shrimp and calcium-set tofu make it **high in protein and calcium**.
steps: Peel the shrimp and put the shells in a pot with about 1½ cups (375 ml) of water per serving. Simmer for 10 minutes, then strain and keep the stock. Keep the peeled shrimp in the fridge.
Soak the vermicelli in hot water for 5 minutes, until pliable, then drain and rinse. Put one portion in a deep bowl with the bean sprouts, and keep the rest of the noodles and sprouts for tomorrow.
Blitz the shallot, lemongrass, galangal, chili, shrimp paste, turmeric and coriander with 3 tablespoons of water into a smooth paste.
Sear the tofu sticks in the oil in a hot non-stick pot for 6 to 8 minutes, turning, until golden. Lift them out.

In the same pot, spoon in the thick cream from the top of the coconut milk and fry the paste over medium heat for 5 minutes, stirring, until it darkens, smells toasty and the oil begins to separate. Add the rest of the coconut milk and the shrimp stock and simmer for 10 minutes. Season with the salt and white pepper.
Add the shrimp and the mustard greens and simmer for 2 to 3 minutes, until the shrimp are pink and curled. Taste: it should be fragrant, salty and a little hot.

Ladle the broth, shrimp and mustard greens over the noodles and sprouts in the bowl, then top with the tofu, the Thai basil and a squeeze of lime. For the second portion, keep the broth, the noodles and the raw shrimp and mustard greens separate, then add the shrimp and mustard greens to the reheated broth for 2 minutes.
tip: If the paste catches, add a splash of water. The paste freezes well, so make a double batch for an even faster laksa another night. A few candlenuts or raw macadamias blitzed into the paste make it richer, if you can find them.
ingredients: raw, peeled weight; buy about 180 g shell-on and keep the shells for the stock
Thai basil, standing in for laksa leaf (daun kesum)

name: Ikan bakar, grilled mackerel with sambal belacan and ulam
inspiredBy: Malay and Indonesian ikan bakar, with a hot, sour sambal belacan and a plate of raw herbs and vegetables (ulam)
about: Mackerel marinated in turmeric, garlic, tamarind and sweet soy, grilled until the skin blisters and crisps, with a fiery sambal belacan and a plate of cucumber, raw long beans and Thai basil to eat alongside. Mackerel is one of the richest sources of **omega-3** you can buy, and the sambal and lime keep it fresh and light.
steps: Mash the garlic, the shallot, the turmeric, tamarind, kecap manis, half the lime juice and a pinch of the salt into a rough paste. Rub it over the fish and leave it for 15 to 20 minutes.

For the sambal, toast the shrimp paste in a dry pan for 1 minute, until crumbly and fragrant (open a window). Pound or blitz it with the chili, the tomato, the rest of the lime juice and the rest of the salt into a coarse sambal. Taste: it should be hot, salty and sour.

Heat a grill, grill pan or the broiler until very hot and brush with the oil. Cook the fish skin-side down for 4 to 5 minutes, until the skin blisters and crisps, then flip it for 3 to 4 minutes, until it just flakes with a fork.

Serve the fish with the rice, a spoonful of sambal, and the cucumber, raw long beans and Thai basil on the side. The raw vegetables and herbs (ulam) are meant to be eaten with the fish and sambal, a bite at a time.
tip: Spanish mackerel or sardines work too. On a barbecue, wrap the fish in a banana leaf for the real thing.
ingredients: fillets with the skin on, or a butterflied whole fish
about 1 lime, split between marinade and sambal
raw long beans, cut into 6 cm lengths

name: Ripe papaya
about: Sweet, soft ripe papaya eaten plain, the way it's enjoyed across the islands. It brings **vitamin C, vitamin A and folate**.
steps: Cut the papaya into chunks and eat it just as it is.
tip: A squeeze of lime helps if the papaya isn't very sweet.

name: Bubur kacang hijau, sweet mung beans in ginger coconut milk
inspiredBy: Indonesian bubur kacang hijau, lighter on coconut milk and sugar
about: Whole mung beans simmered until they burst, in a sweet, gingery coconut milk scented with pandan. It's a classic Indonesian snack that brings **fibre, folate and plant iron**, with only a spoon of coconut milk per bowl. The recipe makes 2 bowls.
steps: Soak about ½ cup (110 g) of mung beans overnight if you can. Put them in a pot with about 1¾ cups (440 ml) of water, the ginger and the pandan. Bring to a boil, then simmer gently for 35 minutes if soaked, or 50 minutes if not, until most of the beans have split and the mixture is thick. Top up with a splash of hot water if it thickens before the beans split.

Fish out the ginger and pandan. Stir in the palm sugar, the coconut milk and the salt, and simmer for 5 more minutes. Serve warm, and keep the second bowl in the fridge to reheat tomorrow with a splash of water.
tip: Not eating it tomorrow? Freeze the second bowl. It reheats well.

name: Rujak-style papaya with tamarind-chili dip
inspiredBy: Indonesian rujak buah
about: Sweet, soft papaya with a sweet, sour and hot tamarind dip, the Indonesian fruit salad called rujak. The papaya brings **vitamin C and folate**, and the tamarind and chili wake it right up.
steps: Stir the tamarind, palm sugar, sambal oelek and 1 tablespoon of warm water into a smooth dip.
Arrange the papaya on a plate and dip each piece.
ingredients: peeled, seeded and cut into chunks

name: Roasted peanuts with chili salt
about: A handful of unsalted roasted peanuts tossed with a pinch of salt and a little fresh chili, the kind of snack you'd find at any warung or sari-sari store. It brings **protein, vitamin E and magnesium**.
steps: Toss the peanuts with the chopped chili and salt, and eat them right away while they're still crunchy.

name: Tempe goreng, crisp tempeh with sambal kecap
inspiredBy: Indonesian tempe goreng
about: Thin slices of tempeh rubbed with garlic and coriander, pan-fried until crisp and golden, with a quick dip of sweet soy and fresh chili, a favourite Indonesian snack. Tempeh brings **plant protein, fibre and iron**.
steps: Crush the garlic with the salt and coriander, rub it over the slices and leave them 5 minutes.
Heat the oil in a non-stick pan over medium heat and fry the tempeh slices for 3 minutes per side, until golden and crisp.
Stir the kecap manis and chili together in a small dish and dip the tempeh in it.

name: Cucumber and tomato with sambal
about: Cool cucumber and ripe tomato with a spoon of sambal and a squeeze of lime, a fresh, lively snack you'd eat alongside almost any Malaysian or Indonesian meal. It adds **vitamin C and potassium** for very few calories.
steps: Stir the sambal and lime juice together. Dip the cucumber and tomato in it.

name: Steamed kalabasa with palm sugar and pandan
inspiredBy: Filipino and Indonesian steamed squash
about: Soft steamed squash mashed with a little palm sugar and a pinch of salt, scented with pandan, a comforting sweet snack in the Philippines and Indonesia. The squash brings **vitamin A and potassium**.
steps: Steam the squash with the pandan leaf for 12 to 15 minutes, until very soft.
Discard the pandan, then mash the squash lightly with the palm sugar and the salt, and eat it warm.
ingredients: kalabasa, peeled, seeded and cut into chunks

name: Boiled egg with chili vinegar
inspiredBy: Filipino sawsawan
about: A boiled egg dipped in cane vinegar with fresh chili and a pinch of salt, the sawsawan on every Filipino table. It gives you **protein and choline**.
steps: Lower the egg into simmering water for 8 minutes, then cool it under cold water and peel it.
Stir the vinegar, chili and salt together, halve the egg and dip it.

name: Blanched okra and tomato with sambal belacan
inspiredBy: Malay ulam with sambal belacan
about: Tender blanched okra and ripe tomato with a hot, tangy sambal belacan to dip in, the way a Malaysian table serves raw and blanched vegetables (ulam). It brings **fibre, vitamin C and vitamin K** for very few calories.
steps: Blanch the okra in boiling water for 3 minutes, until bright green and just tender, then drain.
Toast the shrimp paste in a dry pan for 1 minute, until crumbly and fragrant. Mash it with the chili and lime juice into a coarse sambal, then eat the okra and tomato dipped in it.

name: Blanched kangkong with sambal and lime
about: A big handful of blanched water spinach with a spoon of sambal and a squeeze of lime, a simple Malaysian and Filipino side that makes a fine snack. It's **rich in vitamin K and folate**, and very light.
steps: Blanch the kangkong stems in boiling water for 1 minute, then the leaves for 20 seconds, and drain well.
Stir the sambal and lime juice together and toss with the kangkong.
ingredients: water spinach, cut into 6 cm lengths

name: Ginataang kalabasa, squash simmered in coconut milk
inspiredBy: Filipino ginataang kalabasa
about: Soft squash simmered in a little coconut milk with garlic and ginger, a gentle Filipino merienda. The squash brings **vitamin A and potassium**, and the coconut milk is only a spoonful.
steps: Put the squash, coconut milk, garlic, ginger, salt and a splash of water in a small pot. Cover and simmer gently for 12 to 15 minutes, until the squash is very soft.
Mash a few pieces against the side of the pot to thicken the sauce, and eat it warm.
ingredients: kalabasa, peeled, seeded and cut into chunks

name: Japanese breakfast set: tofu and wakame miso soup, tamagoyaki and brown rice
inspiredBy: a classic Japanese asa-gohan breakfast, with brown rice and a walnut furikake on top
about: A proper Japanese morning: miso soup with tofu and wakame, a rolled omelette (tamagoyaki), warm brown rice under a sprinkle of toasted sesame, nori, bonito and walnuts, and a quick cucumber pickle. With rice from your batch it is about 15 minutes. The **eggs bring protein and choline**, and the soup is warm and easy on the stomach.
steps: Reheat a portion of your batch rice with a splash of water, covered, until steaming. A couple of minutes in the microwave is fine.
Slice the cucumber thinly and toss it with a few drops of the tamari and half the sesame seeds. Leave it to soften while you cook.

Bring about 220 ml (a scant cup) of water to a gentle simmer, add the bonito flakes and steep for 2 minutes, then strain them out and squeeze them dry. Add the wakame (a pinch swells into a lot) and the tofu to the broth, and simmer for 2 minutes.
Turn off the heat. Whisk the miso with a ladle of the broth until smooth, then stir it back in. Don't boil it once the miso is in, which keeps the flavour mellow. Sprinkle with half the scallion.

Start the eggs while the dashi steeps. Beat the eggs with the mirin, the rest of the tamari and the rest of the scallion, finely sliced. Warm the oil in a small non-stick pan over medium-low heat, pour in a thin layer of egg, and roll it up when it has just set. Push the roll to one side, pour in more egg under it, and roll again until the egg is used up.

Toast the squeezed bonito flakes in a dry pan with the chopped walnuts and the rest of the sesame seeds until the flakes are dry and crisp, about 2 minutes. Take the pan off the heat and crumble in the nori. Sprinkle over the rice, and serve with the sliced tamagoyaki, the soup and the pickle.
tip: Short on time? Scramble the eggs softly with the mirin and tamari instead of rolling them. Same flavour, half the fuss.

name: Korean banchan breakfast: soy-braised tofu, soybean sprouts, kimchi, fried egg and rice
inspiredBy: Korean dubu-jorim and kongnamul-muchim, set out the way a home breakfast table has a few small side dishes
about: Golden pan-seared tofu in a garlicky soy, gochujang and gochugaru glaze, with sesame soybean sprouts, a little kimchi, a crisp-edged fried egg and brown rice. The tofu and sprouts are made once and last two mornings, so each breakfast takes about 10 minutes. The **tofu and sprouts bring plant protein and folate**.
steps: The evening before, make the banchan for two mornings (cook double the amounts for 2 portions). Cut the tofu into slabs about 1 cm (½ inch) thick and pat them dry. Warm half the canola oil in a non-stick pan over medium heat and sear the tofu until golden, about 3 minutes a side.

Mince the garlic and scallion. Stir most of them into the tamari, gochujang, gochugaru and a splash of water, pour it over the tofu, and simmer, spooning the sauce over, until it is thick and glossy, about 3 minutes.
Boil the soybean sprouts, covered, in a little water for 5 minutes, until they no longer taste raw. Drain, and toss with the rest of the garlic and scallion, the sesame oil and the sesame seeds.
Cool the tofu and the sprouts and keep them in separate containers in the fridge. They keep for 3 days.
In the morning, reheat the rice and barley with a splash of water, and warm the tofu in the microwave or a small pan for a minute.
Fry the egg in the rest of the canola oil until the white is set and crisp at the edges and the yolk is still soft.
Serve the rice with the tofu and its sauce, the sprouts, the egg and the kimchi.
tip: The evening batch takes about 20 minutes once, and you get two quick mornings out of it.
ingredients: calcium-set, check the label for calcium sulfate

name: Dak-juk, Korean chicken and vegetable rice porridge with walnuts
inspiredBy: Korean dak-juk, made from cooked rice and barley, with walnuts on top like hodu-juk
about: A silky, gently savoury porridge of rice and barley with tender chicken, carrot and zucchini, finished with toasted sesame oil, nori, scallion and crunchy walnuts. It is slow weekend comfort food that makes two bowls, so Sunday's breakfast is already done. The **chicken and barley keep you full** for hours, and the walnuts add plant omega-3.
steps: Mince the ginger and garlic, dice the carrot and zucchini, slice the scallion, and cut the chicken into small pieces.
Warm half the sesame oil in a heavy pot over medium heat. Cook the chicken with the ginger and garlic until it turns white, about 3 minutes.
Add the carrot and the cooked rice and barley, and pour in water to cover the grains by about 3 cm (1 inch). That is roughly 3 parts water to 1 part cooked grain.

Bring to a boil, then simmer over low heat, stirring often and pressing some of the grains against the side of the pot, for about 20 minutes. Add water as it thickens, until the porridge is thick and creamy. Stir in the zucchini and tamari for the last 5 minutes.
Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 2 minutes, then chop them roughly.

Ladle one portion into a bowl and finish with the sesame oil, scallion, walnuts and crumbled nori. Chill the second portion of porridge on its own, and keep its walnuts and nori separate so they stay crisp. Loosen it with a splash of water when you reheat it.
tip: A spoonful of kimchi on the side is very Korean, and wakes the porridge up.

name: Cold soba with chilled tofu and edamame, with a ginger dipping sauce
inspiredBy: Japanese zaru soba, turned into a fuller lunch bowl
about: Chilled buckwheat noodles with cool tofu, edamame and crisp cucumber, dunked in a light, gingery bonito and soy sauce and finished with shredded nori. It is fresh, filling and ready in about 20 minutes. The **tofu and edamame carry the protein**, and the buckwheat gives it a nutty flavour and a little extra fibre.
steps: Make the dipping sauce first so it can chill. Simmer about 60 ml (¼ cup) of water with the bonito flakes, tamari and mirin for 2 minutes, then strain. Stir in the vinegar and half the grated ginger, and cool it quickly in a bowl set over ice, or the night before in the fridge.
Boil the edamame for 3 to 4 minutes, drain and cool them under cold water.

Cook the soba in plenty of boiling water for the time on the package, usually 4 to 5 minutes. Drain, then rinse really well under cold running water, rubbing gently, until the noodles are chilled and no longer slippery.
Pile the noodles on a plate with the tofu, the cucumber cut into matchsticks and the edamame. Scatter over the sesame seeds, the sliced scallion and the nori cut into thin strips with scissors.
Serve with the sauce and the rest of the ginger for dunking.
tip: Stir a little hot noodle water into the leftover sauce and drink it at the end, the Japanese way.
ingredients: calcium-set, check the label for calcium sulfate, chilled, cubed

name: Tofu steak and onigiri bento with broccoli goma-ae and carrot-daikon pickle
inspiredBy: a Japanese bento of onigiri and kohaku namasu, with a soy-glazed tofu steak for the protein
about: Two small rice balls seasoned with bonito flakes and sesame, wrapped in crisp nori, with a sweet-soy tofu steak, broccoli in a sesame dressing and a bright carrot and daikon pickle. It is the lunchbox you can eat cold at your desk. The **tofu brings plant protein**, the broccoli adds vitamin C and folate, and the pickle adds crunch.
steps: The night before, make the tofu, the broccoli and the pickle. Peel the carrot and daikon and cut them into thin matchsticks. Toss with the vinegar and half the mirin, squeeze lightly, and leave to pickle.
In the morning, reheat the rice and barley until steaming hot. The barley makes it sticky enough to shape.

Pat the tofu dry and cut it into two slabs. Sear it in the oil over medium heat until golden, about 3 minutes a side. Add most of the tamari and most of the remaining mirin to the pan and turn the tofu in the sizzling glaze for a minute, until it is sticky and dark.

Cut the broccoli into small florets and boil for 2 minutes, then drain and cool under cold water. Toss with a few drops of the tamari, a drop of the mirin and half the sesame seeds, to make the goma-ae.

Stir the bonito flakes with the last of the tamari until damp, and mix them into the warm rice with the rest of the sesame seeds. Wet your hands and press the rice firmly into 2 triangles or balls, or press it in plastic wrap and twist.
Pack the onigiri with the tofu, broccoli and pickle, and keep the nori separate. Wrap each onigiri in a strip of nori just before eating so it stays crisp.
tip: Everything except the onigiri can be made the night before. Shape the rice in the morning and wrap the balls in plastic wrap.

name: Natto soba with grated daikon, scallion, nori and kimchi, with bok choy ohitashi
inspiredBy: Japanese natto soba, with kimchi for crunch and a simple ohitashi side
about: Cold buckwheat noodles topped with sticky, savoury natto, sharp grated daikon, scallion and nori, with a spoonful of kimchi for crunch and bok choy dressed in soy and sesame on the side. It is a fast, very Japanese lunch if you like natto. **Natto is rich in iron and fibre**, and the bok choy adds calcium.
steps: Simmer about 50 ml (3 tbsp) of water with the bonito flakes, half the tamari and the mirin for 2 minutes, then strain and cool it in the fridge or over ice. This is the noodle sauce.

Boil the bok choy for 1 to 2 minutes, until just tender and still bright green. Drain, cool under cold water, squeeze lightly and cut into chunks. Toss with a few drops of the tamari and the sesame seeds.
Cook the soba in plenty of boiling water for the time on the package, then drain and rinse well under cold running water until chilled.
Grate the daikon and let it drain a little. Stir the natto briskly with chopsticks about 30 times, until it turns pale and stringy, then stir in the rest of the tamari and most of the scallion.

Put the noodles in a bowl and top with the natto, the grated daikon and the kimchi. Crumble the nori over, add the last of the scallion, pour the cold sauce around the noodles, and serve with the bok choy.
tip: Natto keeps well in the freezer, so buy a few packs on your next trip to an Asian grocery. Not a natto fan yet? Stir in extra grated daikon and a splash of vinegar. Both calm the smell and the stickiness.

name: Hot soba in ginger broth with salmon, bok choy and a soft egg
inspiredBy: Japanese hot kake soba and tsukimi soba, with canned salmon as a quick topping
about: Hot buckwheat noodles in a savoury bonito and soy broth with flaked salmon, bok choy, ginger and a soft egg that poaches in the broth. It is a warming Saturday lunch that takes about 20 minutes. The **canned salmon brings omega-3 and vitamin D**, plus calcium from its soft bones.
steps: Simmer about 300 ml (1¼ cups) of water with the bonito flakes for 3 minutes, then strain it back into the pot. Add the tamari, mirin and half the ginger, cut into thin matchsticks, and keep it at a gentle simmer.
Add the bok choy to the broth and simmer for 2 minutes, until the stems are just tender. Add the salmon in chunks. Crack the egg into the broth, cover, and let it poach for 2 minutes.
While the egg poaches, cook the soba in plenty of boiling water for the time on the package. Drain it and rinse briefly so it does not clump.
Put the noodles in a deep bowl and ladle over the broth, salmon, bok choy and egg. Top with the scallion, the rest of the ginger and the crumbled nori.
tip: A shake of shichimi togarashi on top is a good finish, if you have it.

name: Chicken teriyaki with bok choy, carrots and brown rice
inspiredBy: Japanese teriyaki, with mirin and no added sugar in the sauce
about: Juicy pan-seared chicken thigh glazed in a glossy ginger and soy sauce, with tender bok choy, carrots and chewy brown rice and barley. The sauce is just tamari, mirin, ginger and garlic, so it is far less sweet and less salty than the bottled kind. It makes two portions, so tomorrow's **lunch is already packed**.
steps: Stir the tamari, mirin, grated ginger, grated garlic and a splash of water together in a small bowl.

Pat the chicken dry and cut it into broad strips. Warm the oil in a wide non-stick pan over medium-high heat (use two batches if the pan is crowded) and sear the chicken for 2 to 3 minutes a side, until golden. Move it to a plate.
Add the carrot, sliced into thin coins, and a splash of water to the pan, cover and steam for 2 minutes. Add the bok choy and steam 2 minutes more, until the stems are just tender.
Return the chicken to the pan and pour in the sauce. Simmer, stirring, until it turns glossy and clings to the chicken, about 2 minutes. The chicken should be cooked all the way through with no pink.
Reheat the rice and barley. Serve the chicken and vegetables over the rice with a few drops of the vinegar over the bok choy, then the sesame seeds and sliced scallion.
Pack the second portion, rice and all, for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Cold teriyaki chicken is just as good in a bento. Pack some cucumber slices on the side.

name: Miso-glazed salmon with sesame spinach, grilled mushrooms and brown rice
inspiredBy: Japanese miso salmon and spinach gomae
about: A salmon fillet broiled until nearly done, then brushed with a thin miso, mirin and ginger glaze so it caramelizes without scorching, with grilled king oyster mushrooms, spinach in a nutty sesame dressing and brown rice and barley. Salmon brings **omega-3 fats and vitamin D**, and the sesame spinach adds folate and vitamin K.
steps: Heat the broiler to high and line a tray with foil. Stir the miso, mirin and grated ginger together into a thick paste.
Pat the salmon dry and put it on the tray. Toss the mushrooms with the oil and a few drops of the tamari and set them alongside. Broil about 15 cm (6 inches) from the heat for 5 minutes.
Spread the paste thinly over the salmon and broil 3 to 4 minutes more, until the glaze browns in spots and the salmon flakes easily. The mushrooms should be golden and tender.
Meanwhile, boil the spinach for 30 seconds, then drain, rinse under cold water and squeeze it very dry. Cut it into chunks.

Crush the sesame seeds in a mortar, or in a bowl with the back of a spoon, until about half are ground. Stir in the rest of the tamari, the vinegar and a teaspoon of water, then toss the spinach through it.
Reheat the rice and barley. Serve the salmon and mushrooms with the sesame spinach and the rice, with sliced scallion on top.
tip: No broiler? Bake at 220°C (425°F) for 8 minutes, glaze, then 3 to 4 minutes more.

name: Doenjang jjigae with beef, tofu, zucchini and mushrooms, over barley rice
inspiredBy: Korean doenjang jjigae, with a bonito broth in place of dried anchovy
about: A bubbling, savoury Korean stew of thin beef, tofu, zucchini and king oyster mushrooms in a garlicky doenjang broth with a little gochujang and gochugaru, served over barley rice (boribap). It is rustic family food, and it tastes even better the next day. The **tofu and vegetables do most of the work**, with just a little beef for iron and zinc.
steps: Simmer about 350 ml (1½ cups) of water per portion with the bonito flakes for 3 minutes, then strain the broth.
Warm the sesame oil in a medium pot over medium heat. Cook the beef with the minced garlic for 2 minutes, until it has lost its pink colour.
Pour in the broth and bring it to a simmer. Whisk the doenjang with a ladle of the hot broth until smooth, then stir it into the pot with the gochujang and gochugaru.
Add the zucchini and mushrooms, cut into chunky pieces, and simmer for 6 minutes. Add the tofu in big cubes and the scallion cut into lengths, and simmer gently for 3 minutes more.
Taste the broth: it should be savoury and a little earthy, not too salty. Add a splash of water if it is.
Reheat the rice and barley, and serve the stew over or beside it in deep bowls. Pack the second portion, with its rice, for tomorrow's lunch and reheat it gently so the tofu stays tender.
tip: Add an extra spoon of gochujang for a spicier bowl. Barley is about half the grain here, the way Korean boribap is.

name: Salt-grilled mackerel with grated daikon, spinach ohitashi and wakame cucumber
inspiredBy: Japanese saba shioyaki, set out as a teishoku with ohitashi and a vinegared side
about: A mackerel fillet salted and grilled until the skin is crisp and blistered, with a mound of grated daikon and a splash of soy, spinach in a light soy dressing and a sharp wakame and cucumber salad. It is a simple, honest Japanese dinner. Mackerel is one of the best sources of **omega-3 fats**, and the daikon cuts right through its richness.
steps: Sprinkle the mackerel with most of the salt on both sides and leave it for 20 minutes, then pat it dry with paper towel.
Boil the spinach for 30 seconds, then drain, rinse under cold water and squeeze it very dry. Cut it into chunks and toss with a few drops of the tamari and half the sesame seeds.

Slice the cucumber thinly and toss it with a pinch of the salt. After 10 minutes, squeeze out the water. Soak the wakame in cold water for 5 minutes, then drain and squeeze it, and toss both with the vinegar and a few drops of the tamari.
Heat the broiler to high. Broil the mackerel skin side up on a foil-lined tray for 8 to 10 minutes, until the skin is blistered and the flesh is opaque all the way through. No flipping needed.
Grate the daikon and drain it lightly. Reheat the rice and barley. Serve the mackerel with the daikon and the rest of the tamari dribbled over, with the spinach, the salad and the rice.
tip: Open a window and turn on the fan. Grilled mackerel smells like a Japanese izakaya, which is not bad at all.

name: Dubu-kimchi, stir-fried pork and kimchi with seared tofu and rice
inspiredBy: Korean dubu-kimchi, with a little mirin to balance sour kimchi
about: Tender pork, carrot and mushrooms stir-fried with tangy, spicy kimchi, piled beside slabs of golden seared tofu with brown rice and barley. It is fast, punchy and deeply savoury, and a favourite at Korean tables. **Kimchi is already salty and sour**, so the sauce needs very little extra, and the tofu adds plant protein.
steps: Pat the tofu dry and cut it into slabs about 1 cm (½ inch) thick. Warm half the canola oil in a large non-stick pan over medium heat and sear the tofu until golden, about 3 minutes a side. Move it to a plate.
Add the rest of the canola oil to the same pan. Stir-fry the carrot, mushrooms and pork over high heat for 3 minutes, until the pork has lost its pink colour.
Add the garlic and kimchi and stir-fry for 4 to 5 minutes, until the carrot is tender and the kimchi smells toasty and its edges caramelize.
Stir in the tamari, the mirin and a splash of water, and cook 1 minute more. Take it off the heat and stir through the sesame oil.
Reheat the rice and barley. Serve the kimchi and pork beside the warm tofu and the rice, with the scallion and sesame seeds on top.
tip: Older, sour kimchi is best for cooking. Fresh kimchi works too, but add a splash of vinegar.

name: Bibimbap with beef, four namul and a fried egg
inspiredBy: Korean bibimbap, with brown rice and less oil
about: A big bowl of brown rice topped in sections with sesame spinach, soybean sprouts, carrot and shiitake namul, marinated beef and a crisp-edged fried egg, all mixed together with a tangy gochujang sauce. It is the weekend project: lots of small steps, none of them hard, and it makes two portions. The colourful vegetables carry **folate, vitamin A and vitamin K**.
steps: Make the sauce. Stir the gochujang with the vinegar, about a third of the sesame oil, a little of the garlic and a splash of water into a thick, spoonable paste.
Toss the thinly sliced beef with a little tamari, garlic and a few drops of sesame oil, and leave it to marinate while you do the vegetables.

Blanch the spinach for 30 seconds, drain, rinse cold and squeeze dry. Toss it with garlic, a few drops of sesame oil and a few drops of tamari. Boil the soybean sprouts, covered, in a little water for 5 minutes until they no longer taste raw, then drain and season the same way.

Cut the carrot into matchsticks and slice the shiitake. Stir-fry the carrot in a little sesame oil for 2 minutes, then the shiitake for 3 minutes until golden, seasoning each with a few drops of tamari. Keep the vegetables in separate piles.
Cook the beef in a hot pan for 2 minutes, until it is browned and there is no pink left.
In the same pan, with a little more sesame oil, fry an egg, sunny side up, until the white is crisp at the edges and the yolk is still runny.

Reheat the rice and barley with a splash of water. Divide the rice, namul and beef in half. Put one half in a wide bowl, arranged in sections around the edge, with the egg in the middle, a spoonful of the sauce on top and a pinch of sesame seeds. Mix everything together before you eat.
Pack the other half of the rice, namul and beef in a container for tomorrow's lunch, with the sauce on the side. Reheat the beef and rice, and fry a fresh egg then.
tip: Spinach, sprouts, carrot and shiitake can be swapped for any four vegetables you like.

name: Chicken and tofu nabe with napa cabbage and mushrooms, finished with udon
inspiredBy: Japanese mizutaki, finished with udon instead of the usual rice
about: A pot of bonito broth simmered with chicken thigh, tofu, napa cabbage, daikon, king oyster mushrooms and spinach, dipped in a bright soy and mandarin ponzu, then finished with udon noodles and a swirl of egg in the leftover broth. It is a relaxed Sunday supper you can cook right at the table, with **plenty of vegetables in a light broth** and chicken and tofu for protein.
steps: Make the ponzu. Squeeze the mandarin juice into a small bowl and stir in two-thirds of the tamari and the vinegar. Grate a little of the daikon and slice some of the scallion into it, and set it out for dipping.
Simmer about 600 ml (2½ cups) of water with the bonito flakes and the mirin for 3 minutes in a wide, shallow pot, then strain and return the broth to the pot.
Add the chicken, thin rounds of daikon and the white stems of the napa cabbage. Simmer gently for 8 minutes, skimming any foam.
Add the mushrooms (halved lengthwise) and the tofu cubes and simmer for 4 minutes. Add the napa leaves, spinach and scallion for the last minute. The chicken should be cooked through with no pink.
Eat from the pot, dipping everything in the sharp ponzu.

For the finish, add the udon (rinsed under hot water to loosen it) to the remaining broth with the rest of the tamari. Simmer for 2 minutes, then pour in the beaten egg in a slow spiral, cover, and turn off the heat for a minute. Spoon into a bowl with a little scallion.
tip: Any firm white fish works in place of the chicken, and it cooks in about 4 minutes. Fresh or frozen udon is fine too.
ingredients: boneless, skinless, cut into bite-size pieces
calcium-set, check the label for calcium sulfate

name: Warm edamame with sea salt
inspiredBy: Japanese izakaya edamame
about: A bowl of warm shelled edamame with a pinch of salt, the izakaya classic. It is a snack with real staying power. The **edamame bring protein, folate and fibre**.
steps: Boil the edamame for 3 to 4 minutes, or as the package says, then drain well.
Sprinkle with a pinch of salt and eat warm.

name: Mandarin and walnuts
about: A juicy mandarin with a handful of walnuts, the way Jeju mandarins are enjoyed in Korea. It is sweet, crunchy and easy to carry. **Walnuts add plant omega-3 fats**, and the mandarin adds vitamin C.
steps: Peel the mandarin and eat it with the walnuts.

name: Mandarin and toasted almonds
about: A juicy mandarin with a small handful of warm toasted almonds. It is sweet, crunchy and keeps you going. The **almonds bring vitamin E** and calcium, and the mandarin adds vitamin C.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan over medium heat for 3 minutes, until golden and fragrant. Peel the mandarin and eat it with the warm almonds.

name: Mandarin with almonds and walnuts
about: A juicy mandarin with a small handful of almonds and walnuts. It is sweet, crunchy and easy to carry. The **almonds bring vitamin E**, the walnuts bring plant omega-3 fats, and the mandarin adds vitamin C.
steps: Peel the mandarin and eat it with the almonds and walnuts. Toast the nuts in a dry pan for 2 minutes first if you like.

name: Asian pear and walnuts
inspiredBy: Korean fruit and nuts after a meal
about: Cold, crisp, juicy Asian pear slices with a handful of walnuts, a very Korean way to end a meal. It is sweet and crunchy. **Walnuts add plant omega-3 fats** and the pear adds fibre.
steps: Slice the pear and eat it with the walnuts.

name: Asian pear and toasted almonds
inspiredBy: Korean fruit and nuts after a meal
about: Cold, crisp, juicy Asian pear slices with a small handful of warm toasted almonds. It is sweet and crunchy, and a very Korean way to end a meal. The **almonds bring vitamin E**, and the pear adds fibre.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan over medium heat for 3 minutes, until golden and fragrant. Slice the pear and eat it with the warm almonds.

name: Hiyayakko, chilled tofu with ginger and bonito
inspiredBy: Japanese hiyayakko
about: A block of chilled tofu topped with grated ginger, scallion, bonito flakes and a dash of tamari. It is cool, silky and savoury, and takes two minutes. It adds **plant protein and a little calcium**.
steps: Pat the tofu dry and set it on a plate.
Grate the ginger over the top, then add the sliced scallion, bonito flakes and sesame seeds. Dribble with the tamari.

name: Roasted sweet potato (yaki-imo)
inspiredBy: Japanese and Korean street-cart roasted sweet potato
about: A whole sweet potato roasted until the skin crackles and the inside turns jammy and caramelized, the way it is sold from street carts in Japan and Korea in winter. It is naturally sweet with nothing added. It is rich in **vitamin A and fibre**.
steps: Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Pierce the sweet potato a few times with a fork, set it on a tray and roast for 45 to 50 minutes, until it feels very soft and some syrup oozes from the skin.
Let it cool for a few minutes and eat it with the skin on.
tip: Roast a whole tray on Sunday and rewarm one in a toaster oven. They keep for 4 days in the fridge.

name: Cucumber and carrot sticks with miso and sesame dip
inspiredBy: Japanese moro-kyu, cucumber with miso
about: Crunchy cucumber and carrot sticks with a savoury miso and sesame dip, a very Japanese snack that is often served with beer or tea. It is light, crisp and low in calories. The carrot adds **vitamin A**, and the dip brings a little sesame for minerals.
steps: Cut the cucumber and carrot into sticks. Stir the miso, mirin, sesame seeds and a few drops of water into a thick dip, and use it for dunking.

name: Soft-boiled egg with toasted nori
inspiredBy: Korean gim and eggs
about: A soft-boiled egg with crisp toasted nori to tear and wrap around bites of the egg. It is a small, savoury snack with a lot of protein. The egg brings **protein and choline**, and the nori adds iodine.
steps: Boil the egg for 6½ minutes, cool it under cold water and peel it. Dribble with a few drops of tamari and eat it with torn pieces of nori.

name: Soy-glazed almonds and walnuts (nut jorim)
inspiredBy: Korean nut jorim (gyeongwa-jorim)
about: Almonds and walnuts toasted in a pan and glazed with a little tamari and mirin until sticky, like the Korean nut jorim side dish. They are savoury, a little sweet and very crunchy. The **almonds bring vitamin E**, and the walnuts bring plant omega-3 fats.
steps: Toast the almonds and walnuts in a dry pan over medium heat for 3 minutes, until they smell nutty.
Add the tamari and mirin and stir for about a minute, until the glaze is sticky and coats the nuts. Cool on a plate so they crisp up.
tip: Make a jar on Sunday. They keep for a week.

name: Korean spicy cucumber salad (oi-muchim)
inspiredBy: Korean oi-muchim
about: Crunchy cucumber in a quick sesame, garlic, vinegar and gochugaru dressing, a Korean side dish you can snack on. It is cool, tangy and a little spicy, and mostly water and crunch, with **almost no calories**.
steps: Slice the cucumber and squeeze it lightly to push out some of the water.
Toss with the sliced scallion, minced garlic, vinegar, gochugaru and sesame seeds, and eat right away.

name: Lemony chia pudding with raspberries and toasted hazelnuts
inspiredBy: Greek rizogalo, the rice pudding scented with cinnamon and lemon peel, made keto with chia
about: Chia soaked overnight in almond milk with cinnamon and lemon zest until it sets like a soft rice pudding, then topped with a few raspberries and toasted hazelnuts. It is ready when you wake up, and one jar gives you **calcium, magnesium and plenty of fibre**.
steps: The night before, stir the chia, almond milk, cinnamon and lemon zest together in a jar or bowl.
Leave it for 5 minutes, then stir again so the seeds do not clump at the bottom.
Cover and chill overnight. By morning it should be thick and spoonable, like a loose rice pudding.
Toast the hazelnuts in a dry pan over medium heat until they smell nutty, about 2 minutes. Tip them out to cool, then roughly chop them.
Spoon the pudding into a bowl and top with the raspberries and hazelnuts. Add a splash more almond milk if it has set too firm.
tip: Make one jar on Sunday night for Monday, and three on Thursday night for Friday to Sunday. They keep for 3 days in the fridge.
ingredients: unsweetened, fortified with calcium and vitamin D

name: Greek yogurt with walnuts, raspberries and olive oil
inspiredBy: Greek strained yogurt with walnuts and fruit, without the honey
about: Thick, full-fat Greek yogurt with crunchy toasted walnuts and hazelnuts, a few raspberries, a dusting of cinnamon and a drizzle of good olive oil, the way a savoury-sweet Greek breakfast tastes. It is ready in five minutes, and the yogurt, walnuts and flax give you **protein, calcium, fibre and plant omega-3**.
steps: Toast the walnuts and hazelnuts in a dry pan over medium heat until fragrant, about 2 minutes.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl, stir in the ground flax and grate a little lemon zest over it.
Add the raspberries and warm nuts, dust with cinnamon and drizzle with the olive oil.
tip: Squash the raspberries into the yogurt with a fork if you like a pink swirl.

name: Spinach and dill omelette with olives and avocado
inspiredBy: Greek spanakopita filling in an omelette, with no pastry
about: A soft, golden omelette folded around wilted spinach, chopped olives and a good pinch of dill, with sliced avocado on the side. It tastes like the filling of a spanakopita without the pastry, and the eggs and spinach bring **choline, folate and vitamin K** first thing.
steps: Warm half the olive oil in a non-stick frying pan over medium heat. Soften the onion for 2 minutes.
Add the spinach and cook, stirring, until it wilts completely and the pan looks nearly dry, about 2 minutes. Tip it onto a plate.
Beat the eggs with a pinch of salt and plenty of pepper.
Wipe the pan, add the rest of the oil and pour in the eggs. Stir gently for 20 seconds, then let them set into a soft omelette, about 1 minute, a little longer for a bigger omelette.
Scatter the spinach, olives and dill over one half and fold the other half over. Slide it onto a plate.
Slice the avocado alongside and squeeze a little lemon over it.
tip: The olives are salty, so go easy on the salt in the eggs.

name: Garlic shrimp, avocado and fennel salad
inspiredBy: Spanish gambas al ajillo with an almond-garlic dressing
about: Quickly seared garlicky shrimp over crisp romaine, ripe avocado and shaved fennel, dressed with a creamy almond, garlic and lemon sauce. It is bright, rich and ready in 15 minutes, and the avocado and romaine bring **potassium and folate**.
steps: Pat the shrimp dry and toss them with the paprika, garlic and a pinch of salt.
Shave the fennel as thin as you can with a sharp knife or peeler, and toss it with half the lemon juice. This takes the raw edge off while it stays crisp.
Warm a third of the olive oil in a frying pan over medium-high heat. Cook the shrimp until they curl and turn pink, about 2 minutes a side.

Pound the almonds to a coarse paste with the rest of the garlic and a pinch of salt in a mortar, or blitz them in a mini chopper. Stir in the remaining lemon juice, the rest of the olive oil, the pepper and a splash of water until it pours like thick cream, in the style of ajo blanco.
Pile the romaine, fennel and avocado slices on a plate, top with the warm shrimp and spoon the dressing over. Scatter with dill.
tip: Look for shrimp with no added salt or phosphate.

name: Spanish tuna, egg and red pepper salad with olives
inspiredBy: Spanish ensalada de atún with boiled egg, with no potato
about: Tinned tuna and a boiled egg on crisp romaine with red pepper, tomato, creamy avocado, salty olives and capers in a sharp vinegar dressing. It is a very Spanish lunch that needs almost no cooking, and the parsley and pepper bring plenty of **vitamin C**.
steps: Lower the egg into boiling water and cook for 9 minutes. Cool it under cold water, then peel and quarter it.
Rinse the olives and capers under cold water and pat them dry. Tear the romaine into a wide bowl and add the red pepper, tomatoes, onion, olives and capers.
Drain the tuna and flake it into big pieces.
Whisk the olive oil with the vinegar, salt and pepper, and toss with the salad.
Top with the tuna, egg, avocado slices and a generous handful of chopped parsley.
tip: Buy tuna with no salt added.

name: Greek salad with sardines
inspiredBy: Greek horiatiki, with sardines in place of the feta
about: A Greek village salad of juicy tomatoes, crunchy cucumber, red pepper, olives and capers, with sardines laid on top in place of the feta and a splash of vinegar. The soft sardine bones give you **calcium and omega-3**, and the salad keeps the carbs tiny.
steps: Rinse the olives and capers under cold water and pat them dry. Put them in a wide bowl with the cucumber, tomatoes, red pepper and onion.
Whisk the olive oil with the vinegar, oregano and pepper, and pour it over. Toss lightly and let it sit for 5 minutes so the juices mingle.
Drain the sardines, break them into large pieces and lay them on top.
Scatter with parsley and finish with a little more oregano.
tip: Spoon the juices over the sardines and use a fork, since there is no bread.

name: Pork souvlaki with tzatziki and Greek romaine salad
inspiredBy: Greek pork souvlaki with tzatziki, without the pita
about: Lemony, oregano-marinated pork on skewers, served with thick garlicky tzatziki and a crunchy Greek romaine salad with dill and olives. It is the taverna plate without the pita, and the pork brings **thiamin**. The second portion makes tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Cut the pork into bite-size cubes. Mix them with half the olive oil, half the lemon juice, most of the garlic, the oregano, a pinch of salt and pepper. Marinate for at least an hour in the fridge (a few hours is even better).
Make the tzatziki. Grate the cucumber and squeeze it dry with your hands. Stir it into the yogurt with a little grated garlic, half the dill, a drizzle of olive oil and a pinch of salt.

Shred the romaine and slice the onion very thin. Rinse the olives under cold water and pat them dry. Toss everything together with the olives, the rest of the dill, a squeeze of lemon, the last of the olive oil and a pinch of salt.

Thread the pork onto skewers. Cook under a hot grill, on a grill pan or on the barbecue, turning now and then, until golden at the edges and just cooked through, about 8 minutes. Pork tenderloin dries out fast, so do not overdo it.
Serve the skewers with the salad and a big spoonful of tzatziki.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the tzatziki and salad in separate containers. Eat the pork cold, sliced, with the tzatziki, since reheating dries tenderloin out.
tip: Soak wooden skewers for 20 minutes, or just cook the pork as flat kebabs under the grill.

name: Roast trout with zucchini, spinach and almond gremolata
inspiredBy: Italian gremolata, with toasted almonds, over roast trout
about: A crisp-skinned trout fillet roasted on a tray with lemony zucchini, then set on garlicky wilted spinach and finished with a bright gremolata of toasted almonds, parsley, lemon zest and raw garlic. It is **omega-3 and vitamin D** in one pan, and the spinach and zucchini bring folate and potassium.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the zucchini on a tray with about a third of the olive oil, a pinch of salt and the Aleppo pepper.
Roast the zucchini for 8 minutes, then push it to the side and add the trout, skin side down. Rub it with a little olive oil, salt and pepper.
Roast another 8 to 10 minutes, until the trout flakes easily but is still a little translucent in the middle and the zucchini has browned edges.
Meanwhile, toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes, then chop them roughly.
Make the gremolata. Mix the almonds with the finely chopped parsley, lemon zest and the garlic, minced as fine as you can.

Wilt the spinach in a hot pan with a little olive oil and a pinch of salt, about 1 minute. Pile it on a plate with the zucchini and the trout on top, then squeeze over the lemon and spoon the gremolata over the fish.

name: Fennel and rosemary pork tenderloin with garlicky rapini and hazelnut salsa verde
inspiredBy: Tuscan porchetta flavours (fennel, garlic, rosemary) on lean pork tenderloin, with Puglian rapini
about: Lean pork tenderloin rubbed with garlic, fennel seed and rosemary, roasted until blushing and served with garlicky rapini and a punchy parsley, caper and toasted hazelnut salsa verde. It gives you the flavour of Tuscan porchetta in 35 minutes, and the pork and rapini bring **thiamin, folate and iron**. The second portion becomes tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Crush the fennel seeds and rosemary with the back of a spoon and mix them with a little of the minced garlic, a teaspoon of the olive oil, salt and pepper.
Rub this paste all over the pork. Put the onion wedges on a tray, make a gap for the pork, and roast for 10 minutes.
Turn the pork and stir the onion. Roast another 12 to 15 minutes, until the pork is just a little pink inside. Rest it for 5 minutes, then slice it thickly.

Meanwhile, toast the hazelnuts in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes, and chop them roughly. Chop the parsley and capers together and stir in the hazelnuts, half the lemon juice and enough olive oil to make the salsa spoonable, about 1 tablespoon for the two portions.
Blanch the rapini in boiling salted water for 2 minutes, drain well, then toss in a hot pan with the remaining olive oil and garlic until tender and fragrant, about 2 minutes.
Plate the rapini and onion, lay the pork slices on top and spoon over the salsa verde and the rest of the lemon juice.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the salsa verde in its own container. Eat the pork cold, sliced, or warm it very gently so it stays juicy.
tip: Do not overcook tenderloin. It is best at 63°C (145°F), then rested.

name: Garlic shrimp on cauliflower rice with olives and zucchini
inspiredBy: Spanish gambas al ajillo, over cauliflower rice instead of bread
about: Sizzling garlic shrimp with smoked paprika spooned over lemony cauliflower rice, with olives, golden zucchini, silky kale and creamy avocado. It is a quick Spanish-style supper, and the shrimp, cauliflower and kale bring **choline, vitamin C and calcium**.
steps: Pulse the cauliflower in a food processor, or grate it on the coarse side of a box grater, until it looks like rice.

Warm a third of the olive oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Add the cauliflower with a pinch of salt and cook, stirring, until just tender, about 5 minutes. Stir in the rinsed olives and half the lemon juice and move it to a plate.

Add a little more oil and the zucchini to the pan. Cook until golden at the edges and tender, about 4 minutes. Add the kale with a splash of water and cook until silky, about 3 minutes, then put the vegetables with the rice.
Add the rest of the olive oil and the garlic to the pan and let it sizzle for 30 seconds, until fragrant but not brown.
Add the shrimp, paprika, Aleppo pepper and a pinch of salt. Cook until pink and curled, about 2 minutes a side.
Spoon the shrimp and the garlicky oil over the rice. Add sliced avocado, parsley and the remaining lemon juice.
tip: Look for shrimp with no added salt or phosphate.
ingredients: grated or pulsed into rice-size pieces

name: Chicken cacciatore with mushrooms, peppers and olives
inspiredBy: Italian pollo alla cacciatora, with no pasta or bread alongside
about: Chicken thighs braised with plenty of mushrooms, a little red pepper, black olives and capers in a light tomato and herb sauce, a hunter-style stew from Italy. It is even better the next day, and the mushrooms bring **B vitamins and potassium** while the spinach stirred in at the end adds folate.
steps: Pat the chicken dry and season with salt and pepper. Warm half the olive oil in a wide pan or Dutch oven over medium-high heat and brown the chicken well on both sides, about 8 minutes. Set it aside.
Add the rest of the olive oil, the mushrooms and a pinch of salt. Cook until they lose their water and turn golden, about 6 minutes.
Add the onion, red pepper and garlic and cook until soft, about 4 minutes.
Stir in the vinegar, scraping up the browned bits, then add the crushed tomatoes, thyme, rosemary and about ⅓ cup (80 ml) of water.
Return the chicken to the pan, cover and simmer gently for 20 minutes, then take the lid off for the last 5 minutes so the sauce thickens.
Stir in the rinsed olives and capers and the spinach, and cook 2 more minutes, until the spinach wilts.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. It reheats well and keeps for 3 days in the fridge.
tip: Bone-in thighs make an even richer sauce. Brown them the same way and simmer 35 minutes instead of 20.

name: Eggplant and lamb moussaka with zucchini and a yogurt topping
inspiredBy: Greek moussaka, with zucchini for the potatoes and a yogurt and egg topping in place of flour béchamel
about: Layers of roasted eggplant and zucchini under a cinnamon-scented lamb and tomato sauce, finished with a golden yogurt and egg topping. It is the Greek weekend classic with no potato or flour, and the second portion is even better tomorrow. The eggplant brings **fibre and potassium** for very few carbs.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Lay the eggplant and zucchini on lined trays, brush both sides with about half the olive oil (a thin coat is enough on a lined tray), season with salt and roast until soft and golden, about 25 minutes, turning once.
Meanwhile, warm the remaining oil in a large pan. Cook the onion until soft, about 5 minutes, then add the garlic and lamb. Break the lamb up and brown it well, about 8 minutes.

Stir in the cinnamon, oregano, bay leaf, crushed tomatoes, about ½ cup (125 ml) of water for the dish, salt and pepper. Simmer for about 20 minutes, until thick but still saucy. Discard the bay leaf and stir in the parsley.
Lower the oven to 190°C (375°F). In a baking dish, layer half the eggplant and zucchini, then all the meat sauce, then the rest of the vegetables.
Whisk the yogurt with the egg, nutmeg and a pinch of salt. Spread it over the top.
Bake until set and golden in patches, about 30 minutes. Let it rest for 10 minutes before cutting, or it will slump.
Cut it into two portions. Keep the second for tomorrow's lunch; it reheats well and keeps for 3 days.
tip: Ask the butcher to mince a lean leg of lamb. It keeps the moussaka light and not greasy.
ingredients: for the two portions, 1 jumbo egg

name: Roast trout with tomatoes, olives and lemony greens
inspiredBy: Greek plaki, fish baked with tomato, garlic and olive oil
about: Trout fillets roasted on a bed of cherry tomatoes, olives, capers and garlic, served with kale braised until silky in lemon and olive oil, the way Greek horta are served. It is a Greek-island plaki dinner, and the trout brings **omega-3 and vitamin D** while the kale adds calcium and vitamin C.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Rinse the olives and capers under cold water and pat them dry. Toss the tomatoes, onion, sliced garlic, olives and capers on a tray with about half the olive oil, the oregano and a pinch of salt.
Roast for 10 minutes, until the tomatoes start to burst.
Pat the trout dry, rub it with a little olive oil, salt and pepper, and lay the fillets skin side up on the tomatoes.
Roast another 8 to 10 minutes, until the skin is blistered and the flesh flakes easily.

While it cooks, strip the kale from its stems and chop it. Warm a little olive oil in a pan with a splash of water and cook the kale with a pinch of salt until silky, about 6 minutes. Take it off the heat and dress with half the lemon juice and the rest of the olive oil.
Plate the kale, then the trout and tomatoes, and spoon the tomato juices over the fish. Finish with parsley and the remaining lemon.
ingredients: leaves only, most of a small bunch

name: Warm olives with rosemary and hazelnuts
inspiredBy: Spanish tapas bar olives and nuts
about: Black olives and whole hazelnuts warmed in olive oil with rosemary and a squeeze of lemon, which makes them taste like a bar snack in Catalonia. The hazelnuts give you **vitamin E and magnesium** with very few carbs.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a small pan over medium heat. Add the hazelnuts and rosemary and toast for 2 minutes, stirring, until the hazelnuts smell nutty.
Add the rinsed olives and warm through for 1 minute.
Tip into a bowl and squeeze a little lemon over the top.

name: Garlic mushrooms with parsley and lemon
inspiredBy: Spanish champiñones al ajillo
about: Mushrooms sautéed hard in olive oil until golden, then tossed with sizzling garlic, parsley and a squeeze of lemon. It is a classic Spanish tapa, and mushrooms are a surprisingly good source of **B vitamins and potassium**.
steps: Heat the olive oil in a wide frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms in one layer with a pinch of salt and cook, without stirring too much, until golden, about 6 minutes.
Add the garlic and Aleppo pepper and cook for 30 seconds, just until fragrant.
Take the pan off the heat and toss with parsley and a squeeze of lemon.

name: Avocado with lemon, olive oil and oregano
inspiredBy: Spanish and Greek avocado with lemon, olive oil and herbs
about: A whole ripe avocado, halved and dressed with generous olive oil, lemon, oregano and Aleppo pepper. It is simple and creamy, and avocado is a great source of **potassium, folate and fibre**.
steps: Halve the avocado and remove the stone.
Drizzle with the lemon juice and olive oil, then sprinkle over the oregano, Aleppo pepper and a pinch of salt.
Eat it straight from the skin with a spoon.

name: Olive and caper tapenade with cucumber dippers
inspiredBy: Provençal and Ligurian olive tapenade
about: A coarse tapenade of black olives, capers, garlic and lemon, scooped up with crunchy cucumber. The olives and olive oil are the Mediterranean fats at their purest, and they bring **vitamin E**.
steps: Rinse the olives and capers under cold water and pat them dry. Chop them with the garlic and parsley until they make a coarse paste, or pulse them a few times in a food processor.
Stir in the lemon juice, olive oil and pepper.
Cut the cucumber into dippers and serve with the tapenade.

name: Raspberries and walnuts with cinnamon
inspiredBy: Greek fruit and walnuts, without the honey
about: Juicy raspberries with a handful of toasted walnuts and a pinch of cinnamon. It is sweet-tart and crunchy, with plant omega-3 from the walnuts and plenty of **fibre** from the berries.
steps: Toast the walnuts in a dry pan over medium heat until fragrant, about 2 minutes.
Put the raspberries in a bowl, add the warm walnuts and dust with cinnamon.

name: Toasted hazelnuts with rosemary and lemon
inspiredBy: Spanish and Piedmontese toasted hazelnuts
about: Whole hazelnuts toasted in a dry pan until golden and fragrant, then tossed with rosemary, a pinch of salt and a squeeze of lemon. Hazelnuts are grown across Spain and Italy, and a small handful gives you **vitamin E, magnesium and healthy fats** with hardly any carbs.
steps: Toast the hazelnuts in a dry pan over medium heat, shaking now and then, until golden and fragrant, about 4 minutes.
Take the pan off the heat and toss with the olive oil, rosemary and salt.
Add a squeeze of lemon and let them cool for a couple of minutes so they crunch.

name: Avocado filled with tuna and lemon
inspiredBy: Spanish and Italian tuna with avocado and lemon
about: A ripe avocado half filled with flaked tuna, lemon, parsley and a drizzle of olive oil. It is rich, creamy and filling, with **protein and potassium** in one easy bite.
steps: Halve the avocado and remove the stone.
Flake the tuna with the lemon juice, chopped parsley, olive oil, pepper and a pinch of salt.
Pile the tuna into the hollow of the avocado and eat with a spoon.

name: Poached shrimp with lemon and smoked paprika
inspiredBy: Spanish gambas cocidas
about: Shrimp poached in a pot of lemony water for a couple of minutes, then tossed with olive oil, smoked paprika and parsley and eaten cold, like a plate of Spanish gambas cocidas. It is a cold plate of shrimp to pick at, with plenty of **protein** for almost no carbs.
steps: Bring a small pot of salted water to a boil with a squeeze of the lemon.
Add the shrimp and cook until pink and curled, about 2 minutes. Drain and cool under cold water.
Toss with the olive oil, paprika, parsley and the rest of the lemon juice.
tip: Look for shrimp with no added salt or phosphate.

name: Tuna-stuffed eggs with capers and parsley
inspiredBy: Spanish huevos rellenos de atún
about: Hard-boiled egg halves filled with a creamy mash of the yolk, flaked tuna, capers, parsley and lemon, a classic Spanish tapa. It is a small, salty, filling snack, and the egg and tuna bring **choline and protein**.
steps: Lower the egg into boiling water and cook for 9 minutes. Cool it under cold water, then peel and halve lengthwise.
Pop out the yolk and mash it with the drained tuna, chopped capers, parsley, lemon juice and olive oil until creamy.
Spoon the filling back into the whites and dust with the paprika.

name: Marinated olives with oregano, garlic and lemon
inspiredBy: Greek meze marinated olives
about: Black olives tossed with olive oil, a little garlic, oregano and lemon and left to sit for a few minutes, the way every meze table in Greece starts. They are salty, fruity and satisfying, and a handful of olives is a classic Mediterranean source of **healthy fats and vitamin E**.
steps: Rinse the olives under cold water, pat them dry and put them in a small bowl.
Add the olive oil, lemon juice, finely grated garlic, oregano and chopped parsley, and toss well.
Leave them to marinate for 10 minutes if you can, then eat with a fork or toothpicks.

name: Almonds fried in olive oil with pimentón
inspiredBy: Spanish almendras fritas
about: Whole almonds fried in olive oil until golden, then tossed with smoked paprika and a pinch of salt, the kind of snack a Spanish bar puts out with a glass of sherry. They are warm, crunchy and rich, and bring **vitamin E and magnesium**.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a small frying pan over medium heat.
Add the almonds and fry, stirring, for about 3 minutes, until they are golden and smell toasty.
Tip them and the oil onto a plate, toss with the pimentón and salt, and let them cool for a couple of minutes so they crisp up.

name: Foul medames with boiled eggs, tahini, raw onion and radish
inspiredBy: Jordanian and Palestinian foul, the breakfast of the foul stands in Amman, with a little chickpea in the pot as Lebanese cooks like it
about: Warm, creamy fava beans and chickpeas mashed with garlic, cumin and lemon, with a swirl of tahini, two boiled eggs and a pile of raw onion, radish, tomato and parsley on top. Scoop it all up with warm whole-wheat pita. The beans bring **fibre, folate and iron**, and the eggs add choline.
steps: Lower the eggs gently into a small pot of boiling water and cook for 8 minutes, then cool them under cold water and peel.

Mash the garlic with the salt into a paste. Warm the fava beans and chickpeas in a small pot with the garlic, the cumin and a splash of water, stirring now and then, until they are steaming hot, about 5 minutes.
Mash roughly with a fork. You want a creamy base with some whole beans left in it. Stir in the lemon juice and half the olive oil.
Stir the tahini with a spoonful of water until it is pourable, like thin cream.
