Spoon the beans into a shallow bowl, drizzle with the tahini and the rest of the olive oil, and pile the tomato, onion, radish and parsley on top. Add the halved eggs.
Warm the pita in a dry pan or the toaster, tear it up and use it to scoop.
tip: A 400 g tin of foul makes two portions, so two foul mornings need only one tin. A pinch of chili flakes or a few chopped pickles on top is welcome.
ingredients: from a tin, drained and rinsed

name: Za'atar pita with labneh, olives, egg and cucumber
inspiredBy: the za'atar and olive oil breakfast of Jordan and Lebanon, in the style of a man'oushe
about: Warm pita brushed with za'atar and olive oil, a swirl of labneh, a soft-boiled egg, olives, cucumber and fresh mint. It is the everyday breakfast table in one plate. The labneh and egg bring **protein, calcium and choline**.
steps: Lower the egg gently into a small pot of boiling water and cook for 7 minutes for a jammy yolk. Cool it under cold water, then peel. You can boil a few ahead and keep them in the fridge.
Stir the za'atar into most of the olive oil to make a paste. Spread it over the pita and warm it in a dry pan or a hot oven for a couple of minutes, until it smells toasty.
Stir a pinch of salt into the labneh and swirl it onto a plate. Pour the rest of the olive oil into a little well in the middle.
Halve the egg and arrange it with the olives, sliced cucumber and mint around the labneh. Tear the pita and scoop.
tip: No labneh? Spoon thick Greek yogurt into a sieve lined with a clean cloth the night before, stir in a pinch of salt and let it drain in the fridge.

name: Balila, warm chickpeas with tahini, lemon, cumin and a boiled egg
inspiredBy: Lebanese and Palestinian balila, the warm chickpea breakfast
about: Warm, soft chickpeas in a little of their liquid with lemon, garlic and cumin, finished with a spoon of tahini, parsley and a good pour of olive oil, with a boiled egg alongside. It is simple, savoury and very filling. The chickpeas bring **fibre and protein** and the egg adds choline.
steps: Lower the egg gently into a small pot of boiling water and cook for 8 minutes, then cool it under cold water and peel.
Mash the garlic with the salt into a paste. Warm the chickpeas in a small pot with the garlic, the cumin and a splash of water for 5 minutes, until they are very hot and soft.
Mash a few of them against the side of the pot so the liquid turns creamy, and stir in the lemon juice.
Whisk the tahini with a spoonful of water until pourable.
Spoon the chickpeas and some of their liquid into a bowl. Drizzle over the tahini and the olive oil and scatter with the parsley.
Halve the egg and lay it on top. Warm the pita and serve with the radish on the side.
tip: Add a pinch of chili flakes or a few drops of hot sauce, the way balila is often served in Beirut.

name: Ijjeh, a herb and chard omelette with radish and mint salad
inspiredBy: Levantine ijjeh (eggah), with chard folded in and no flour
about: A thick, green, herby omelette packed with parsley, chard, onion and a little grated halloumi, cut into wedges and eaten with warm pita, crunchy radishes, cucumber and mint. It makes two portions, and the cold wedge is just as good tomorrow morning. The eggs bring **protein and choline**, and the parsley and chard bring vitamin K.
steps: Finely chop the parsley, chard and onion. Keep the chard stems, they stay pleasantly crisp.
Beat the eggs in a bowl with the baharat and half the salt, then stir in the grated halloumi, herbs, chard, onion and walnuts. It should look more green than yellow.

Heat the broiler. Warm half the oil in a medium oven-safe non-stick pan over medium-low heat. Pour in the egg mixture, cover, and cook gently until the edges are set and the top is almost firm, about 8 minutes.
Brush the top with the rest of the oil and slide the pan under the broiler for 2 minutes, until puffed and golden. Cut into wedges.
Slice the radishes and cucumber, toss with the mint, lemon juice and the rest of the salt, and serve beside a wedge with warm pita.
Wrap the second portion for tomorrow. Make a fresh salad then, and eat the wedge cold or tucked into pita.
tip: Leave out the walnuts if you like it softer. A pinch of cinnamon is traditional in some Syrian kitchens.

name: Lamb kafta pita with roasted cauliflower, tarator and tomato
inspiredBy: Lebanese and Palestinian kafta sandwiches, made with lean lamb and finished with tahini sauce and roasted cauliflower, as karnabeet is eaten
about: Finger-shaped patties of lean lamb, parsley and onion with baharat, tucked into warm whole-wheat pita with golden roasted cauliflower, tomato, a sumac onion salad and a lemony tahini sauce. It is street food you can make at home. The lamb brings **iron, zinc and vitamin B12**, and the tahini adds calcium.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C. Toss the cauliflower with half the olive oil and a pinch of salt on a tray and roast until golden at the edges, about 20 minutes.
Pulse the lamb cubes in a food processor, in short bursts with a splash of ice water, until finely ground and sticky. Or ask the butcher to grind lean leg of lamb twice.

Squeeze the grated onion in your hands to get rid of the extra juice. Mix it with the lamb, most of the parsley, the baharat, black pepper and half the salt, kneading for a minute or two. Shape into 3 or 4 fingers about 8 cm long.
Warm the rest of the oil in a non-stick pan over medium-high heat and cook the kafta, turning now and then, until browned all over and cooked through, about 8 minutes.

Make the tarator. Stir the tahini with the lemon juice, the garlic (mashed to a paste), the rest of the salt and 2 to 3 tablespoons of cold water, until pale and pourable. Toss the sliced onion with the rest of the parsley and the sumac.
Warm the pita, fill it with the kafta, cauliflower, sliced tomato and sumac onions, and drizzle with the tarator.
tip: Roast the cauliflower and shape the kafta on Wednesday night while the oven is hot for the salmon. At lunch, fry the kafta and assemble. You can also freeze the shaped raw fingers.
ingredients: most for the kafta, a little for the salad

name: Fattoush with chickpeas and grilled halloumi
inspiredBy: Lebanese fattoush, with chickpeas and halloumi to make it a meal
about: A big, crunchy salad of romaine, radish, cucumber, tomato and mint under shards of toasted pita, with a sumac and pomegranate molasses dressing, spiced chickpeas and slices of golden halloumi. It is sharp, juicy and salty at once. The chickpeas and halloumi bring **protein and calcium**.
steps: Split the pita, tear it into pieces, toss with a little of the oil and toast in a dry pan or a hot oven until golden and crisp, about 5 minutes.
Make the dressing. Mash the garlic with a pinch of salt and whisk it with the lemon juice, pomegranate molasses and the rest of the olive oil.
Toss the chickpeas in a bowl with half the sumac, a pinch of salt and a spoonful of the dressing so they take on some flavour.
Slice the halloumi and cook it in a dry non-stick pan over medium-high heat for about 1 minute per side, until golden.
Chop the romaine, radish, cucumber and tomato into bite-size pieces, tear in the mint and toss with most of the dressing.
Pile on a plate, top with the chickpeas and halloumi, sprinkle with the rest of the sumac and add the pita pieces just before eating.
tip: Grilled chicken or a handful of toasted almonds are good on top too. Use a squeeze of extra lemon if you have no pomegranate molasses.

name: Musakhan-style sumac chicken and onions on pita
inspiredBy: Palestinian musakhan, roasted sumac chicken on bread soaked in onions, made with boneless thighs and a lighter hand with the oil
about: Chicken thighs rubbed with sumac and baharat and roasted until golden, piled on whole-wheat pita with a heap of slowly cooked sumac onions and toasted pine nuts. It is Palestine's best-loved dish, scaled down for a Saturday lunch. The chicken brings **protein and zinc**, and the onions bring plenty of flavour for very little fat.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C. Rub the chicken with half the sumac, the baharat, the black pepper, a third of the oil and half the salt. Spread it on a small tray.
Roast until golden and cooked through, 25 to 30 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook the onions in the rest of the oil with the rest of the salt in a wide pan over medium-low heat, stirring now and then, until completely soft and golden, about 20 minutes, with a splash of water if they start to stick. Stir in the rest of the sumac and the lemon juice for the last minute.
Toast the pine nuts in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until golden, and watch them closely.
Warm the pita in the oven for the last 5 minutes. Spread the onions over it, lay the chicken on top and scatter with the pine nuts and parsley. Cut it into wedges and eat with your hands.
tip: Serve it with a spoonful of labneh or yogurt on the side if you like. Traditional musakhan is made with much more olive oil, and it is delicious.

name: Adas bi hamod, lemony lentil and chard soup
about: A sunny, sharp Lebanese lentil soup with plenty of chard, finished with crushed garlic and cilantro fried in olive oil and a good squeeze of lemon. It is cosy, hearty and better the next day, so it makes two portions. The lentils and chard bring **iron, folate and fibre**, and the lemon helps your body use that iron.
steps: Soften the onion in half the olive oil in a big pot over medium heat until golden, about 8 minutes.
Add the rinsed lentils and cover with plenty of water, about 4 times their volume. Bring to a boil, then simmer gently until the lentils are nearly tender, about 20 minutes.
Slice the chard stems and add them with a little salt. Cook for 5 minutes, then stir in the leaves and cook until they wilt and soften, about 5 minutes more.

Crush the garlic with a pinch of salt and the cilantro. Warm the rest of the olive oil in a small pan and fry this paste for a minute, until it smells wonderful. Stir it into the soup with the lemon juice.
Taste and add more lemon or salt until it is properly sharp and savoury. Tear the pita into pieces, toast them in a dry pan until crisp and scatter over each bowl.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. The soup thickens as it sits, so loosen it with a splash of water when you reheat it.
tip: For a creamier soup, blitz a ladleful and stir it back in.

name: Shish tawook with parsley tabbouleh and toum-style garlic sauce
inspiredBy: Lebanese shish tawook, with a lighter whipped garlic sauce in place of full toum and a tabbouleh that is mostly parsley
about: Chunks of chicken marinated in yogurt, lemon and garlic and grilled until charred at the edges, with a bright tabbouleh that is mostly parsley and a sharp, punchy garlic sauce. It makes two portions, so tomorrow's lunch is covered. The chicken brings **protein and niacin**, and all that parsley brings vitamins K and C.
steps: Stir the yogurt with a third of the garlic (mashed to a paste), a third of the lemon juice, the baharat, the black pepper and half the salt. Add the chicken and turn to coat. Marinate for at least 30 minutes and up to 6 hours in the fridge.
Cover the bulgur with hot water and leave it for 15 minutes, until tender, then drain well and squeeze out the water.
Mix the bulgur with the parsley, mint, onion, half the remaining lemon juice, half the olive oil and a pinch of salt. Keep the tomato aside and add it at serving, so the tabbouleh stays fresh.
Thread the chicken onto skewers, or spread it on a tray, and grill or broil on high, turning once or twice, until charred at the edges and cooked through, 10 to 12 minutes.

Make the garlic sauce. Pound the rest of the garlic with a pinch of salt, then slowly whisk in the rest of the olive oil and the last squeeze of lemon, a few drops at a time, until it turns thick and creamy. It is a quick toum.
Serve the chicken with the tabbouleh, the tomato, the sauce and the romaine leaves to scoop. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the tomato and sauce in separate containers.
tip: Chicken breast works too, but thighs stay juicier. If the garlic sauce splits, whisk in a teaspoon of cold water.
ingredients: boneless, skinless thighs, cut in 3 cm chunks

name: Samke harra, Lebanese spicy cilantro and walnut baked salmon with tomato bulgur
inspiredBy: Lebanese samke harra from Tripoli, with salmon in place of white fish, baked with a hot cilantro paste and topped with toasted walnuts
about: Salmon fillet rubbed with a fiery paste of cilantro, garlic, chili, cumin and lemon and baked until it flakes, with a tomato bulgur pilaf (burghul bi banadoura) and a handful of toasted walnuts on top. It is the Lebanese coast on a plate. The salmon brings **omega-3 fats and vitamin D**, and the walnuts add crunch.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C. Soften half the onion, diced, in a third of the olive oil in a small pot, about 5 minutes, without browning it. Add half the chopped tomato and cook for 3 minutes, then stir in the bulgur, add double its volume of water and a pinch of salt, cover and simmer on low for 12 minutes. Leave it covered.
Meanwhile, pound or blitz the cilantro, garlic, chili, all the cumin, half the lemon juice, half the remaining oil and a pinch of salt into a rough, spoonable paste.
Rub the paste all over the fish, pressing it in well. Set the fish on a lined tray and bake until it flakes easily with a fork, 12 to 15 minutes.
Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until they smell nutty, and chop them roughly.
Toss the rest of the tomato and the sliced onion with the rest of the lemon juice, the last of the oil and a pinch of salt.
Serve the fish on the bulgur, scattered with the walnuts, with the tomato salad on the side.
tip: Sea bass, grouper, cod or halibut make the traditional version, and trout is lovely too. Use a smaller chili or leave out the seeds if you want less heat.
ingredients: seeded if you like less heat
chopped, half for the pilaf and half for the salad
half diced for the pilaf, half sliced for the salad

name: Mujadara hamra, lentils and bulgur with caramelised onions and malfouf salad
inspiredBy: Lebanese and Palestinian mujadara hamra, the version made with bulgur
about: Brown lentils and bulgur cooked with cumin and baharat and topped with deeply browned onions, with a crunchy mint, lemon and olive oil cabbage and carrot salad on the side. It is humble, filling and very much a Levantine home dinner. The lentils and bulgur bring **iron and fibre**, the carrot brings vitamin A, and it makes two portions for tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Simmer the lentils with the cumin in plenty of water for about 15 minutes, until they are almost tender but still have some bite. Drain, keeping the cooking water.

While they cook, cook the sliced onions in two-thirds of the olive oil with a pinch of salt in a wide pan over medium-low heat, stirring often, until they are deep golden brown and sweet, 30 to 35 minutes. Most of this time is hands-off. Lift out about a third for the top.

Add the lentils, bulgur, baharat and the rest of the salt to the pan with the remaining onions. Pour in enough of the lentil water to cover by about 1 cm, bring to a simmer, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes.
Turn off the heat and leave it covered for 10 minutes so the bulgur finishes steaming, then fluff with a fork.
Make the cabbage salad, salata malfouf. Mash the garlic with a pinch of salt and toss it with the cabbage, carrot, lemon juice, mint and the rest of the olive oil.
Top the mujadara with the caramelised onions and serve with the salad. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the salad dressed fresh. It reheats well, or eat it at room temperature.
tip: Slow, patient onions are the secret. If they start to catch, add a splash of water and keep going.

name: Spicy tomato sardines on toasted pita with parsley and onion salad
inspiredBy: the chili, garlic and tomato fish dishes of the Lebanese and Palestinian coast, made with canned sardines
about: Canned sardines warmed through in a garlicky, chili-spiked tomato sauce and spooned over toasted pita, with a sharp parsley, onion and sumac salad. It is on the table in about 35 minutes. Sardines are one of the best sources of **omega-3, calcium and vitamin D**, because you eat the soft bones.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Cook the diced onion until soft, about 5 minutes, then add the garlic, chili and cumin and stir for a minute, until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes and half the salt. Simmer, pressing them down with the back of a spoon, until they collapse into a thick, jammy sauce, 12 to 15 minutes.
Nestle the sardines into the sauce, spoon some over the top and warm them gently for 3 to 4 minutes without stirring, so they stay in nice pieces.
Toss the sliced onion with the parsley, sumac, half the lemon juice and a pinch of salt. Toast the pita until crisp at the edges.
Squeeze the rest of the lemon over the sardines and serve with the pita and the parsley salad.
tip: Fresh sardines or small mackerel, seared and slipped into the sauce, are the classic version if you can find them at a fishmonger or Middle Eastern market. Use about 200 g of cleaned, butterflied fish.

name: Baked kibbeh with spiced lamb and walnut filling and tomato sumac salad
inspiredBy: Lebanese and Syrian kibbeh bil sanieh, made with lean lamb and plenty of bulgur
about: A tender layer of spiced lamb and bulgur dough over a savoury filling of onion, spiced lamb and walnuts, baked until the top is crisp and golden, with a tomato, onion and sumac salad. It is the weekend project dish. Lamb and bulgur bring **iron, zinc and B vitamins**, and it makes two portions.
steps: Rinse the bulgur, cover it with cold water and leave it for 20 minutes, then squeeze it very dry. Heat the oven to 200 C and brush a 20 cm square baking dish with a little of the oil.
Pulse the lamb cubes in a food processor, in short bursts, until finely ground. Or ask the butcher to grind lean leg of lamb twice. Set a third aside for the filling.

Make the filling. Soften half the kibbeh onion, finely chopped, in a spoonful of the oil. Add the reserved lamb and cook, breaking it up, until browned, about 5 minutes. Stir in the walnuts, a third of the baharat and a pinch of salt. Set aside to cool slightly.

Make the dough. Grate or blitz the other half of the kibbeh onion. Put the rest of the lamb, the squeezed bulgur, the grated onion, the rest of the baharat, the black pepper and the salt in the food processor and pulse in short bursts, adding a spoonful of ice water, until it is a smooth, sticky paste. Chill it for 15 minutes if it feels too soft.
With wet hands, press half the dough into the dish in a flat, even layer. Spread the filling over it, then pat the rest of the dough over the top, smoothing it to seal in the filling.
Score the top in diamonds with a wet knife, drizzle with the rest of the oil and bake until deep golden brown and crisp at the edges, 35 to 40 minutes. Rest for 10 minutes before cutting.
Meanwhile, slice the tomato and the salad onion very thinly, and toss with the parsley, sumac, lemon juice and a pinch of salt. Serve a portion with the salad.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. Reheat the kibbeh in a hot oven and make a fresh salad.
tip: Keep the dough and the knife wet, it is what makes the top smooth. Kibbeh freezes very well, baked or unbaked.
ingredients: most for the kibbeh, a little for the salad

name: Baked mackerel on collapsed eggplant with tarator
inspiredBy: the Levantine pairing of fish with tarator, the tahini and lemon sauce, served over silky roasted eggplant
about: Mackerel fillets roasted over eggplant that has collapsed into a soft, silky bed with lemon, garlic and parsley, drizzled with a creamy tahini tarator. It is bold, rich and ready in about an hour, mostly in the oven. Mackerel is one of the richest sources of **omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the tahini adds calcium.
steps: Heat the oven to 230 C. Score the cut side of the eggplant halves in a diamond pattern, brush with half the olive oil and sprinkle with half the salt and the cumin. Roast cut side down on a tray until completely soft and collapsing, about 30 minutes.
Mash half the garlic with a pinch of salt. Mix it with a third of the lemon juice and a little of the olive oil, and chop most of the parsley into it.

Turn the eggplant cut side up and scoop and mash the flesh roughly with a fork on the tray. Spoon over the dressing, tuck the tomato halves around it and lay the mackerel on top, skin side up. Brush the fish with the rest of the olive oil.
Roast for 10 to 12 minutes more, until the fish flakes easily and the skin is crisp.
Make the tarator. Stir the tahini with the rest of the garlic, the rest of the lemon juice, a pinch of salt and 3 to 4 tablespoons of cold water until pale and pourable.
Serve the fish on the eggplant, drizzled with the tarator and the rest of the parsley, with warm pita.
tip: Any oily fish works here. The roasted eggplant keeps well, so roast extra for a baba ghanoush-style spread.

name: Silky hummus with radish and cucumber sticks
about: A proper creamy hummus made from a tin of chickpeas, with plenty of tahini and lemon, served with crunchy radishes and cucumber. Make the batch once and it covers both hummus snacks, with some left for the table. The chickpeas and tahini bring **fibre, protein and calcium**.
steps: Make a batch of 4 portions: blitz 1 tin of chickpeas (about 240 g drained) with 4 tablespoons of tahini, the juice of 1 lemon, 2 cloves of garlic, a pinch of cumin, a good pinch of salt and 4 to 6 tablespoons of ice-cold water for 3 to 4 minutes, until pale and silky. Keep it in the fridge for up to 4 days.
Spoon one portion (about a quarter of the batch) into a bowl, make a well in the middle and drizzle with the olive oil. Serve with the radish and cucumber sticks.
tip: Ice-cold water and a long blitz are the secret to a smooth, pale hummus. Rubbing the skins off the chickpeas makes it even silkier.

name: Dried figs and almonds
about: Chewy dried figs and a small handful of almonds, a pairing found on every Levantine market stall. It is sweet, crunchy and easy to carry. The figs bring **calcium and fibre** and the almonds bring vitamin E.
steps: Put the figs and almonds in a small bowl or a bag and eat together.
tip: In fig season, two or three fresh figs or a bunch of grapes are lovely in place of the dried figs.

name: Pomegranate seeds with toasted almonds
about: Juicy pomegranate seeds with a small handful of toasted almonds, sweet-sour with a crunch. It is bright, cool and a little festive. The almonds bring **vitamin E and protein** and the pomegranate brings fibre and vitamin C.
steps: Tip the pomegranate seeds into a small bowl.
Scatter with the toasted almonds and eat with a spoon.
tip: Pomegranates are in season in the fall. The rest of the year, buy a tub of seeds, or use fresh figs or grapes in season.

name: Grilled halloumi, cucumber and mint in pita
about: A few slices of golden grilled halloumi tucked into warm whole-wheat pita with cool cucumber and fresh mint, the way it is eaten in Lebanon and Jordan. It is salty, chewy and fresh. The halloumi brings **calcium and protein**.
steps: Slice the halloumi and cook it in a dry non-stick pan over medium-high heat for about 1 minute per side, until golden.
Warm the pita, tuck in the halloumi, sliced cucumber and mint, and add a squeeze of lemon.

name: Pomegranate seeds with walnuts
inspiredBy: the pomegranate and walnut pairing of Levantine muhammara
about: Juicy pomegranate seeds with a handful of walnuts, sweet and sour with a crunch, like the flavours of a muhammara dip. The walnuts bring **omega-3 fats** and the pomegranate brings vitamin C and fibre.
steps: Tip the pomegranate seeds into a small bowl.
Scatter with the walnuts and eat with a spoon.

name: Pita with tahini and dried figs
inspiredBy: tahini with date or grape molasses, a Levantine breakfast sweet, made with figs
about: Warm whole-wheat pita spread with tahini and topped with chopped dried figs, nutty and sweet. It is a good, filling snack. The tahini and figs bring **calcium and copper**.
steps: Warm the pita in a dry pan or the toaster.
Spread with the tahini, scatter over the chopped figs and fold.

name: Pomegranate bowl with mint and lemon
about: Juicy pomegranate seeds with torn mint and a squeeze of lemon, sweet, sour and very refreshing. It is a light bowl after a rich meal. The pomegranate brings **vitamin C and fibre**.
steps: Tip the pomegranate seeds into a bowl.
Tear over the mint and squeeze over the lemon juice.
tip: Pomegranates are in season in the fall. The rest of the year, buy a tub of seeds.

name: Za'atar pita with olives
inspiredBy: the zeit w za'atar plate of Jordan and Lebanon
about: Warm whole-wheat pita brushed with olive oil and za'atar, with a few olives on the side. It is a simple snack from a Levantine breakfast table. The whole-wheat pita brings **fibre and B vitamins**.
steps: Stir the za'atar into the olive oil and brush it over the pita.
Warm the pita in a dry pan or a hot oven for 2 minutes and serve with the olives.

name: Dried figs stuffed with walnuts
inspiredBy: the figs and walnuts of Levantine sweet trays
about: Soft dried figs with a walnut half tucked into each one, chewy and nutty. They taste like a sweet from a Levantine tray but are made of just two ingredients. The walnuts bring **omega-3 fats** and the figs bring calcium and fibre.
steps: Snip the stems off the figs and slit each one open.
Tuck a walnut half into each fig and eat the rest of the walnuts alongside.
tip: In fig season, use fresh figs or a bunch of grapes with the walnuts.

name: Yogurt with chopped figs and toasted almonds
about: Thick, cool yogurt with chopped dried figs for sweetness and crunchy toasted almonds on top. It is creamy, a little sweet and very quick. The yogurt brings **calcium and protein**, and the figs add more calcium.
steps: Stir most of the chopped figs into the yogurt.
Spoon into a bowl and top with the rest of the figs and the almonds.

name: Pita with olives, cucumber and mint
about: Warm whole-wheat pita with crunchy cucumber, a few olives and torn mint, the kind of plate you might pick at on a Levantine afternoon. It is fresh and filling. The cucumber and mint bring **vitamin K and potassium**.
steps: Slice the cucumber and toss it with the olives, mint, olive oil and salt.
Warm the pita and eat it with the salad, tucked inside or on the side.

name: Labneh, olive and mint pita roll
inspiredBy: the labneh sandwiches of Lebanese bakeries
about: Warm whole-wheat pita spread with labneh, olive oil and chopped olives, rolled up with fresh mint. It is a quick, filling snack. The labneh brings **protein and calcium**.
steps: Warm the pita in a dry pan or the toaster.
Spread it with the labneh, drizzle with the olive oil, scatter over the olives and mint, and roll it up.

name: Moong dal chilla with fenugreek and mint chutney
inspiredBy: Punjabi and Gujarati moong dal cheela (puda), with fresh fenugreek leaves
about: Thin, savoury pancakes of ground yellow moong dal with onion, grated carrot, spinach and fresh fenugreek leaves, hot off the pan with a sharp mint and cilantro chutney. Moong dal is the classic steady-energy breakfast: **plenty of protein and fibre**, and it digests slowly.
steps: Drain the soaked dal and blend it with the ginger, half the green chili, the hing, the turmeric, half the salt and a few spoonfuls of cold water until completely smooth. The batter should pour like thin pancake batter, so add a splash more water if it is thick.
Stir in the onion, carrot, spinach, fenugreek leaves, cumin and half the cilantro.
Make the chutney: blitz the mint, the rest of the cilantro and green chili, the lemon juice, a pinch of salt and a splash of water until it is a bright, loose green sauce.

Warm a non-stick pan over medium heat and wipe it with a little of the oil. Pour in a ladle of batter and spread it gently with the back of the ladle into a round a little thicker than a crêpe. Cook until the top looks set and the underside is golden with brown spots, about 3 minutes.
Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edge, flip and cook for 1 minute more. Repeat with the rest of the batter and eat the chillas hot with the chutney.
tip: Soak the dal the night before, and mornings take about 15 minutes. Frozen methi works if fresh is hard to find. If a chilla sticks or tears, the pan is too cool or the batter too thick.
ingredients: split yellow moong dal, soaked for 4 hours or overnight
half for the batter, half for the chutney
half in the batter, half in the chutney

name: Foxtail millet vegetable upma
inspiredBy: South Indian rava upma, made with foxtail millet (thinai) and lots of vegetables
about: A soft, peppery upma with mustard seeds, curry leaves and tender, nutty chana dal, loaded with carrot and cabbage. Foxtail millet is an intact grain, so it digests more slowly than semolina, and the chana dal adds **protein and fibre**.
steps: The night before, soak the millet and the chana dal together in plenty of water. In the morning, drain them well.
Warm the oil in a pan. Add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then the drained chana dal, and stir for about 2 minutes until the dal turns golden. Add the curry leaves and hing.
Add the onion, ginger and green chili and cook until the onion is soft, about 4 minutes. Add the carrot and cabbage with a splash of water and cook for 4 minutes.

Stir in the turmeric, the salt and the drained millet and stir for a minute. Pour in boiling water, about twice the volume of the millet and dal together, cover and cook over low heat until the millet and dal are tender and the water is gone, about 15 minutes. Rest it, covered, for 5 minutes.
Fluff with a fork, squeeze over the lemon, scatter with cilantro and serve hot.
tip: Soak both the night before, and it is about 20 minutes in all. Unsoaked chana dal stays hard, so do not skip it.
ingredients: split chana dal, soaked with the millet

name: Methi besan thepla with curd
inspiredBy: Gujarati methi thepla, with extra chickpea flour for a slower, more filling bite, and sunflower seeds where many cooks use sesame
about: Soft, speckled Gujarati flatbreads with fresh fenugreek leaves, ajwain and a sprinkle of sunflower seeds, made with chickpea flour next to the whole wheat. Served with cold curd and tomato, they are a breakfast with **protein, calcium and fibre**, and they travel well too.
steps: Mix the two flours in a bowl with the ajwain (rub it between your palms first), the turmeric, Kashmiri chili, hing and sunflower seeds. Rub in about a teaspoon of the oil with your fingertips.

Add the squeezed-dry fenugreek leaves, the grated garlic, the minced green chili and a spoonful of the curd, then the salt last so the leaves do not go wet. Knead into a soft dough. The leaves let out water as you knead, so add a little more curd only if it is still dry. Then rest it, covered, for 10 minutes.
Divide the dough into balls and roll each one into a thin round, dusting with a little flour. Besan makes the dough delicate, so go gently. If it sticks, roll it between two sheets of parchment.

Heat a flat pan or tawa over medium-high heat. Cook each thepla for about a minute, flip, brush with a little oil and cook until golden with brown spots, about 1 minute more. Press the edges so it puffs a little.
Serve the theplas warm with the rest of the curd and the sliced tomato.
tip: Cook the theplas the night before and reheat them in a dry pan. Do not knead the dough ahead, as the leaves turn it soggy. Frozen methi from a South Asian grocery works when fresh is hard to find.
ingredients: fresh fenugreek leaves, picked, chopped and squeezed dry
a spoonful in the dough, the rest on the side

name: Chana chaat with sprouted moong
inspiredBy: Delhi and Lahore street chana chaat
about: A tangy, crunchy bowl of chickpeas and sprouted moong with cucumber, tomato, raw onion, cold yogurt and a squeeze of tamarind, finished with chaat masala and roasted peanuts. It is a no-cook lunch with **fibre and plant protein in every spoonful**, and the sourness is the point.
steps: Whisk the yogurt with the tamarind paste, the lemon juice and a splash of water until smooth, then stir in the chaat masala, black salt, crushed cumin and Kashmiri chili.
Tip the chickpeas into a big bowl. Mash a handful of them with the back of a spoon so the dressing clings.
Add the sprouts, cucumber, tomato, onion, green chili and cilantro. Pour over the dahi dressing and toss well.
Taste and add more lemon or chaat masala if you like it sharper. Top with the crushed peanuts just before you eat, so they stay crunchy.
tip: Dress it just before eating. Blanch store-bought sprouts for a minute, or sprout your own: soak the moong 8 hours, drain, and wait 24 to 36 hours. For a packed lunch, keep the dressing and the peanuts in a small jar.

name: Chicken do pyaza with a roti and cucumber salad
inspiredBy: Punjabi and Pakistani chicken do pyaza, "two onions"
about: Tender chicken thighs in a thick black pepper and ginger gravy, with the onions added twice, once cooked soft and once left with a little bite, served with one fresh roti and a crisp cucumber and onion salad. It is mostly **protein and vegetables**, which keeps the plate steady, and it is just as good cold.
steps: Warm the oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds for 15 seconds, then the chopped onion for the gravy and cook, stirring, until deep golden, about 9 minutes.

Add the ginger, garlic and green chili and stir for 1 minute. Stir in the turmeric, the crushed coriander, the Kashmiri chili and the black pepper, then the chopped tomato, and cook until it breaks down into a thick paste, about 5 minutes.

Add the chicken and the salt and stir over medium-high heat for 5 minutes until it turns opaque. Add a splash of water, cover and cook for 10 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through and the gravy clings to it.
Stir in the onion wedges and the garam masala and cook uncovered for 3 minutes, so the onions soften but keep a little bite. Finish with half the cilantro.

Knead the atta with a little water into a soft dough, rest it 15 minutes and roll it into one thin round. On the lighter sizes it is a small roti, about the size of your palm, and that is plenty next to everything else on the plate. Cook it on a hot dry pan until it puffs and has brown spots on both sides.
Toss the cucumber and the sliced onion with the lemon juice, the rest of the cilantro and a pinch of salt, and eat the salad first, then the chicken with the roti.
tip: Cook it the night before and reheat it for lunch. It keeps 3 days, so a double batch on Sunday covers two lunches. If you want it milder, use half the black pepper. Knead dough for four rotis at once and keep it in the fridge for 2 days, or use a frozen whole-wheat roti from the South Asian grocer.
ingredients: skinless thighs, cut in bite-size pieces
90 g chopped for the gravy, 35 g in wedges added at the end, the rest sliced for the salad

name: Lauki chana dal with a roti and onion salad
inspiredBy: Punjabi and Gujarati dudhi chana dal
about: Split chickpeas cooked soft with tender bottle gourd in a garlicky cumin tadka, with one fresh whole-wheat roti and an onion and lemon salad. Chana dal is one of the **lowest glycaemic dals** there is, and the lauki makes it light and sweet.
steps: Soak the dal in plenty of water for 1 hour, then drain. Put it in a pot with the tomato, chopped onion, ginger, turmeric, salt and plenty of water, about three times the volume of dal. Simmer partly covered until the dal is nearly soft, about 25 minutes, then add the lauki and cook for 15 minutes more, until both are completely soft.

While the dal cooks, knead the atta with a little water into a soft dough and rest it for 15 minutes. Roll it into one thin round. On the lighter sizes it is a small roti, about the size of your palm, and that is plenty next to everything else on the plate.
Mash the dal lightly with a spoon so it turns creamy, and add hot water if it is too thick. Stir in the garam masala and amchur.

Warm the ghee in a small pan. Add the cumin seeds, then the hing and the sliced garlic, and cook until the garlic is golden, about 1 minute. Take the pan off the heat, stir in the Kashmiri chili and pour the tadka over the dal.

Cook the roti on a hot dry pan until it puffs and has brown spots on both sides. Toss the sliced onion with the lemon juice, the green chili, the cilantro and a pinch of salt, and serve with the dal and roti.
tip: The dal freezes well, so cook a double batch and keep half for another night. Knead dough for four rotis at once and keep it in the fridge for 2 days, or use a frozen whole-wheat roti from the South Asian grocer.
ingredients: split chana dal, soaked for 1 hour
peeled and cut in small cubes
30 g chopped, the rest sliced for the salad

name: Rajma masala with brown basmati and onion-tomato salad
inspiredBy: Punjabi rajma chawal, with the beans taking the lead and a small rice portion
about: Red kidney beans in a thick, gingery onion and tomato gravy, spooned beside a little brown basmati and a sharp onion and tomato salad. The beans carry **iron, folate and slow carbohydrate**, and the salad comes first so you start with the crunch.
steps: Use the Sunday brown basmati: boil about 100 g raw in plenty of water for 25 minutes, drain, cool and keep it up to 4 days in the fridge, freezing a portion for later in the week. Warm your portion with a splash of water. On the lighter sizes it is just a spoonful or two, and that is the idea.
Warm the oil in a pan over medium heat. Add the bay leaf and cumin seeds and let them sizzle for 15 seconds, then add the chopped onion and cook until deep golden, about 8 minutes.

Add the ginger and garlic and stir for 1 minute. Stir in the crushed coriander, turmeric and Kashmiri chili, then the tomato for the gravy, and cook, pressing with the spoon, until it becomes a thick jammy paste that leaves oil at the edges, about 6 minutes.

Add the kidney beans, the salt and about a cup of water. Simmer for 15 minutes, mashing a few beans against the side of the pan so the gravy thickens. Stir in the garam masala and the kasuri methi (crush it between your fingers).
Toss the sliced onion and the rest of the tomato, diced, with the lemon juice, cilantro and a pinch of salt for the salad.
Serve the rajma with the rice, with the salad to eat first. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, and keep the salad separate so it stays crisp.
tip: The rajma freezes well. Warm the Sunday rice while the beans simmer and both are ready together.
ingredients: 60 g chopped for the gravy, the rest sliced for the salad
100 g for the gravy, the rest for the salad

name: Kerala-style mackerel curry with cabbage and carrot thoran and brown basmati
inspiredBy: Kerala ayala (mackerel) curry, soured with tamarind in place of kudampuli, and cabbage and carrot thoran
about: Mackerel simmered in a tangy red tamarind gravy with ginger, green chili and curry leaves, with a quick cabbage and carrot thoran dressed in fresh coconut and a spoonful or two of brown basmati. The mackerel brings **omega-3 and B12**, and the thoran is your fresh, crunchy vegetable.
steps: Use the Sunday brown basmati: boil about 100 g raw in plenty of water for 25 minutes, drain, cool and keep it up to 4 days in the fridge, freezing a portion for later in the week. Warm your portion with a splash of water. On the lighter sizes it is just a spoonful or two, and that is the idea.

Warm half the oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Add the fenugreek seeds for 10 seconds, then the onion, ginger, most of the garlic, half the green chili and half the curry leaves. Cook until the onion is soft and just golden, about 6 minutes.

Stir in most of the turmeric and the Kashmiri chili for 30 seconds, then the tomato, and cook until it breaks down, about 4 minutes. Add the tamarind, the salt and about half a cup of water and simmer for 5 minutes.

Slide the fish into the gravy, spoon some of it over the top and simmer gently, partly covered, until the fish is just cooked through, about 8 minutes. Swirl the pan rather than stirring so the fish stays whole.

Make the thoran while the fish simmers. Warm the rest of the oil in a second pan, pop the mustard seeds, then add the rest of the curry leaves, the cabbage and carrot, a pinch of salt and the pepper. Cook, stirring, until the vegetables are tender but still have a bite, about 5 minutes. Crush the coconut with the rest of the green chili and garlic and the last pinch of turmeric, and stir it in at the end.
Serve the fish curry with the rice and the thoran, starting with the thoran. Eat this one fresh rather than saving it for tomorrow.
tip: Coconut oil is the traditional Kerala cooking fat, but canola keeps the saturated fat lower here. Sardines or kingfish work too.
ingredients: cleaned, cut into steaks or fillets
for the thoran; fresh grated, or unsweetened desiccated

name: Gujarati-style tuvar dal with spinach, bhindi and a roti
inspiredBy: the Gujarati dal, rotli and shaak plate, with tamarind for the sweet-sour and no sugar or jaggery
about: A thin, sweet-sour Gujarati tuvar dal with cloves, cinnamon and a sizzling ghee tadka, a dry okra sabzi, and one fresh roti. The dal is the big part of the plate, so it brings **plenty of protein and fibre** along with its slow carbohydrate.
steps: Rinse the dal and cook it with the tomato, most of the turmeric and plenty of water, about three times the volume of dal, until completely soft, about 40 minutes, or 12 minutes in a pressure cooker. Whisk it smooth.

Add the tamarind, the ginger, half the green chili, the clove, cinnamon, salt and the spinach, with enough hot water to make it pourable like thin soup. Simmer for 10 minutes, until the spinach has melted in.

Make the bhindi: warm the canola in a wide pan over medium-high heat, add the okra in two batches so it browns instead of steaming, and cook, stirring only now and then, until it is browned and no longer sticky, about 8 minutes in all. Add the crushed coriander, the last pinch of turmeric, a pinch of the cumin and a pinch of salt.

Knead the atta with a little water into a soft dough and rest it for 15 minutes. Roll a thin round for each portion (a small, palm-sized one on the lighter sizes) and cook on a hot dry pan until it puffs and has brown spots.

Warm the ghee in a small pan. Add the cumin and mustard seeds and let them pop, then the garlic, hing, curry leaves and the rest of the green chili. Take the pan off the heat, stir in the Kashmiri chili and pour the tadka over the dal. Stir in the cilantro.
Serve the dal with the bhindi and a roti each. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, and warm the roti in a dry pan or wrapped in foil.
tip: An Instant Pot or pressure cooker gets the dal done in about 12 minutes. Soak the dal for 30 minutes and it takes about 25 in an open pot. Kokum is the traditional souring agent if you have it. Knead dough for four rotis at once and keep it in the fridge for 2 days, or use a frozen whole-wheat roti from the South Asian grocer.
ingredients: washed, dried well and cut in rounds

name: Tandoori chicken tray with roasted chickpeas, kachumber and mint raita
inspiredBy: Punjabi tandoori chicken, baked on a tray at home
about: Chicken thighs marinated in yogurt and Kashmiri chili, roasted on one tray with cauliflower, carrot, onion and chickpeas until the edges char, with a cooling mint raita and a tomato and onion kachumber. The chickpeas and vegetables give **protein, fibre and crunch** next to the chicken, with one roti for the starch.
steps: Make the marinade: stir the marinating yogurt with the grated ginger and garlic, half the lemon juice, the Kashmiri chili, garam masala, cumin, coriander, turmeric, kasuri methi (crushed between your fingers), about half a teaspoon of the oil and the salt. Coat the chicken and leave it for at least 30 minutes, or overnight in the fridge.

Heat the oven to 230°C (450°F) and line a big tray. Toss the chickpeas with a little of the oil and a pinch of salt and roast them alone for 10 minutes while the oven finishes heating and the chicken sits.

Toss the cauliflower, carrot and onion wedges with the rest of the oil and a pinch of salt, add them to the tray with the chickpeas and nestle the chicken on top. Roast for 25 to 30 minutes, turning the chicken once, until it is charred at the edges and cooked through, and the chickpeas are crisp.

Make the raita: stir the chopped mint and a pinch of salt into the remaining yogurt. Toss the tomato and the rest of the onion, finely chopped, with the remaining lemon juice and the chaat masala for the kachumber.

Knead the atta with a little water into a soft dough, rest it 15 minutes and roll it into one thin round. On the lighter sizes it is a small roti, about the size of your palm, and that is plenty next to everything else on the plate. Cook it on a hot dry pan until it puffs and has brown spots.

Toast the almonds in a dry pan and scatter them over the tray. Serve the chicken tray with the kachumber first, then the raita and the roti. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the raita and kachumber in separate containers.
tip: Marinate it in the morning if you can; even 15 minutes helps. Reheat the leftover tray for 8 minutes at 200°C so the edges crisp again. Knead dough for four rotis at once and keep it in the fridge for 2 days, or use a frozen whole-wheat roti from the South Asian grocer.
ingredients: skinless thighs, cut in big chunks
about 3 tablespoons for the marinade, the rest for the raita
55 g in wedges for the tray, the rest for the kachumber
toasted and chopped, for the top

name: Pepper and tamarind salmon with parippu and spinach mallung
inspiredBy: Sri Lankan ambul thiyal (sour fish curry, usually tuna), with parippu and a mallung
about: Salmon rubbed with black pepper and tamarind and cooked until sticky, with a creamy red lentil parippu, a spinach mallung and a spoonful or two of brown basmati. It is a Sri Lankan rice-and-curry plate where the lentils and greens take up most of the room, and the salmon brings **omega-3 and vitamin D**.
steps: Use the brown basmati you froze on Sunday, thawed overnight in the fridge, and warm your portion with a splash of water. Cooking this on its own? Boil about 100 g raw in plenty of water for 25 minutes, drain, and keep the rest up to 4 days

Make the parippu: put the lentils in a pot with half the turmeric, the cinnamon, the cardamom, half the garlic, half the onion and plenty of water. Simmer until the lentils collapse into a creamy dal, about 18 minutes. Stir in half the coconut and half the salt. Finish the parippu with a quick tempering: pop a few of the mustard seeds and a few curry leaves in about half a teaspoon of the oil and stir it in.
Mix the black pepper, half the turmeric, the tamarind, the ginger, the lemon juice and a pinch of salt into a paste and rub it over the salmon.
Warm half of the remaining oil in a non-stick pan over medium heat. Cook the salmon for 3 to 4 minutes per side, spooning over any paste left in the bowl, until it is sticky and just cooked through.

Make the mallung: in a second pan, warm the last of the oil, pop the rest of the mustard seeds, then add the rest of the curry leaves, the Kashmiri chili, the rest of the garlic and onion and the green chili. Add the spinach and a splash of water, cook for 2 to 3 minutes until wilted, then stir in the rest of the coconut and a pinch of salt.
Serve the salmon with the parippu, the mallung and the rice, starting with the greens. Eat this one fresh rather than saving it for tomorrow.
tip: Ambul thiyal cooks dry in a clay pot with tuna and goraka (a sour fruit), so this is a quicker pan version with tamarind. Mackerel works as well as salmon.
ingredients: skinless fillet, in two or three pieces
half for the parippu, half for the mallung; fresh grated, or unsweetened desiccated
30 g for the parippu, 30 g for the mallung

name: Barley haleem with goat and dals
inspiredBy: Pakistani and Hyderabadi haleem, with barley doing most of the wheat's job
about: The slow, rich Pakistani stew of tender goat, barley and lentils beaten smooth and finished with fried onions, ginger, lemon and fresh herbs, with a crisp cucumber and onion salad. Barley digests slowly, and together with the dals it makes a pot **full of fibre and protein**.
steps: Soak the barley and the dals in plenty of water for at least 4 hours or overnight, then drain.

Warm the canola in a heavy pot over medium heat. Fry the thinly sliced onion, stirring often, until it is deep golden brown and crisp at the edges, about 12 minutes. Lift out about two thirds and keep it for the top.

Add the chopped onion to the pot with the bay leaf, cumin, clove and cinnamon and cook for 4 minutes. Add the grated ginger, the garlic and the goat, and brown the meat for about 5 minutes. Stir in the turmeric, Kashmiri chili, coriander, black pepper and salt.
Add plenty of water to cover and simmer the goat, partly covered, until it is very tender, about 1 hour 15 minutes, or 30 minutes in a pressure cooker.
Add the drained barley and dals and more hot water, and cook gently, stirring now and then, until everything is falling apart, about 45 minutes, or 25 minutes in a pressure cooker.

Pick out any bones and the bay leaf. Beat the haleem hard with a wooden spoon, or give it a few pulses with a hand blender, until the meat shreds and it turns thick and stretchy. Stir in the garam masala and the ghee.

Toss the cucumber with the onion you kept for the salad, thinly sliced, a squeeze of the lemon and a pinch of salt. Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden. Serve the haleem topped with the fried onions, the almonds, the ginger strips, the rest of the lemon juice, the green chili and the cilantro, with the salad to eat first.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. Haleem keeps for 4 days in the fridge and freezes well.
tip: Make a double batch in a pressure cooker, which cuts the cooking to about an hour, and freeze two portions. Boneless lamb or beef works in place of goat.
ingredients: bone-in or boneless goat stewing meat, cut in chunks
35 g sliced thinly for frying, 20 g for the salad, the rest chopped
half grated, half cut in thin strips to serve

name: Palak paneer with a roti and cucumber-onion salad
inspiredBy: Punjabi palak paneer
about: Soft cubes of paneer in a smooth, garlicky spinach gravy with ginger and garam masala, with one fresh whole-wheat roti and a cucumber and onion salad. The spinach brings **folate and vitamin A**, and the paneer and yogurt are the protein.
steps: Boil a pot of water, drop in the spinach and push it under for 1 minute, then drain and rinse under cold water so it stays bright green. Squeeze it lightly and blend with the green chili to a smooth purée.
Warm the oil in a pan over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds, then the onion for the gravy and cook until golden, about 7 minutes. Add the ginger and garlic and stir for 1 minute.
Stir in the turmeric, the crushed coriander and the Kashmiri chili, then the chopped tomato, and cook until it breaks down into a thick paste, about 5 minutes.

Pour in the spinach purée with a splash of water and simmer for 5 minutes. Add the paneer, the salt and the garam masala, crush the kasuri methi in over the top and simmer for 3 minutes more. Take the pan off the heat and stir in the yogurt.

Knead the atta with a little water into a soft dough, rest it 15 minutes and roll it into one thin round. On the lighter sizes it is a small roti, about the size of your palm, and that is plenty next to everything else on the plate. Cook it on a hot dry pan until it puffs and has brown spots on both sides.
Toss the cucumber and the sliced onion with the lemon juice and a pinch of salt, and serve with the palak paneer and the roti, eating the salad first.
tip: Firm tofu cubes are a good swap for the paneer, and they take on the gravy just as well. Knead dough for four rotis at once and keep it in the fridge for 2 days, or use a frozen whole-wheat roti from the South Asian grocer.
ingredients: 55 g for the gravy, the rest sliced for the salad

name: Guava chaat with almonds
inspiredBy: Pakistani and Punjabi roadside fruit chaat
about: Ripe guava chunks tossed with lemon and chaat masala, with a small handful of almonds for crunch. Guava is one of the **highest-fibre fruits**, and the almonds bring protein and healthy fat, so the fruit never comes on its own.
steps: Toss the guava with the lemon juice, chaat masala and black salt, and eat it with the almonds.
ingredients: cut in chunks, seeds and all

name: Oven-roasted masala chickpeas
inspiredBy: Indian roasted chana, made from canned chickpeas
about: Crunchy chickpeas roasted with chaat masala, amchur and a little Kashmiri chili. A **protein and fibre snack** you can keep in a jar for a day or two.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Pat the chickpeas completely dry with a towel, since dry chickpeas get crunchy.
Toss them with the oil, chaat masala, amchur, Kashmiri chili and salt, spread them on a tray and roast for 25 to 30 minutes, shaking the tray halfway, until crisp.
Squeeze over the lemon juice and eat warm.
tip: Roast a double batch and keep half in a jar for another day. Once cooled, they stay crunchy for a day or two.

name: Chickpea sundal
inspiredBy: Tamil sundal
about: Tamil temple-style chickpeas with mustard seeds, curry leaves and a bit of raw onion. Warm, savoury and full of **plant protein and fibre**.
steps: Warm the oil in a pan. Pop the mustard seeds, then add the Kashmiri chili, curry leaves, hing and chopped green chili for 20 seconds.
Add the chickpeas and the salt and toss for 3 minutes until hot. Stir in the onion and finish with the lemon juice.

name: Cucumber and mint raita
inspiredBy: North Indian and Pakistani raita
about: Cold yogurt with grated cucumber, mint and roasted cumin, with a pinch of black salt. **High in protein and calcium**, it is a snack you eat with a spoon.
steps: Loosen the yogurt with a splash of water, then stir in the grated cucumber, mint, crushed cumin and black salt.
ingredients: thinned with a splash of water

name: Sprouted moong kosambari
inspiredBy: Karnataka kosambari
about: A Karnataka salad of sprouted moong with carrot, tomato, a little coconut and lemon, tempered with mustard seeds. Crunchy, light and a good **hit of protein and fibre** for very few calories.
steps: Toss the sprouts, carrot, tomato, coconut, cilantro and green chili in a bowl.
Warm the oil in a small pan, pop the mustard seeds, and pour it over the salad with the lemon juice and the salt. Toss and eat right away.

name: Masala peanuts
inspiredBy: Indian and Pakistani masala peanuts
about: Warm roasted peanuts tossed with chopped onion, tomato, green chili, lemon and chaat masala, as sold at every Pakistani and Indian street corner. A small bowl gives you **protein and healthy fats** with some freshness on top.
steps: Toss the peanuts with the onion, tomato, cilantro and green chili, then add the lemon juice, chaat masala and salt. Eat it right away so the peanuts stay crunchy.

name: Masala boiled egg with carrot sticks
inspiredBy: Indian masala egg
about: A hard-boiled egg with chaat masala, black pepper and lemon, with crunchy carrot sticks on the side. Small, quick and **a good source of choline**.
steps: Lower the egg into boiling water and cook for 9 minutes. Cool it in cold water, peel and halve.
Sprinkle the egg with the chaat masala, pepper, salt and lemon juice and eat it with the carrot sticks.
tip: Boil a few eggs on Sunday and keep them in their shells in the fridge for the week.

name: Egg chaat
inspiredBy: Pakistani and Delhi anda chaat
about: A boiled egg chopped with raw onion, tomato, cilantro and green chili, with lemon and chaat masala, the way it is sold from street carts in Pakistan and Delhi. Small, sharp and a good source of **choline and protein**.
steps: Lower the egg into boiling water and cook for 9 minutes. Cool it in cold water, peel and chop it roughly.
Toss the egg with the onion, tomato, cilantro and green chili, then add the lemon juice, chaat masala, pepper and salt and eat it right away.
tip: Use one of the Sunday eggs and it is ready in 5 minutes, or boil one while you chop.

name: Toor dal rasam in a mug
inspiredBy: Tamil milagu rasam
about: A thin, peppery South Indian rasam with a spoon of toor dal, tomato, garlic and curry leaves, sipped warm. It gives you **a little protein and fibre** and a lot of flavour.
steps: Simmer the dal with plenty of water until very soft, about 30 minutes (12 in a pressure cooker), and whisk it smooth.
Add the tomato, garlic, tamarind, rasam powder, pepper, salt and a cup of water and simmer for 10 minutes.
Warm the oil in a small pan, pop the mustard seeds and curry leaves, pour it in and finish with cilantro. Sip it hot.
tip: Make a double batch on Sunday and keep it in the fridge for 3 days; reheat a mug at a time.

name: Haldi doodh with cardamom and almonds
inspiredBy: Indian haldi doodh (turmeric milk)
about: Warm milk simmered with turmeric, black pepper and cardamom, with finely crushed almonds on top and no sugar. A glass gives you **calcium, protein and B12**, and it is a lovely way to end a day.
steps: Stir the turmeric into a splash of the cold milk until no lumps are left, then pour it into a small pot with the rest of the milk, the pepper and the cardamom. Warm, stirring, until it just starts to steam, about 5 minutes. Do not let it boil over.
Crush the almonds very fine, pour the milk into a mug and stir them in.
tip: No sugar is needed, but a pinch of cinnamon makes it taste sweeter.

name: Moong dal shorba in a mug
inspiredBy: Pakistani and Punjabi dal shorba
about: A light, lemony moong dal soup with ginger, garlic and cumin, sipped warm. Moong cooks to a soft, silky soup and gives you **plant protein and fibre** in a mug.
steps: Rinse the dal and simmer it with the tomato, half the ginger, the turmeric and plenty of water until completely soft, about 20 minutes. Whisk it smooth.
Warm the oil in a small pan and cook the cumin, the rest of the ginger and the garlic until fragrant, about 1 minute. Stir it into the soup with the pepper and the salt.
Finish with the lemon juice and cilantro and sip it hot.
tip: It keeps for 3 days in the fridge. Add a splash of water when you reheat it.

name: Paneer tikka bites with mint
inspiredBy: Punjabi paneer tikka
about: Cubes of paneer rubbed with Kashmiri chili, ajwain and lemon and roasted until the edges are golden, with fresh mint. A small, **high-protein** snack that holds its shape.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the paneer cubes with the oil, Kashmiri chili, ajwain, half the lemon juice and the salt.
Roast on a tray for 10 to 12 minutes, turning once, until golden at the edges.
Toss with the mint, the chopped green chili, the chaat masala and the rest of the lemon juice, and eat them warm.

name: Chakchouka with green pepper, harissa and two eggs
inspiredBy: Chakchouka, the Algerian and Tunisian cousin of shakshuka
about: Eggs poached in a thick, spicy sauce of tomato, green pepper, harissa and caraway, with warm khobz for scooping. It is the everyday breakfast across Algeria and Tunisia. The eggs add **protein and choline**, and the tomato and pepper bring vitamin C.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Cook the onion and green pepper until soft and just turning golden, about 8 minutes.
Stir in the garlic, harissa, cumin, paprika and caraway for a minute, until it smells toasty. Add the crushed tomato and the salt.
Simmer for 8 minutes, stirring now and then, until the sauce is thick and jammy.
Make two wells with the back of a spoon and crack an egg into each. Cover and cook for 4 to 5 minutes, until the whites are set and the yolks are still soft.
Scatter with the cilantro. Warm the pita in a dry pan and tear it up for scooping.
tip: Make the sauce the night before. In the morning, reheat it and crack in the eggs, which takes about 8 minutes.

name: Bissara with olive oil, cumin and olives
inspiredBy: Moroccan bissara, made in a pot of two so the second breakfast is already waiting
about: A thick, silky Moroccan fava bean soup, served warm with a pool of olive oil, cumin and paprika and a few olives, with khobz for dunking. It is the street breakfast of Marrakech and Fes. The fava beans bring **fibre, folate and iron**.
steps: The evening before, while another pot is simmering, rinse the dried fava beans and put them in a pot with the garlic and plenty of water, about 4 times their volume for the two portions. Use split, peeled fava, which cook in about 40 minutes. Whole ones need an overnight soak, peeling and about 1½ hours.
Simmer gently for about 40 minutes, until the beans fall apart when pressed, adding hot water if they get dry.
Blitz with a stick blender or mash well until thick and silky. Stir in half the cumin and the salt, and thin with hot water to a soupy hummus.
Ladle one portion into a bowl, make a pool in the middle for the olive oil, then dust with the paprika and the rest of the cumin and add the olives.
Warm the pita and use it to dunk. Chill the second portion, and reheat it with a splash of water when you want it.
tip: A tin of fava beans in a hurry works too. Blitz about 400 g of beans and their liquid with the garlic and cumin, and heat it through for 8 minutes.
ingredients: dried, split and peeled if you can find them

name: Cinnamon oat porridge with dates, orange, almonds and walnuts
inspiredBy: Inspired by the warm, milky cereals of the Maghreb, made here with oats
about: Creamy oats cooked in milk with cinnamon and a whisper of orange blossom water, sweetened by soft dates and topped with orange segments and a toasted almond and walnut crunch. The milk and nuts bring **calcium, vitamin E and plant omega-3**.
steps: Toast the almonds and walnuts in a dry pan over medium heat until golden and fragrant, about 3 minutes. Tip them out so they do not burn.
Put the oats, milk, cinnamon and salt in a small pot over medium heat. Stir often for 6 to 7 minutes, until thick and creamy.
Stir in the dates and the orange blossom water and let the dates soften for a minute.
Spoon into a bowl and top with the orange and the toasted nuts.
tip: A spoonful of honey is lovely on top if your dates are not very sweet. Toast a handful of almonds and walnuts the Sunday before so they are ready all week.

name: Whole-wheat msemen-style flatbread with fried eggs, olives and tomato
inspiredBy: Moroccan msemen, made with whole-wheat flour and a quicker fold
about: A flaky, pan-cooked flatbread folded around a little olive oil, served with two fried eggs, olives and juicy tomato. It is the slow weekend breakfast of Moroccan homes, in a whole-wheat version. The eggs and whole grain bring **protein, choline and fibre**.
steps: Mix the flour and half the salt with about 60 ml warm water and a teaspoon of the olive oil. Knead for 8 minutes, until smooth and soft, then cover and rest for 30 minutes.

Divide the dough into 2 balls. Oil your counter and your hands, then stretch each ball into a thin sheet about the size of a saucer. It may tear in places, so just patch the holes with a pinch of dough.
Brush each sheet with olive oil and fold it into a small square, like an envelope. Press it flat with your palm.
Cook each square in a dry non-stick pan over medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes a side, until golden with flaky layers.
Wipe the pan, add a little oil and fry the eggs with the cumin and a pinch of salt until the whites are set.
Serve the msemen with the eggs, olives, tomato and cilantro. Tear and scoop.
tip: Real msemen is made with white flour, semolina and butter. This version keeps the folded, flaky idea with whole-wheat flour. Skip the eggs and drizzle honey for a sweet version.
ingredients: part in the dough, part for folding and the pan

name: Moroccan carrot and orange salad with tinned mackerel on khobz
inspiredBy: Moroccan carrot and orange salad, with the tinned mackerel that North African cooks love on bread
about: Sweet grated carrot and juicy orange dressed with lemon, cinnamon and a touch of orange blossom water, with a lemony mash of tinned mackerel spread on warm khobz. Sunny, crunchy and quick. The carrot and orange bring **vitamin A and vitamin C**, and the mackerel brings **omega-3 and vitamin D**.
steps: Whisk half the lemon juice with the olive oil, cinnamon, orange blossom water and the salt in a large bowl.
Add the grated carrot, orange pieces, olives and half the parsley and toss well.
In a small bowl, mash the mackerel with the rest of the lemon juice, the cumin, the grated onion and the rest of the parsley.
Warm the pita, spread it with the mackerel, and serve it with the salad.
tip: The salad keeps well for a day, so pack it for the office and keep the mackerel and pita separate.

name: Slata mechouia with tuna, egg and olives
inspiredBy: Tunisian slata mechouia. Tuna and egg are the traditional toppings
about: Peppers and tomatoes charred until sweet and smoky, chopped with garlic, caraway, harissa and lemon, then topped with tuna, a boiled egg and olives. It is the Tunisian salad you find on every table, served with bread. The peppers and tomato bring **vitamin C**, and the tuna and egg bring protein.
steps: Heat your oven grill (broiler) to high. Lay the peppers and tomatoes on a tray and char them, turning now and then, until the skins blacken and blister, about 15 to 20 minutes.
Meanwhile, lower the egg into boiling water and cook for 9 minutes, then cool under cold water and peel.
Pop the peppers in a bowl, cover, and leave for 10 minutes so the skins loosen. Peel off the skins and the tomato skins, and pull out the pepper seeds.
Chop the peppers and tomatoes roughly with a knife until it is a chunky, juicy mash.
Mash the garlic with the salt and stir it in with the harissa, caraway, lemon juice and olive oil.
Spoon onto a plate, then top with the tuna, the halved egg, olives and parsley. Warm the pita and scoop.
tip: Char the peppers and tomatoes the night before while the oven is already hot from dinner. Keep them in the fridge and dress them at lunch.

name: Sardine kefta in khobz with warm zaalouk
inspiredBy: Moroccan sardine balls (boulettes de sardines) simmered with zaalouk, shaped as patties for a quicker lunch
about: Little patties of tinned sardines, parsley, cilantro and cumin, seared briefly and finished in a silky, garlicky zaalouk of eggplant and tomato, then tucked into warm khobz. Sardines with their soft bones bring **calcium, omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the eggplant brings fibre and potassium.
steps: Put the eggplant, crushed tomato, garlic, half the olive oil, half the cumin, half the paprika and half the salt in a pan with a splash of water. Cover and simmer for 20 to 25 minutes, until the eggplant is completely soft.
Mash the zaalouk with a fork until chunky. Stir in half the lemon juice and half the cilantro.
Mash the sardines in a bowl with the onion, parsley, the rest of the cilantro, cumin, paprika, lemon juice and salt, and the flour. Chill for 15 minutes, then shape into 4 small patties.
Sear the patties in the rest of the olive oil over medium heat for 2 minutes a side, until golden. Turn them gently, since they are soft.
Slide the patties into the warm zaalouk and simmer for 3 minutes so they take on the sauce.
Warm the pita and open it. Fill it with the sardine kefta and the zaalouk.
tip: Make the zaalouk on Friday night while the mackerel roasts. On Saturday, mix, sear and warm the kefta through the zaalouk in about 20 minutes.

name: Moroccan chicken tagine with apricots, almonds and chickpeas
inspiredBy: Moroccan chicken tagine with apricots, with chickpeas and pumpkin added for more fibre and vitamin A
about: Tender chicken thigh simmered with onion, saffron, ginger, cinnamon and ras el hanout, with sweet dried apricots, chickpeas and golden pumpkin, and crunchy toasted almonds on top. A lemon squeeze at the end keeps it bright. The chicken and chickpeas bring **protein and iron**, and the pumpkin and apricots bring **vitamin A**.
steps: Rub the chicken with the ras el hanout, ginger, pepper, half the cinnamon and the salt. Brown it in the olive oil in a wide, heavy pot over medium-high heat, about 5 minutes. Lift it out.
Crush the saffron into 2 tablespoons of warm water. Soften the onion in the same pot until golden, about 8 minutes.
Return the chicken with the chickpeas, apricots, the saffron water, the rest of the cinnamon and about 250 ml of water. Cover and simmer gently for 15 minutes.
Add the pumpkin and simmer, partly covered, for another 20 minutes, until the pumpkin is tender and the sauce is thick and glossy.
Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes.
Stir the lemon juice and half the cilantro into the tagine. Scatter with the almonds and the rest of the cilantro and serve with warm khobz. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: No tagine pot needed. A heavy pot with a tight lid does the same job.
ingredients: in big chunks, butternut or kabocha squash works

name: Harira with lentils, chickpeas and tomato
inspiredBy: Moroccan harira, vegetarian, with mashed lentils instead of the flour thickener
about: The thick, fragrant Moroccan soup, with lentils, chickpeas, tomato and celery, scented with cinnamon and pepper and thickened with beaten egg, then finished with lots of cilantro and parsley and a squeeze of lemon. It is hearty enough for dinner. The lentils and chickpeas bring **iron, folate and fibre**, and the lemon helps your body absorb the iron.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a large pot over medium heat. Cook the onion and celery until soft, about 8 minutes.
Stir in the turmeric, ginger, cinnamon and pepper, then add the crushed tomato, the lentils, the salt and 1 litre of water for the two portions.
Bring to a boil, then simmer gently for 25 minutes, until the lentils are soft.
Add the chickpeas and simmer for 15 more minutes. Mash a ladleful against the side of the pot to thicken the soup.
Turn the heat to low. Pour in the 2 beaten eggs in a thin stream, stirring, so they set in silky threads. Stir in the cilantro, the parsley and the lemon juice, and add salt if it needs it.
Serve with warm khobz. Cool the second portion and keep it in the fridge for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Many Moroccan cooks add a few cubes of lamb too. Harira is traditionally the soup that breaks the fast in Ramadan, eaten with dates.
ingredients: 2 eggs for the pot of two, beaten

name: Chermoula sardines roasted over potatoes and carrots
inspiredBy: Moroccan sardines mchermla, roasted rather than fried, with chermoula carrots alongside
about: Fresh sardines rubbed with chermoula, the garlicky cilantro, cumin and preserved lemon paste of Morocco, then roasted on a tray over potato, carrot and tomato. A sizzling tray, ready in about 45 minutes, mostly in the oven. Sardines bring **omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the carrot brings vitamin A.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the potato slices and carrot sticks with half the olive oil and half the salt on a large baking tray. Roast for 15 minutes.

Meanwhile, make the chermoula. Mash the garlic with the rest of the salt, then chop or blitz it with the cilantro, parsley, cumin, paprika, preserved lemon rind, lemon juice and the rest of the olive oil.
Rub most of the chermoula over the sardines, inside and out, keeping a spoonful for the vegetables.
Toss the spoonful of chermoula through the vegetables, add the tomato slices, nestle the sardines on top, and roast for 10 to 12 minutes, until the skin is blistered and the flesh flakes easily.
Scatter with the olives and serve from the tray.
tip: Ask the fishmonger for sardines scaled and gutted, with the heads on. Frozen ones work well once thawed. Open a window, since sardines are fragrant. Mackerel works too.

name: Algerian-style couscous with beef, chickpeas and vegetables
inspiredBy: Inspired by Algerian couscous with meat and vegetables, with whole-wheat couscous and more vegetables
about: Fluffy whole-wheat couscous under a fragrant stew of tender beef, carrot, zucchini and chickpeas, with a dab of harissa on the side. It is the Friday-table dish of Algeria, built with extra vegetables. The chickpeas and vegetables bring **fibre and vitamin A**, and the beef brings iron and zinc.
steps: Heat most of the olive oil in a large pot and brown the beef in batches, about 5 minutes. Lift it out.
Soften the onion in the same pot for 6 minutes. Stir in the cinnamon, pepper and ras el hanout until fragrant.
Return the beef with the crushed tomato, the salt and 600 ml of water for the two portions. Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer gently for 45 minutes.
Add the carrots and chickpeas and simmer for 15 minutes, then add the zucchini and simmer for 10 more minutes, until the beef is tender and everything is soft.

While it simmers, put the dry whole-wheat couscous for both portions in a bowl and pour over about 1¼ times its weight of boiling water, just enough to wet the grain. Cover and rest for 10 minutes, then rub in the rest of the olive oil and fluff with a fork.
Pile the couscous on plates, ladle the beef and vegetables over it, scatter with cilantro and serve with the harissa on the side.
Whisk the yogurt with a little cold water and a pinch of salt into a thin, cool drink, the lben-style glass that often goes with couscous.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow, with the couscous and the drink in separate containers.
tip: On a weeknight, use a pressure cooker: the beef is tender in 25 minutes. Keep the stew and the couscous apart in the fridge so it does not go soggy. Buttermilk (lben) is the classic drink if you can find it.

name: Tunisian harissa mackerel with barley and chickpea salad and a chopped salad
inspiredBy: Tunisian mackerel with harissa, a pairing that suits oily fish well
about: Mackerel fillets rubbed with harissa, garlic, caraway and lemon and roasted until the skin crackles, with a warm barley and chickpea salad with preserved lemon, olives and lots of parsley, and a crunchy diced tomato and cucumber salad. Mackerel carries **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**, and the barley brings fibre.
steps: Cover the barley with plenty of boiling water and simmer for 25 to 30 minutes, until tender but still a little chewy. Drain well.
Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Mix the harissa, garlic, caraway, half the lemon juice and a pinch of salt and rub it all over the mackerel.
Lay the fillets skin side up on a lined tray and roast for 10 to 12 minutes, until the skin is crisp and the flesh flakes.
Toss the warm barley with the chickpeas, preserved lemon, olives, most of the parsley and half the olive oil.
Toss the tomato and cucumber with the rest of the parsley, the rest of the lemon, the rest of the olive oil and a pinch of salt.
Serve the mackerel over the barley with the salad on the side.
tip: Cook the barley earlier in the week if you like, since it keeps 4 to 5 days in the fridge. Then Friday is just the fish and the salads.

name: Lamb and prune tagine with toasted almonds and a cucumber and carrot salad
inspiredBy: Moroccan lamb tagine with prunes and almonds, the kind served at celebrations
about: Lamb shoulder slowly braised with onion, cinnamon, ginger and pepper until it falls apart, then finished with sweet prunes, honey and toasted almonds. A lemony cucumber and carrot salad cuts the richness. The lamb brings **iron, zinc and B12**, and the prunes bring potassium.
steps: Brown the lamb in the olive oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat, about 6 minutes. Add the onion, cinnamon, ginger, pepper and the salt.
Add 300 ml of water. Cover and simmer very gently for 1 hour 15 minutes, until the lamb is tender.
Add the prunes and honey and simmer uncovered for 15 minutes, until the sauce is thick and syrupy.
Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes.
Toss the cucumber, grated carrot and parsley with the lemon juice, the cumin and a pinch of salt.
Spoon the tagine over the plates, scatter with the almonds and serve with the salad and warm pita. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: In a pressure cooker the lamb takes 30 minutes. Finish the prunes uncovered on the stove.

name: Algerian chicken tajine zitoune with potatoes and chard
inspiredBy: Algerian tajine zitoune, the chicken and green olive tagine
about: Chicken thighs braised in a golden, gentle sauce of onion, ginger and saffron with green olives, preserved lemon, potato and wilted chard. A pot of comfort that is tangy and savoury. The chard brings **vitamins K and A**, and the chicken brings protein.
steps: Brown the chicken in the olive oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat, about 5 minutes. Add the onion and garlic and cook for 5 minutes.
Crush the saffron into 2 tablespoons of warm water and add it with the ginger, pepper and the salt.
Add the potatoes and 250 ml of water. Cover and simmer gently for 25 minutes, until the potatoes and chicken are tender.
Stir in the olives, preserved lemon and chard stems. Simmer for 5 minutes.
Add the chard leaves until just wilted, about 2 minutes. Stir in the lemon juice and the parsley.
Serve in a shallow bowl with the sauce spooned over.
tip: Rinse the olives if they are very salty. Add a handful of sliced mushrooms with the potatoes if you like.

name: Yogurt with dried apricots, honey and cinnamon
inspiredBy: Inspired by the yogurt and dried fruit snacks of Algeria and Morocco
about: Thick yogurt with chopped dried apricots, a drizzle of honey and a pinch of cinnamon. Creamy and sweet. The yogurt brings **calcium and protein**.
steps: Stir the apricots into the yogurt, drizzle with the honey and dust with the cinnamon.

name: Yogurt with chopped dates and cinnamon
inspiredBy: Inspired by the yogurt and dried fruit snacks of Algeria and Morocco
about: Thick yogurt with chopped soft dates and a pinch of cinnamon, sweet enough without any honey. Creamy and a little chewy. The yogurt brings **calcium and protein**, and the dates bring potassium.
steps: Stir the dates into the yogurt and dust with the cinnamon.

name: Plain yogurt with a spoon of honey
about: Thick, cold yogurt with a spoon of honey, the simplest end to an afternoon. The yogurt brings **calcium and protein**.
steps: Spoon the honey over the yogurt and eat it straight away.

name: Sardines on khobz with tomato, onion and harissa
inspiredBy: Moroccan tinned sardine sandwich
about: Tinned sardines on warm khobz with sliced tomato, raw onion and a smear of harissa, the street-stall sandwich of Moroccan ports. The sardines bring **omega-3, calcium and vitamin D**.
steps: Warm the pita in a dry pan and open it. Smear the inside with the harissa.
Fill with the sardines, tomato and onion, squeeze over the lemon juice and press closed.

name: Dates stuffed with almonds
inspiredBy: Inspired by the stuffed dates served with tea in Morocco and Algeria
about: Soft medjool dates with a toasted almond tucked into each. A tiny sweet that goes with mint tea across the Maghreb. The almonds bring **vitamin E and magnesium**.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes. Split the date, remove the pit, tuck two almonds inside and eat the rest alongside.

name: Dried apricots with toasted almonds
about: Chewy dried apricots with a handful of toasted almonds, as served with tea across Morocco. The almonds bring **vitamin E and magnesium**, and the apricots bring potassium.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes. Eat with the apricots.

name: Khobz with olives and olive oil
