about: Warm whole-wheat khobz with salty green olives and a little olive oil for dipping and a pinch of cumin. Simple and satisfying. The whole grain brings **fibre**.
steps: Warm the pita in a dry pan. Tear it up, stir the cumin into the olive oil and dip. Eat with the olives.

name: Dates and walnuts with warm milk and cinnamon
about: Soft dates and a few walnuts with a mug of warm milk and cinnamon. Algerian and Tunisian hosts serve dates and walnuts together, and milk is the old companion. The milk brings **calcium**, and the walnuts bring plant omega-3.
steps: Warm the milk in a small pot or the microwave with the cinnamon. Drink it with the dates and walnuts on the side.

name: Boiled egg with cumin and salt
inspiredBy: Moroccan and Tunisian street-cart boiled egg with cumin
about: A warm boiled egg with a little cumin and flaky salt for dipping, the street-cart snack of Morocco and Tunisia. The egg brings **protein and choline**.
steps: Lower the egg into boiling water and cook for 9 minutes, then cool it under cold water and peel.
Mix the cumin and the salt and dip the egg into it as you eat.

name: Roasted chickpeas with cumin and paprika
inspiredBy: Inspired by the cumin chickpeas sold in paper cones by Moroccan street vendors
about: Crunchy oven-roasted chickpeas with cumin, paprika and a squeeze of lemon. A savoury snack in the style of Moroccan street-cart chickpeas. The chickpeas bring **protein and fibre**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Pat the chickpeas very dry.
Toss with the oil, cumin, paprika and salt on a tray.
Roast for 25 minutes, shaking the tray halfway, until crisp. Squeeze over the lemon juice and let them crisp more as they cool.
tip: They stay crunchy for about 3 days in a jar. Roast a fresh batch the day before you want them.

name: Orange slices with cinnamon and orange blossom
inspiredBy: Moroccan orange with cinnamon
about: Juicy orange slices with cinnamon and a few drops of orange blossom water, a Moroccan classic that works as a snack or dessert. The orange brings **vitamin C**.
steps: Arrange the orange on a plate, sprinkle with the orange blossom water and dust with the cinnamon.

name: Overnight oats with Greek yogurt, figs and almonds
inspiredBy: Greek yogurt with honey, figs and nuts, turned into make-ahead oats
about:
Rolled oats soaked overnight in thick Greek yogurt with chopped dried figs and a little chia, then topped with chopped almonds and a drizzle of honey. It is **ready when you wake up**, creamy, a little sweet and nicely crunchy on top.

The oats and chia add fibre, the figs add a little calcium and the almonds bring vitamin E.
steps: The night before, stir the oats, yogurt, chia and chopped figs together in a jar or bowl with about 100 ml (⅓ cup) of milk or water. It should look a little too runny, since the oats and chia will drink it up.
Cover and chill overnight. The figs soften and sweeten the oats as they sit.
In the morning, give it a stir. It should be thick and spoonable, and a splash more milk or water loosens it if it has gone stiff.
Roughly chop the almonds and scatter them on top with a drizzle of honey.
tip: Swap the figs for berries or a chopped orange, whatever you have. Make a few jars at once on Sunday, Tuesday and Thursday evenings.

name: Strapatsada, Greek tomato and feta scrambled eggs with spinach
inspiredBy: Greek strapatsada, with a handful of spinach folded in
about: Soft eggs scrambled into juicy cherry tomatoes with crumbled feta, oregano and a little spinach, with an orange on the side. It is a proper hot breakfast in **about ten minutes**. Eggs bring protein and choline, and the tomatoes and orange bring vitamin C.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a non-stick pan over medium heat. Add the tomatoes with the oregano and cook, pressing them with the back of a spoon, until they collapse into a thick, jammy sauce, about 4 minutes.
Stir in the spinach until it wilts.
Beat the eggs with the salt and pour them in. Stir gently until they are softly set and still glossy, about 2 minutes.
Crumble the feta over the top and eat right away, with the orange alongside.
tip: In the winter, canned crushed tomato works well here when fresh tomatoes are pale.

name: Spanish potato and kale tortilla with tomato salad
inspiredBy: Spanish tortilla española, with kale folded in and less oil
about:
A thick, soft omelette of slow-cooked potatoes, sweet onion, kale and eggs, served in wedges with a juicy tomato and cucumber salad. It is a slow weekend breakfast that makes two portions, and the cold slice is **just as good tomorrow morning**.

The eggs bring protein and choline and the potato brings potassium.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a non-stick frying pan over medium-low heat. Add the potatoes and onion with a pinch of the salt, cover and cook, stirring now and then, until the potatoes are completely tender but not browned, about 15 minutes. Add a little more oil if it starts to catch.
Stir in the kale and cook until it is tender and bright green, about 3 minutes, then tip everything into a bowl and let it cool for a few minutes.
Beat the eggs with a pinch of salt and fold in the potato mixture. Let it sit for 5 minutes so the egg soaks in.
Pour it back into the pan over low heat and cook until the edges are set and the middle is just a little wobbly, about 6 minutes.
Put a plate over the pan, flip the pan over so the tortilla drops onto the plate, then slide it back into the pan and cook 3 minutes more, until golden on both sides.

Toss the tomatoes and cucumber with the parsley, lemon juice and a few drops of olive oil, and serve a wedge with the salad. Wrap the second portion for tomorrow's breakfast and make a fresh batch of the salad then.
tip: Skip the flip and finish the top under a hot grill if turning it feels scary.

name: Greek meze plate with quick hummus, tzatziki and a boiled egg
inspiredBy: Greek and Cypriot meze tables, built as a quick lunch
about:
A lunch plate to graze from: lemony hummus, a quick garlicky yogurt dip, feta, a boiled egg, olives and crunchy fennel, cucumber and cherry tomatoes. Only the egg gets cooked, and **the hummus comes from your Sunday night batch**.

Chickpeas, yogurt, egg and feta make it a solid protein lunch, and the raw vegetables bring vitamin C.
steps: Make the hummus on Sunday night for the week. The batch uses a whole can of chickpeas (about 240 g drained), 1 tbsp of tahini, a little garlic, most of a lemon's juice and a pinch of salt, blitzed with a few spoonfuls of ice-cold water for 2 to 3 minutes until pale and silky. It keeps 4 days in the fridge, and today's plate uses a portion of it (the ingredient list shows that portion).
Lower the egg gently into a small pot of boiling water, cook for 8 minutes, then cool it under cold water and peel.
Grate a third of the cucumber, squeeze out the water and stir it into the yogurt with the rest of the garlic, finely grated, and a pinch of salt.

Cut the rest of the cucumber and the fennel into sticks and halve the tomatoes. Spoon the hummus and the yogurt dip onto a plate, squeeze over the remaining lemon juice, and arrange the vegetables, feta, olives and the halved egg around them. Finish with chopped parsley.
tip: Boil a few eggs on Sunday as well, and this lunch takes five minutes. A fresh tub of hummus works too.

name: Village-style salad with chickpeas and feta
inspiredBy: Greek horiatiki, with chickpeas to turn it into a lunch
about:
Chunky tomatoes, cucumber, pepper and red onion with olives, a slab of feta, a spoon of cool yogurt and a pile of chickpeas, all dressed with olive oil, red wine vinegar and oregano. The tomatoes make their own dressing as it sits, so it is **better after five minutes**.

Chickpeas, feta and yogurt make it a real lunch, and the pepper and tomato bring vitamin C.
steps: Halve the tomatoes, cut the cucumber and pepper into thick pieces and slice the red onion thinly.
Toss them in a big bowl with the olives and chickpeas.
Whisk the olive oil, vinegar, oregano and salt together and pour over, then toss well.
Lay the feta on top in one slab, spoon alongside the yogurt, stirred with the finely grated garlic and a pinch of salt, scatter with parsley and let it sit for 5 minutes before eating.
tip: In summer, use big ripe tomatoes cut into wedges. Pack the dressing separately if you take it to work.

name: Sicilian-style fava bean, orange and fennel salad with egg
inspiredBy: Sicilian orange and fennel salad, with fava beans for a lunch, and feta standing in for ricotta salata
about:
Juicy orange segments, shaved fennel, olives and red onion with creamy fava beans, toasted almonds and parsley, in a lemony olive oil dressing with a pinch of chili. It is **bright, crunchy and a little sweet**.

The fava beans, egg and feta carry the protein, and the orange and lemon give you plenty of vitamin C.
steps: Lower the egg gently into boiling water for 8 minutes, then cool and peel it. Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes, then chop roughly.
Slice the fennel very thinly and the red onion into fine rings. Peel the orange, removing the white pith, and cut it into rounds or segments over the bowl so the juice falls in.
Add the fava beans, olives, parsley, the feta, crumbled, and the egg, quartered, to the bowl.
Whisk the olive oil, lemon juice, salt and chili together, pour over and toss gently. Top with the toasted almonds.
tip: Leave out the chili for a milder salad.
ingredients: canned or frozen, cooked and drained

name: Greek lemon chicken with oregano potatoes and red peppers
inspiredBy: Greek kotopoulo lemonato, with roasted kale and a garlicky yogurt on the side
about:
Chicken thighs roasted with lemony oregano potatoes and red peppers until the edges are golden, with kale roasted on a second tray until crisp and a cool garlic yogurt to spoon over. It makes two portions, so **tomorrow's lunch is already done**.

The chicken brings protein, niacin and zinc, and the kale brings calcium and vitamin K.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C. Toss the potato wedges and pepper strips on a big tray with half the olive oil, the oregano, half the lemon juice and most of the salt. Spread them out in a single layer so they roast instead of steaming.
Roast for 20 minutes, until the potatoes are starting to colour.
Rub the chicken with half the garlic, the rest of the oil and a little of the lemon juice, tuck it in among the potatoes and roast until the chicken is cooked through and golden, 25 to 30 minutes.
Put the kale on a second tray with a few drops of oil and a pinch of salt and roast for the last 8 to 10 minutes, until the leaves are crisp at the edges.
Stir the rest of the garlic, finely grated, and the chopped parsley into the yogurt with a pinch of salt.
Serve one portion now with the kale, the yogurt and a squeeze of lemon. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Leave the skin on if you like, and the chicken stays even juicier. Reheat the second portion in the oven or air fryer for 10 minutes, or eat it at room temperature. A microwave makes roast potatoes sad.

name: Sardines on garlicky white beans with kale and almonds
inspiredBy: Spanish sardines with beans and Italian white bean and sardine toasts, without the bread
about:
Creamy white beans simmered with garlic, onion and smoky paprika, with kale wilted in and canned sardines warmed on top. Toasted almonds, a squeeze of lemon and an optional pinch of chili finish it.

Sardines eaten with their soft bones are **one of the best food sources of calcium**, and they bring omega-3 and vitamin D too.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan over medium heat until golden and fragrant, about 3 minutes, then tip them out and chop roughly.
In the same pan, warm the olive oil over low heat and soften the onion and garlic with the chopped anchovies until sweet and golden and the anchovies have melted away, about 6 minutes.
Stir in the smoked paprika and the chili, if using, then add the beans, a splash of water and the salt and simmer for 6 minutes, mashing a few beans against the pan to thicken the sauce.
Stir in the kale and cook until it is bright green and just tender, 3 to 4 minutes.
Lay the sardines on top for a minute to warm through, then finish with the lemon juice, parsley and toasted almonds.
tip: Mackerel fillets in olive oil work just as well as sardines. Leave out the chili for a mild version.
ingredients: canned in olive oil, with bones

name: Fakes, Greek lentil soup with spinach and feta
inspiredBy: Greek fakes, with spinach stirred in and a splash of vinegar at the end
about:
A thick, comforting Greek lentil soup with tomato, barley and oregano, finished with a splash of red wine vinegar, a raw drizzle of olive oil and crumbled feta. **The vinegar is the secret**, since it wakes everything up.

It makes two bowls and tastes even better tomorrow, and the lentils are a great source of iron, folate and fibre.
steps: Warm half the olive oil in a large pot and soften the onion over medium heat until it is translucent, about 8 minutes.
Stir in the garlic and oregano for a minute until fragrant.

Add the lentils, barley, crushed tomato and about four times as much water as lentils. Bring to a boil, then simmer gently, partly covered, until the lentils and barley are completely soft and the soup is thick, 35 to 40 minutes. Add the salt near the end.
Stir in the spinach until it wilts, then take the pot off the heat.
Stir in the vinegar and parsley, taste for salt, and finish each bowl with crumbled feta, a dollop of yogurt and a drizzle of the rest of the olive oil.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. It thickens overnight, so add a splash of water and a fresh splash of vinegar when you reheat it.
tip: In a hurry? Use canned lentils, drained, and simmer for 20 minutes.

name: Salmon with tomatoes, olives and anchovy on lemony barley
inspiredBy: Southern Italian puttanesca flavours, with barley in place of pasta
about:
Salmon roasted over blistered cherry tomatoes, black olives and a few melted anchovies, served on chewy lemony barley with tender kale stirred through. The tomatoes burst into a sauce all on their own.

Salmon is **one of the best food sources of omega-3** and a good source of vitamin D, and the kale adds calcium while the barley adds fibre.
steps: Rinse the barley and simmer it in plenty of salted water until tender but still chewy, about 25 minutes. Add the kale for the last 3 minutes, then drain well.

Meanwhile, heat the oven to 200 C. Chop the anchovies and toss them with the tomatoes, thin onion wedges, garlic and olives on a small tray with half the olive oil and the oregano. Roast for 10 minutes, until the tomatoes begin to burst and the anchovies have melted into the juices.
Nestle the salmon among the tomatoes, brush it with a little of the remaining oil and roast until it just flakes, 10 to 12 minutes.
Toss the drained barley and kale with the lemon juice and the rest of the oil.
Serve the salmon and the tomato juices over the barley and scatter with parsley.
tip: The anchovies melt away and just add savoury depth, so even anchovy skeptics usually enjoy it. Add a pinch of chili flakes if you like heat.

name: Espinacas con garbanzos, Andalusian chickpea and spinach stew
inspiredBy: the Seville tapas classic, with almonds ground into the base instead of fried bread
about:
A smoky, garlicky chickpea and spinach stew thickened with ground toasted almonds, with cumin, paprika and a splash of vinegar to finish. A halved boiled egg, a spoon of cool yogurt and a scatter of crunchy almonds go on top.

It makes two portions, and the **chickpeas, egg and yogurt bring protein** while the almonds bring vitamin E and the chickpeas bring iron and fibre.
steps: Boil the eggs for 8 minutes, cool them under cold water and peel them. Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden. Set a few aside to chop for the top, and blitz or pound the rest with a third of the garlic, a pinch of salt and a splash of the vinegar into a rough paste.
Warm the olive oil in a wide pot and soften the onion with the rest of the garlic, sliced, over medium heat, about 6 minutes.
Stir in the cumin, smoked paprika and the chili, if using, for 30 seconds, until fragrant.
Add the crushed tomato, chickpeas and a mug of water and simmer until the sauce has thickened, about 12 minutes.
Stir in the almond paste, then the spinach in handfuls until it all wilts, about 3 minutes.

Finish with the rest of the vinegar, taste for salt, and top each bowl with a halved egg, a spoonful of yogurt and the chopped almonds. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch and boil a fresh egg to go on top of it.
tip: Leave out the chili for a milder stew.

name: Shrimp saganaki with feta and lemony potatoes
inspiredBy: Greek garides saganaki, with potatoes on the side instead of bread
about:
Plump shrimp in a bright tomato sauce with oregano, topped with feta that melts into creamy pockets, served with warm lemony potatoes to mop it all up. It is **on the table in 30 minutes**.

Shrimp are a lean protein with plenty of selenium, and the feta adds calcium.
steps: Halve the potatoes if they are large and boil them in salted water until tender, about 15 minutes. Drain, then toss with half the lemon juice and a little of the parsley.

Meanwhile, warm the olive oil in a skillet and soften the onion and red pepper over medium heat, about 5 minutes. Stir in the garlic, oregano and the chopped anchovies for a minute, until the anchovies dissolve.
Add the crushed tomato and simmer until thick and saucy, about 8 minutes.
Slide in the shrimp and cook until they are pink and curled, 3 to 4 minutes.
Crumble the feta over the top, cover for a couple of minutes until it softens, then finish with the rest of the lemon juice and parsley.
Serve with the potatoes alongside.
tip: Mussels are a classic swap for the shrimp. Add them to the sauce, cover until they open, about 5 minutes, and discard any that stay shut. Pre-cooked shrimp only need the last minute.

name: Saffron barley with chicken, peas and red pepper
inspiredBy: Spanish paella, made with pearled barley in place of rice
about:
A golden, creamy pot of chicken, red pepper, peas and chewy pearled barley, cooked in a smoky tomato sofrito and perfumed with saffron, then topped with toasted walnuts for crunch. It is a **slow weekend dish that makes two portions**.

Barley is full of fibre, and the chicken and peas make this a complete one-pot dinner.
steps: Steep the saffron in a mug of hot water. Rinse the barley. Toast the walnuts in a dry pan until fragrant and chop them roughly.
Warm half the olive oil in a wide, deep pan and brown the chicken on all sides over medium-high heat, then set it aside.

Add the rest of the oil and soften the onion and red pepper over medium heat for 8 minutes. Stir in the garlic and smoked paprika, then the crushed tomato, and cook until the sofrito turns dark and jammy, about 5 minutes.
Stir in the barley to coat it in the sofrito, then pour in the saffron water and enough hot water to come to about 2½ to 3 times the barley's volume. Add the salt and the chicken.
Simmer gently, stirring now and then and topping up with hot water if it gets dry, until the barley is tender and the pot is creamy rather than soupy, about 30 minutes.
Scatter the peas over the top for the last 5 minutes, then take the pan off the heat and let it rest, covered, for 5 minutes.
Finish with the lemon juice, parsley and toasted walnuts. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. It reheats well with a splash of water.
tip: Use boneless thighs for an even juicier pot, or add a handful of mussels or shrimp for the last 5 minutes for a seafood version. Barley will not form a crisp base like rice does, so the walnuts bring the crunch.

name: Greek yogurt with honey, walnuts and figs
about: Thick yogurt with chopped dried figs, crunchy walnuts and a drizzle of honey. It is the classic Greek sweet snack, with protein and calcium from the yogurt and **plant omega-3 from the walnuts**.
steps: Spoon the yogurt into a bowl, top with the chopped figs and walnuts, and drizzle with the honey.

name: Greek yogurt with honey, figs and toasted almonds
about: Thick yogurt with chopped dried figs, warm toasted almonds and a drizzle of honey. It is a classic Greek sweet snack, with protein and calcium from the yogurt and **vitamin E from the almonds**.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes. Spoon the yogurt into a bowl, top with the chopped figs and warm almonds, and drizzle with the honey.

name: Fig and almond bites
inspiredBy: Spanish pan de higo and Greek fig and nut sweets
about: Sticky dried figs chopped with almonds and rolled into little balls. They are **chewy, sweet and crunchy at once**, with vitamin E and a little calcium.
steps: Chop the figs and almonds very finely and mash them together with a few drops of lemon juice until they stick.
Roll the mixture into small balls.
tip: Make a batch and keep the balls in a container in the fridge for the week.

name: Orange and toasted almonds
about: A juicy orange with a handful of warm toasted almonds. The **vitamin C and the crunch of the nuts** make a snack that keeps you going, and the almonds bring vitamin E.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes. Peel the orange and eat it with the warm almonds.

name: Quick lemony hummus with fennel and cucumber sticks
about: Creamy lemon and garlic hummus with crunchy fennel and cucumber sticks for dipping. The chickpeas and tahini add **iron and fibre**, and tahini adds calcium.
steps: Use a portion of Sunday night's hummus (the batch is a whole can of chickpeas, about 240 g drained, with 1 tbsp of tahini, garlic, lemon and salt). The ingredient list shows this snack's portion. If you are starting fresh, blitz that amount with a few spoonfuls of ice-cold water until pale and silky.
Cut the fennel and cucumber into sticks and dip away.
tip: Thursday is the last day the Sunday batch is at its best.

name: Dried figs and almonds
about: A few soft dried figs with a handful of warm toasted almonds. It is a sweet, chewy and crunchy snack, with **fibre, calcium and vitamin E**.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes, and eat them with the figs.

name: Garlic mushrooms with lemon and parsley
inspiredBy: Spanish champiñones al ajillo
about: Mushrooms sizzled in a hot pan with garlic until golden, then finished with lemon and a handful of parsley. They work as a **small savoury snack or a starter**, they are meaty and savoury, and they are a good source of niacin and B vitamins.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a pan over medium-high heat and cook the mushrooms until golden and their water has cooked off, about 6 minutes.
Add the garlic and stir for 30 seconds, then finish with the lemon juice, salt and parsley.

name: Garlic mushrooms with soft eggs and parsley
inspiredBy: Spanish champiñones al ajillo, with eggs on top
about: Mushrooms sizzled with garlic, lemon and parsley, with two soft-boiled eggs to break over the top. It works as a **small savoury snack or a starter**, and it gives you protein, choline and niacin.
steps: Lower the eggs gently into boiling water for 6 to 7 minutes for a soft yolk, then cool and peel them.
Warm the olive oil in a pan over medium-high heat and cook the mushrooms until golden and their water has cooked off, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and stir for 30 seconds.
Finish with the lemon juice, salt and parsley and serve with the halved eggs on top.

name: Orange and toasted walnuts
about: A juicy orange with a handful of warm toasted walnuts. The vitamin C and the crunch of the nuts make a snack that keeps you going, and the walnuts bring **plant omega-3**.
steps: Toast the walnuts in a dry pan until fragrant, about 3 minutes, and eat them with the peeled orange.

name: Greek yogurt with orange and honey
about: Thick Greek yogurt with juicy orange pieces and a drizzle of honey. It is a bright, simple snack with protein, calcium and **plenty of vitamin C**.
steps: Peel the orange, cut it into pieces over the bowl so the juice falls in, spoon over the yogurt and drizzle with the honey.

name: Sardine tapa with lemon, cucumber and olives
inspiredBy: Spanish and Portuguese tinned fish tapas
about:
A few canned sardines on cool cucumber rounds with a squeeze of lemon, a few olives and a pinch of smoked paprika. It is the kind of thing you would be served with a drink in a Spanish bar, and a hungry-day extra on the larger plans.

Sardines bring omega-3, vitamin D and **calcium from their soft bones**.
steps: Slice the cucumber into thick rounds, top each with a piece of sardine, and finish with the lemon juice, olives, a dusting of smoked paprika and chopped parsley.
ingredients: canned in olive oil, with bones

name: Tzatziki with cucumber and fennel dippers
about: A quick garlicky yogurt and cucumber dip with a drizzle of olive oil, with cucumber rounds and fennel strips for scooping. It is **cool and fresh**, with plenty of protein.
steps: Grate a third of the cucumber, squeeze out the water, and stir it into the yogurt with the finely grated garlic, lemon juice, chopped parsley, salt and the olive oil.
Slice the rest of the cucumber into rounds, cut the fennel into strips and dip away.
tip: Chopped mint or dill is lovely in the dip if you have some.

name: Chilaquiles verdes with fried eggs and baked tortillas
inspiredBy: Chilaquiles verdes from Mexico City and central Mexico, with the tortillas baked instead of fried and lime-thinned yogurt in place of Mexican crema
about: Crisp baked tortilla wedges tossed in a bright, tangy tomatillo and epazote salsa, then topped with fried eggs, queso fresco, a spoon of lime-thinned yogurt and ripe avocado. Baking the tortillas instead of frying them keeps the crunch and saves most of the oil. The eggs bring protein and **choline**, and the tomatillo brings vitamin C.
steps: Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Cut the tortillas into wedges, spread them on a tray and bake until crisp and pale gold, about 12 minutes, turning them once.
While they bake, simmer the tomatillos, jalapeño and garlic in a small pot of water until the tomatillos turn olive green and soft, about 8 minutes. Drain.
Blend them with the epazote, cilantro, half the onion and the salt until smooth and bright green.

Warm half the oil in a wide pan, pour in the salsa and let it bubble for 3 minutes, until it thickens a little. Toss in the baked tortillas for less than a minute, just until they are coated, so they keep their bite.
Fry the eggs in the rest of the oil in a second pan, with the yolks still soft.

Stir the yogurt with the lime juice to make a quick crema. Pile the chilaquiles on a plate and top with the eggs, the sliced raw onion, queso fresco, crema and avocado. Eat right away, before they go soft.
tip: On Sunday, bake a double tray of tortilla wedges and blend a double batch of salsa; they keep 4 days, so Monday and Thursday take 10 minutes. Shredded chicken from the tinga is the classic add-in. Epazote is sold fresh or dried at Latin grocers; leave it out if you cannot find it. Use a mild poblano instead of the jalapeño for kids.
ingredients: a day or two old is best
5 or 6 fresh leaves, or a pinch of dried
half in the salsa, half sliced thin for the top
stirred with a squeeze of lime, standing in for Mexican crema

name: Huevos rancheros with salsa ranchera and pinto beans
inspiredBy: Huevos rancheros, with a little oil and a side of beans instead of fried potatoes
about: Two fried eggs on crisped corn tortillas, under a smoky roasted tomato and jalapeño salsa, with warm mashed pinto beans, a little queso fresco and avocado. It is the classic ranch breakfast, and it is filling without being heavy. The beans and eggs bring **protein, iron and folate** before the day has started.
steps: Use the beans from your Sunday pot (see the plan notes), or canned beans at about three times the dry weight, drained and rinsed. Warm them with a splash of water and mash roughly with a fork.
Set a dry skillet over high heat and char the tomato, jalapeño and onion, turning them now and then, until blistered and blackened in spots, about 8 minutes.

Blend them with the garlic, half the cilantro, the cumin, oregano and salt into a chunky salsa. Pour it back into the skillet with a splash of water and simmer for 5 minutes, until it thickens and darkens.
Heat a little of the oil in a pan and crisp the tortillas for about a minute on each side. Move them to a plate.
Fry the eggs in the rest of the oil. Set them on the tortillas, spoon the salsa around them and add the beans.
Finish with the queso fresco, avocado and the rest of the cilantro.
tip: The salsa keeps for 4 days, so a double batch covers both mornings. Char and blend it the night before. Chopped serrano makes it hotter.

name: Huevos a la mexicana with pinto beans and warm tortillas
inspiredBy: Huevos a la mexicana, the everyday scrambled eggs with tomato, onion and chile
about: Soft scrambled eggs cooked with tomato, onion, jalapeño and tender nopalitos, the red, white and green of the Mexican flag, served with warm mashed pinto beans, avocado and warm tortillas. It is one of the most common breakfasts in the country, and it is ready in about 20 minutes. The eggs and beans bring **protein, choline and folate**.
steps: Use the beans from your Sunday pot (see the plan notes), or canned beans at about three times the dry weight, drained and rinsed. Warm them with a splash of water and mash roughly with a fork.
Finely chop the tomato, onion and jalapeño. Warm the oil in a pan over medium heat and cook the onion and jalapeño until soft, about 3 minutes.
Rinse the nopalitos well and add them with the tomato, the oregano and a pinch of the salt. Cook until the tomato softens and the juices thicken, about 4 minutes.
Beat the eggs with the rest of the salt, pour them into the pan and stir gently until they are softly set and still glossy, about 2 minutes.
Warm the tortillas in a dry pan. Serve the eggs with the beans, tortillas, avocado, queso fresco and the cilantro.
tip: A chopped serrano or a spoon of salsa makes it hotter. Leave the jalapeño out for kids.

name: Ensalada de nopales with pinto beans, queso fresco and pepitas
inspiredBy: Ensalada de nopales from central Mexico, with pinto beans and pepitas added to make it a full lunch
about: Tender cactus paddles tossed with tomato, red onion, jalapeño, cilantro and lime, folded through pinto beans and finished with queso fresco, toasted pepitas and avocado. It is cool, tangy and fresh, with warm tortillas to scoop it up. The beans and cactus bring **fibre and potassium**, and the pepitas bring zinc and magnesium.
steps: Use the beans from your Sunday pot (see the plan notes), or canned beans at about three times the dry weight, drained and rinsed.
Rinse the nopalitos in a colander under cold water until the slippery coating is gone, then drain well.
Toast the pepitas in a dry pan for 2 to 3 minutes until they puff and pop. Tip them out to cool.
Chop the tomato, red onion and jalapeño. Toss them in a big bowl with the nopales, beans, lime juice, oil, oregano, salt and most of the cilantro.
Top with the queso fresco, pepitas, sliced avocado and the rest of the cilantro.
Warm the tortillas in a dry pan or directly over a gas flame for a few seconds a side and serve them with the salad.
tip: Fresh nopales are worth trying: boil the diced paddles with a piece of onion for 10 minutes, then rinse. It packs well; keep the avocado and tortillas separate.
ingredients: jarred nopalitos, rinsed well under cold water

name: Quesadillas de rajas with corn, pinto beans and raw tomatillo salsa
inspiredBy: Quesadillas de rajas con elote, a street and home favourite across central and southern Mexico
about: Corn tortillas folded around melted Oaxaca cheese, charred poblano strips and sweet corn, served with warm pinto beans, a spoonful of lime crema and a sharp raw tomatillo salsa. Blackening the poblanos is what gives rajas their smoky flavour. The cheese and beans carry **protein and calcium**.
steps: Use the beans from your Sunday pot (see the plan notes), or canned beans at about three times the dry weight, drained and rinsed.

Blacken the poblanos directly over a gas flame or under a very hot broiler, turning them until the skin is charred all over, about 10 minutes. Drop them into a covered bowl for 10 minutes to sweat, then peel off the skin, pull out the seeds and slice into strips (rajas).

Warm half the oil in a wide pan and cook the onion over medium-high heat until soft and speckled with brown, about 5 minutes. Add the rajas, corn and a pinch of salt and cook 2 minutes more. Tip into a bowl.

Make the salsa: blend the raw tomatillo, jalapeño, most of the cilantro, half the lime juice and a pinch of salt until almost smooth. Warm the beans with a splash of water and a pinch of salt, mashing a few as they heat.

Wipe out the pan. Lay the tortillas in it a couple at a time, scatter cheese and the filling over one half and fold them over. Cook in the rest of the oil until the cheese melts and the tortillas are golden and crisp at the edges, about 3 minutes a side.
Stir the yogurt with the rest of the lime juice to make a quick crema. Serve the quesadillas with the crema, beans and salsa, and the rest of the cilantro.
tip: Real Oaxaca cheese (quesillo) is stringy and mild. If you cannot find it, mozzarella is the best swap. Char, peel and cook the rajas on Tuesday night, so lunch is 15 minutes.
ingredients: stirred with a squeeze of lime, standing in for crema

name: Tlayuda-inspired tostadas with black beans, guajillo beef and quesillo
inspiredBy: Oaxacan tlayuda with tasajo (thin dried-style beef), usually one large toasted tortilla; this is a smaller, lighter version
about: Crisp baked tortillas spread with garlicky black beans and topped with thin guajillo-rubbed beef in the style of Oaxacan tasajo, melted Oaxaca cheese, shredded cabbage, grated carrot, sliced tomato and avocado. A real tlayuda is one huge toasted tortilla, and this is the same idea in a smaller, lighter size. The black beans and beef bring **iron, zinc and folate**.
steps: Use the beans from your Sunday pot (see the plan notes), or canned beans at about three times the dry weight, drained and rinsed.

Soak the guajillo in hot water for 10 minutes. Blend it with half the garlic, half the lime juice, the oregano and a pinch of salt into a thick red paste, adding a spoon of the soaking water if you need it. Rub it all over the beef.
Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Brush the tortillas lightly with a little of the oil, lay them on a tray and bake until crisp and pale gold, about 8 minutes.
Heat the rest of the oil in a hot pan and sear the beef for about 1 minute a side, until browned at the edges. Rest it for a minute, then slice it thinner still.
Warm the beans in a small pot with the rest of the garlic, minced, the rest of the salt and a splash of water. Mash roughly.

Spread the beans over the crisp tortillas, scatter on the cheese and return the tray to the oven for 3 to 4 minutes, until it melts. Top with the beef, cabbage, grated carrot, tomato and avocado, and squeeze over the rest of the lime.
tip: A large tortilla from a Latin grocery makes it closer to the real thing. A dab of salsa on top is never wrong.
ingredients: round or flank steak, sliced against the grain as thin as you can
1 to 2 dried guajillo chiles, stemmed and seeded

name: Pollo en tinga with black beans
inspiredBy: Tinga poblana from Puebla, served with black beans on warm tortillas
about: Shredded chicken simmered in a smoky tomato and chipotle sauce with soft onion, piled onto warm tortillas with black beans, a crunchy cabbage and carrot slaw and a sprinkle of queso fresco. It is a Puebla favourite, and it tastes even better the next day. Chicken and black beans bring **protein, folate and niacin**.
steps: Use the beans from your Sunday pot (see the plan notes), or canned beans at about three times the dry weight, drained and rinsed.

Put the chicken in a pot with a quarter of the onion, a clove of the garlic, a pinch of salt and enough water to cover. Simmer gently until cooked through and tender, about 18 minutes. Lift it out, save a cup of the broth and shred the meat with two forks.
Blend the tomatoes, chipotles with their sauce, the rest of the garlic, the oregano, cumin, the rest of the salt and the cup of broth until smooth.
Warm the oil in a wide pan and cook the rest of the onion, sliced, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Pour in the sauce and simmer for 8 minutes until it thickens and darkens.
Stir in the chicken and cook for 5 minutes so it soaks up the sauce. Warm the beans with a splash of water.
Serve on warm tortillas with the beans, cabbage, carrot and queso fresco. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch; tinga keeps well for 4 days.
tip: A small can of chipotles in adobo lasts a while: freeze the rest flat in a bag and snap off a chile when you need one. Tinga is great on a crisp tostada too.
ingredients: chipotles in adobo, about 1 chile and a spoonful of sauce per portion

name: Baja-style salmon tacos with cabbage slaw and lime crema
inspiredBy: Tacos de pescado estilo Baja, made with salmon and a yogurt crema in place of fried fish
about: Ancho-rubbed seared salmon flaked into warm corn tortillas with a crunchy lime cabbage and carrot slaw, cool lime crema and avocado, with a spoonful of black beans on the side. It borrows the Baja fish taco and swaps in salmon for a richer, oilier bite. One serving gives you **omega-3 and B12**, and helps with vitamin D.
steps: Use the beans from your Sunday pot (see the plan notes), or canned beans at about three times the dry weight, drained and rinsed. Warm a spoonful per plate with a splash of water.
Soak the ancho in hot water for 10 minutes. Blend it with the garlic, half the lime juice and half the salt into a smooth red paste. Rub it over the salmon and let it sit while you make the slaw.
Toss the cabbage with the carrot, red onion, jalapeño, most of the cilantro and a pinch of salt.
Stir the yogurt with the rest of the lime juice and salt to make a thin, tangy crema.

Heat a non-stick pan over medium heat and sear the salmon, skin side down first, until the crust is deep red and it flakes easily, about 4 minutes a side. It releases its own fat, so you do not need oil.
Warm the tortillas in a dry pan. Flake the salmon into them, add the slaw, avocado and a drizzle of crema, and finish with the rest of the cilantro. Serve the warm black beans on the side.
tip: Not a salmon fan? Use any firm fish like cod or tilapia. A little diced mango in the slaw is lovely.
ingredients: 1 dried ancho chile, stemmed and seeded

name: Caldo de res with chickpeas, chayote and corn
inspiredBy: Caldo de res from northern and central Mexico, with chickpeas the way many home cooks add them
about: A big, comforting beef and vegetable soup made on bone-in beef short rib or shank, with cabbage, carrot, chayote, corn and potato in a clear, savoury broth and plenty of cilantro. Chickpeas are a normal addition in many homes, and a squeeze of lime goes in the bowl. It is a full meal in a bowl, rich in **zinc, iron and potassium**.
steps: The night before, cover the chickpeas with plenty of cold water and leave them to soak. Drain before using.

Put the beef and chickpeas in a large pot with the onion, garlic, tomato, salt and enough water to cover well. Bring to a boil, skim off the foam, then cover and simmer gently for 90 minutes, until the meat is nearly tender.
Add the potato, carrot and corn and simmer for 15 minutes.
Add the cabbage and chayote and simmer for 10 minutes more, until the vegetables are tender but not mushy.
Taste the broth and add salt if you need it. Stir in the cilantro.
Ladle into deep bowls with a piece of everything, with lime wedges to squeeze over and warm tortillas to dip in. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch; the broth gets better overnight.
tip: Most of the simmering is hands-off. In an olla exprés (pressure cooker), the beef and chickpeas take 35 minutes. A chopped serrano and a few drops of lime at the table make it feel like the real thing.
ingredients: bone-in beef shank or short rib; buy about 200 g with the bone
peeled and cut into wedges; zucchini works
about half an ear, cut into rounds

name: Sardine tostadas with beans, jícama slaw and salsa
inspiredBy: Tostadas de sardina, the coastal Mexican tostada made with canned sardines, with a spread of beans added for fibre and iron
about: Crisp baked tortillas spread with warm pinto beans, topped with flaked sardines, a crunchy jícama and carrot slaw, a spoon of fresh tomato salsa and creamy avocado. It is quick, fresh and a little spicy, in the style of seaside tostadas on the Pacific coast. The sardines bring **omega-3 and calcium from the soft bones**.
steps: Use the beans from your Sunday pot (see the plan notes), or canned beans at about three times the dry weight, drained and rinsed.
Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Lay the tortillas on a tray and bake until crisp and pale gold, about 8 minutes, turning once. These are your tostadas.
Warm the beans in a small pot with a splash of water and a pinch of salt, mashing them roughly.

Toss the jícama, cabbage, carrot, red onion, half the jalapeño and half the cilantro with half the lime juice and half the salt. Stir the chopped tomato with the rest of the jalapeño, cilantro, lime juice and salt for a quick salsa.
Flake the sardines into big pieces with a fork.
Assemble right away: spread beans over each tostada, add the sardines and a pile of the slaw, then a spoon of salsa and sliced avocado. Eat them while the base is still crisp.
tip: Pick sardines packed in olive oil if you like a richer taste. A dash of hot sauce on top never hurts.
ingredients: canned in oil or water, with the bones, drained; sardines in tomato sauce are common in Mexico too

name: Pozole verde with chicken, hominy and pepitas
inspiredBy: Pozole verde from Guerrero, made with chicken and canned hominy for a weeknight
about: A bright green, tangy soup of chicken and chewy hominy in a tomatillo, epazote and toasted pepita sauce, topped with queso fresco, oregano and lime. It comes from Guerrero on the Pacific side, where Thursday is pozole day. The pepitas bring **magnesium and zinc**, and the tomatillo brings vitamin C.
steps: Put the chicken in a pot with half the onion, half the garlic, a pinch of salt and about 5 cups of water. Simmer gently until the chicken is cooked through, about 20 minutes. Lift it out and shred it. Keep the broth.
Toast the pepitas in a dry pan for 2 to 3 minutes until they puff and pop.
Simmer the tomatillos and jalapeño in a little of the broth for 8 minutes. Blend them with the toasted pepitas, epazote, cilantro, the rest of the onion and garlic, and a ladle of broth until smooth.
Warm the oil in the soup pot and fry the green sauce, stirring, for 5 minutes, until it darkens and thickens. Pour in the broth, add the hominy and the rest of the salt and simmer for 20 minutes.
Return the chicken to the pot and heat through for 5 minutes. Taste for salt.
Ladle into bowls and top with the queso fresco, a pinch of ground oregano and a lime wedge. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Radish slices and a few baked tortilla strips are traditional at the table. Leave the epazote out if you cannot find it and add a little more cilantro.
ingredients: canned white hominy, drained and rinsed; one large 29 oz can makes two portions
3 fresh leaves, or a pinch of dried

name: Cochinita pibil with pickled red onion
inspiredBy: Cochinita pibil from the Yucatán, normally slow-roasted in a pit; this is the oven version with a leaner cut
about: Pork shoulder marinated in a bright achiote, orange and lime rub, wrapped up and baked low and slow until it falls apart, then piled into warm tortillas with sharp pink pickled onion and carrot, a slice of fresh chile and avocado. It comes from the Yucatán, where it is a weekend feast. The pork is a great source of **thiamin and B12**.
steps: The night before, mash the achiote paste with the orange juice and half the lime juice until it dissolves, then blend with the garlic, oregano, pepper, cumin and most of the salt into a red marinade.
Cut the pork into big chunks. Rub the marinade all over it, cover and chill overnight, or at least 2 hours.

Heat the oven to 160°C (325°F). Put the pork and every drop of marinade on a big piece of foil or parchment, fold it into a tight parcel and set it in a baking dish. A banana leaf is traditional if you can find one.
Bake for 2½ to 3 hours, until the meat shreds easily with a fork.
While it finishes, make the pickle: cover the red onion, jalapeño and carrot with the rest of the lime juice and a pinch of salt and leave for 30 minutes, until the onion is bright pink.
Shred the pork right in its juices. Warm the tortillas in a dry pan and fill the tacos with pork, the pickle and sliced avocado. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Achiote paste (recado rojo) comes in small blocks or jars at Latin grocers and many supermarkets, and it is what gives cochinita its colour and earthy flavour. Sour orange is the usual juice; orange plus extra lime is the close swap.
ingredients: pork shoulder, trimmed of the thick fat cap

name: Frijoles charros with pork, tomato and jalapeño
inspiredBy: Frijoles charros from Jalisco and the north, made with less meat and no bacon or sausage
about: A cowboy-style pot of pinto beans simmered with a little pork, tomato, onion, ancho chile and epazote, finished with cilantro and queso fresco and served with warm tortillas. It is hearty, smoky and very much northern Mexico. The beans and pork bring **iron, thiamin and fibre**.
steps: Cover the beans with water in a pot, add a quarter of the onion and the epazote and simmer until very tender, about 1 hour 15 minutes, topping up the water if you need to. Or use about three times the dry weight in cooked Sunday beans or canned, drained, and simmer them for 20 minutes only.
Toast the ancho in a dry pan for 30 seconds a side, then soak it in hot water for 10 minutes and blend it with the tomato into a smoky sauce.
Warm the oil in a second pot and brown the pork cubes over medium-high heat, about 5 minutes, until golden at the edges.

Add most of the rest of the onion, chopped, with the jalapeño and garlic and cook, stirring, until soft and fragrant, about 4 minutes. Pour in the tomato and ancho sauce and cook until thick, about 5 minutes.
Tip in the beans with a cup of their cooking liquid and the salt. Simmer for 15 minutes, mashing a few of the beans against the side of the pot, until it is thick and stew-like.
Stir in most of the cilantro, then serve with the queso fresco, the rest of the cilantro, the last of the onion, raw, a squeeze of lime and the warm tortillas.
tip: Chopped chorizo or bacon are traditional; a small spoonful is plenty. Make a double pot and freeze half.
ingredients: dried; cooked in the pot, see the steps
1 dried ancho or pasilla chile, stemmed and seeded
a sprig, or a pinch of dried

name: Papaya and almond licuado with yogurt
about: A thick, cold blend of yogurt and sweet papaya and a spoonful of almonds with a pinch of cinnamon, the way a juice stand would make it. It is creamy and refreshing, and quick. The yogurt and almonds bring **protein, calcium and vitamin E**, and the papaya brings vitamin C.
steps: Blend everything with a splash of cold water and a few ice cubes until thick and smooth.
Pour into a tall glass and eat it with a spoon if it is very thick.

name: Chía fresca with lime
inspiredBy: Chía fresca, the traditional chia agua fresca of Mexico, lightly sweetened with orange juice instead of sugar
about: Chia seeds soaked in water with lime juice and a splash of orange juice until they turn plump and jelly-like, a classic Mexican agua fresca. It is cool, tangy and slightly sweet. Chia brings **omega-3, calcium and magnesium** in a very Mexican way.
steps: Stir the chia into a tall glass of cold water (about 250 ml) and leave it for 10 minutes, stirring once or twice, until it plumps up.
Add the lime juice, orange juice, a tiny pinch of salt and ice, and stir well.

name: Yogurt with orange and toasted pepitas
about: Cold yogurt with juicy orange segments and a handful of toasted pepitas. It is simple, creamy and crunchy, and a very easy snack. The yogurt and pepitas bring **protein, calcium and zinc**.
steps: Toast the pepitas in a dry pan for 2 to 3 minutes, until they puff and pop.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl, top with the orange segments and the pepitas.

name: Jícama sticks with lime and chile
about: Crunchy jícama sticks tossed with lime juice, ground guajillo and a pinch of salt, the way it is sold at street stalls in Mexico. It is juicy, sharp and refreshing. Jícama brings **fibre and vitamin C**, with very few calories.
steps: Peel the jícama and cut it into sticks. Toss with the lime juice, ground guajillo and salt, and eat it cold.
ingredients: toasted and ground guajillo, or chile powder

name: Orange with chile and lime
about: Juicy orange segments sprinkled with ground guajillo, a squeeze of lime and a pinch of salt, an everyday Mexican fruit snack. It is sweet, sour and a little spicy. Orange brings **vitamin C and folate**.
steps: Peel the orange and cut it into segments or slices.
Sprinkle with the ground guajillo and lime juice.
ingredients: toasted and ground guajillo, or chile powder

name: Papaya with lime and chile
about: Cold papaya cubes with a squeeze of lime and a dusting of ground guajillo, a popular fruit cup in Mexico. The lime makes the sweetness taste brighter. Papaya brings **vitamin C and vitamin A**.
steps: Scoop out the seeds, peel the papaya and cut it into cubes.
Toss with the lime juice and ground guajillo.
ingredients: toasted and ground guajillo, or chile powder

name: Esquites, warm corn in a cup with lime and queso fresco
inspiredBy: Esquites, the warm corn cup sold at street stalls across central Mexico, with lime yogurt in place of mayonnaise and crema
about: Sweet corn kernels sautéed until a little charred, tossed with lime juice, ground guajillo, queso fresco and a spoonful of lime yogurt, served in a cup. It is warm, sweet and salty, and a Mexican street classic. Corn brings **fibre and B vitamins**, and the queso fresco brings calcium.
steps: Warm the oil in a pan over high heat and cook the corn, stirring now and then, until it is hot and some kernels are browned, about 6 minutes.
Tip into a cup and stir in the yogurt, lime juice and ground guajillo. Top with queso fresco and cilantro.
ingredients: frozen kernels, no need to thaw
toasted and ground guajillo, or chile powder

name: Baked sweet potato with cinnamon
about: A sweet potato baked until soft and caramelized, split open and dusted with cinnamon. Camotes are sold hot by street vendors in the evening in Mexico City. Sweet potato brings **vitamin A and potassium**.
steps: Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Prick the sweet potato with a fork, put it on a tray and bake until very soft and oozing, about 45 minutes.
Split it open and dust with the cinnamon.
tip: Bake two or three at once and keep them in the fridge; reheat a few minutes in a hot oven or microwave.

name: Guacamole with baked tostadas
about: Chunky avocado mashed with lime, red onion, cilantro and a little tomato, scooped up with crisp baked tortilla chips. It is creamy and fresh. Avocado brings **vitamin E, potassium and healthy fat**.
steps: Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Spread the tortilla triangles on a tray and bake until crisp, about 8 minutes.
Mash the avocado roughly with the lime juice and salt, then fold in the tomato, red onion and cilantro, all finely chopped.
Scoop with the warm chips.

name: Chía fresca with orange
inspiredBy: Chía fresca, the traditional chia agua fresca of Mexico, made with orange instead of sugar
about: Chia seeds plumped in cold water with fresh orange juice and a squeeze of lime, a sweeter take on the classic agua fresca. It is bright and refreshing, and the seeds give it a pearly, jelly-like texture. Chia brings **omega-3, calcium and magnesium**.
steps: Stir the chia into a tall glass of cold water (about 200 ml) and leave it for 10 minutes, stirring once or twice, until it plumps up.
Add the orange juice, lime juice and ice, and stir well.

name: Yogurt with orange and toasted almonds
about: Cold yogurt with juicy orange segments and a handful of toasted almonds. It is simple, creamy and crunchy, and a very easy snack. The yogurt and almonds bring **protein, calcium and vitamin E**.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan for 4 to 5 minutes, until they smell nutty.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl, top with the orange segments and the almonds.

name: Almonds with lime and chile
about: Almonds toasted in a dry pan and tossed with lime juice, ground guajillo and a pinch of salt, in the style of the spiced nuts sold by Mexican street vendors. They are crunchy, warm and tangy. Almonds bring **vitamin E, magnesium and calcium**.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan over medium heat for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring, until they smell nutty.
Toss with the lime juice, ground guajillo and salt while still warm.
ingredients: toasted and ground guajillo, or chile powder

name: Shakshuka masri, eggs in garlicky tomato and red pepper with baladi bread
inspiredBy: Egyptian shakshuka, the home version with plenty of sweet red pepper, garlic and cumin
about: Two eggs set in a thick, garlicky tomato sauce with soft sweet red pepper and a pinch of chili, finished with a spoonful of nutty dukkah and served with warm bread for scooping. The eggs bring **protein and choline**, and the dukkah brings vitamin E.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a small, wide pan. Cook the onion and red pepper over medium heat until the onion is soft and just golden, about 6 minutes.
Add the garlic, cumin, paprika and chili and stir for 30 seconds, until it smells toasty.
Pour in the crushed tomato with the salt and a splash of water. Simmer, stirring now and then, until it turns thick and jammy, about 8 minutes.
Make two little wells with the back of a spoon and crack an egg into each. Cover and cook on low for 4 to 5 minutes, until the whites are set and the yolks are still soft.
Scatter with the parsley and finish with a spoonful of dukkah, the way Egyptians do with eggs. Warm the bread in a dry pan, tear it up and scoop.
tip: Make the tomato sauce the night before and keep it in the fridge. In the morning, heat it, crack in the eggs and breakfast is ready in 8 minutes.

name: Ful medames with tinned sardines, tahini, lemon and cucumber
inspiredBy: Cairo and Alexandria ful, with the tinned sardines many Egyptians keep in the cupboard for a quick plate
about: Warm, creamy fava beans mashed with garlic, cumin and lemon, with tinned sardines broken over the top, a drizzle of tahini and a pile of cucumber, onion and parsley. The beans bring **fibre, folate and iron**, and the sardines add omega-3, B12 and calcium from their soft bones.
steps: Mash the garlic with the salt into a paste. Warm the beans with some of their liquid in a small pot with the garlic and cumin, stirring now and then, until steaming hot, about 5 minutes.
Mash roughly with a fork, leaving some whole beans. Stir in the lemon juice and most of the olive oil.
Stir the tahini with a spoonful of water until it pours like thin cream.
Spoon the ful into a shallow bowl. Break the sardines over the top, drizzle with the tahini and the rest of the oil, and pile on the cucumber, onion and parsley. Add the shatta on the side.
Warm the bread in a dry pan or the toaster, tear it up and scoop.
tip: A tin of ful makes two portions. Keep the other half for the next ful morning, or slow-cook dried fava until creamy in a slow cooker or a pressure cooker.
ingredients: a tin, with a little of its liquid
tinned in water or brine, drained

name: Ful medames with tahini, lemon and a boiled egg
inspiredBy: the Cairo breakfast ful, the way a home cook finishes it with tahini, lemon and an egg
about: Warm, creamy fava beans mashed with garlic, cumin and lemon, with a boiled egg, a drizzle of tahini and a pile of tomato, onion and parsley. The beans bring **fibre, folate and iron**, and the egg adds choline.
steps: Use an egg boiled the night before, or lower one into boiling water for 8 minutes, then cool it under cold water and peel.
Mash the garlic with the salt into a paste. Warm the beans with some of their liquid in a small pot with the garlic and cumin, stirring now and then, until steaming hot, about 5 minutes.
Mash roughly with a fork, leaving some whole beans. Stir in the lemon juice and most of the olive oil.
Stir the tahini with a spoonful of water until it pours like thin cream.
Spoon the ful into a shallow bowl. Drizzle with the tahini and the rest of the oil, pile on the tomato, onion and parsley, and set the halved egg on top. Add the shatta on the side.
Warm the bread in a dry pan or the toaster, tear it up and scoop.
tip: Boil Thursday's and Friday's eggs together on Wednesday night. They keep 4 days in the fridge.
ingredients: a tin, with a little of its liquid

name: Eggs with basterma-style pastrami and tomato, with olives and baladi bread
inspiredBy: the Cairo breakfast of eggs fried with basterma, made here with beef pastrami as the nearest widely sold cured beef
about: Peppery, smoky cured beef crisped in the pan, then softened tomato and red pepper with two eggs cooked right on top and a spoonful of dukkah to finish. Salty and rich, so a little goes a long way. The eggs and beef bring **protein, choline and B12**.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a small pan. Add the pastrami strips and fry for about 2 minutes, until the edges are crisp and it smells peppery and smoky.
Add the tomato and red pepper and cook until they soften, about 4 minutes.

Crack the eggs over the top, sprinkle with the cumin and pepper, cover and cook for 3 to 4 minutes until the whites are set and the yolks still soft. The pastrami is salty, so you should not need extra salt.
Scatter with parsley and finish with a spoonful of dukkah. Serve with the olives and warm bread.
tip: Real basterma has a fenugreek and garlic crust. If you find it at a Middle Eastern shop or an Armenian deli, use it the same way.
ingredients: sliced thin, then cut in strips

name: Sudanese-style ful with egg, white cheese, tomato, sesame and rocket
inspiredBy: the Sudanese breakfast ful, finished with white cheese, sesame and plenty of raw rocket
about: Fava beans mashed with garlic, lemon and chili, with a boiled egg, crumbled white cheese, tomato, onion, toasted sesame and a big handful of peppery rocket. It is a different mood from Egyptian ful. The beans and rocket bring **iron, folate and vitamin K**, and the egg and cheese add choline and calcium.
steps: Use an egg boiled the night before, or lower one into boiling water for 8 minutes, then cool it under cold water and peel.
Toast the sesame seeds in a dry pan until golden and nutty, about 2 minutes.
Mash the garlic with the salt into a paste. Warm the beans with a splash of their liquid, the garlic, cumin and the shatta, stirring, until steaming hot, about 5 minutes.
Mash with a fork until mostly creamy. Stir in the lemon juice and half the olive oil.
Spoon into a shallow bowl. Pour the rest of the olive oil over the middle and scatter on the white cheese, tomato, onion, sesame and rocket. Halve the egg and set it on top.
Warm the bread and tear it up to scoop.
tip: In Sudan the oil is often toasted sesame oil. A teaspoon in place of half the olive oil is lovely. Gebna beida is salty, so taste before adding more salt.
ingredients: a tin, with a little of its liquid

name: Baked green ta'meya with cucumber and rocket salad, tahini and olives
inspiredBy: Egyptian ta'meya, the fava falafel of Cairo and Alexandria, baked instead of deep-fried
about: Green fava patties packed with parsley and dill, crusted in sesame and baked until crisp, with a peppery cucumber and rocket salad, a lemony tahini sauce and a few black olives. The fava and herbs bring **protein, folate, iron and vitamin K**. This makes two portions, so Sunday's breakfast is done.
steps: The night before, cover the fava with plenty of cold water and soak for at least 12 hours. Drain well. Do not cook them first, they should be raw and just soft.
Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Line a tray with parchment and brush it with a little of the oil.
Pulse the fava, parsley, dill, onion, garlic, half the sesame, cumin and salt in a food processor until it looks like coarse green crumbs. It should hold together when you squeeze a handful.
Shape into small flattened patties, about 6 per portion. Press the edges into the rest of the sesame seeds, set them on the tray and brush with the remaining oil.
Bake for 12 minutes, flip, and bake another 10 to 12 minutes until deep golden and crisp outside, still green inside.
While they bake, stir the tahini with half the lemon juice, a pinch of salt and enough water to make a pourable sauce. Toss the cucumber and rocket with the rest of the lemon.

Serve the ta'meya with the salad, the tahini sauce, the olives and warm bread, with a little dukkah for dipping. Keep the second portion for tomorrow's breakfast and re-crisp it in a hot oven or toaster oven for 8 minutes.
tip: Peeled split dried fava from a Middle Eastern grocer gives the greenest, lightest ta'meya. Whole dried fava from the supermarket works too, but peel the skins after soaking. Canned fava will not work, the raw soaked fava is what holds the patties together.
ingredients: dried, soaked overnight, peeled and split if you can find them
half in the mix, half to coat

name: Sardine, tomato and rocket in baladi bread with tahini and lemon
inspiredBy: the Egyptian tinned sardine sandwich, a lunch-hour classic in Cairo
about: Mashed tinned sardines with onion, cumin and lemon, stuffed into a toasted pocket with tomato, rocket and a tahini and lemon sauce with a pinch of dried mint. The soft sardine bones bring **calcium and omega-3**, and it comes together in ten minutes.
steps: Mash the sardines roughly with a fork with half the lemon juice, the cumin, the chili and the onion.
Stir the tahini with the olive oil, the dried mint, the salt and a spoonful of water to make a thick sauce.
Split the pita and toast it for a minute in a dry pan or toaster.
Spread the sauce inside, then fill with the sardines, tomato, rocket and parsley. Squeeze the rest of the lemon over the top and eat it right away.
tip: Pack the pita, filling and salad separately if you are taking it to work and assemble at lunch so the bread stays crisp.
ingredients: tinned in water or brine, drained

name: Tinned mackerel in garlicky tomato with salata baladi and baladi bread
inspiredBy: a cheap, quick Cairo supper of tinned fish warmed in tomato and scooped up with bread, with the everyday salad on the side
about: Tinned mackerel warmed through in a garlicky, cumin-scented tomato sauce, scooped up with warm bread, with a crunchy salata baladi of cucumber, tomato, onion and parsley on the side. The mackerel brings **omega-3, B12 and vitamin D**, and the cooked tomato brings lycopene and vitamin C.
steps: Warm the olive oil with the crushed garlic in a small pan over low heat for 1 minute, without letting it brown.
Add the crushed tomato, cumin, chili, half the lemon juice and half the salt. Simmer for about 4 minutes, until it thickens.
Flake in the mackerel and warm it through for 2 minutes. Do not stir too hard, you want big flakes.
Toss the cucumber, fresh tomato, onion and parsley with the rest of the lemon juice and a pinch of salt.
Warm the bread in a dry pan. Scoop the mackerel and sauce up with the bread and eat the salad alongside.
tip: Tinned sardines work the same way. Mash the soft bones in with a fork for extra calcium.

name: Molokhia with chicken and brown rice, with garlic and coriander taqliya
inspiredBy: Cairo molokhia, the green jute leaf soup, served over brown rice rather than white
about: Silky, deep green jute leaves in chicken broth, finished with a sizzle of garlic and coriander, spooned over brown rice and tender chicken, with sharp onion in vinegar on the side. The jute brings **vitamins A and K, folate and calcium**, and the chicken and rice make it a full meal.
steps: Start the brown rice first, in a pot with twice its volume of water. It needs about 40 minutes.

Put the chicken, the quartered onion, bay leaf, cardamom, pepper and half the salt in another pot with enough water to cover, about 700 ml for two portions. Simmer, covered, until the chicken is just tender, 18 to 20 minutes.
Lift out the chicken and keep it warm. Strain the broth back into the pot and bring it to a gentle simmer.
Stir in the molokhia, still frozen is fine, and the rest of the salt. Bring back to a gentle simmer, not a hard boil, and cook for 5 minutes. It should be glossy and fall off the spoon in ribbons.

Make the taqliya. Warm the olive oil in a small pan and fry the garlic with the ground coriander for 1 to 2 minutes, until the garlic is just golden. Do not let it brown. Tip it sizzling into the pot and stir once.
Toss a few thin slices of raw onion with the vinegar and a pinch of salt.

Serve the rice with the molokhia ladled over and the chicken on top, with the onions and lemon wedges on the side. Squeeze the lemon over at the table, since it dulls the green if it cooks. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the rice in a separate container.
tip: Ghee is the traditional fat for the taqliya, and a teaspoon of it is delicious here if you have some. Molokhia freezes well, so a double batch makes a quick dinner later.
ingredients: frozen minced molokhia, or fresh, or dried
quartered, plus a little thinly sliced

name: Koshari with lentils, chickpeas and a little pasta
inspiredBy: Cairo koshari, reimagined with brown rice and lentils doing most of the work, and a small handful of whole-wheat pasta
about: The Cairo street classic: lentils, rice, pasta and chickpeas under a spiced tomato sauce, crisp onions and a sharp garlic and vinegar splash. Here it leans on lentils and chickpeas for **fibre, iron and slow carbs**, with less rice and pasta than the street version.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the sliced onions with most of the oil and a pinch of salt and spread them in a single layer over two trays. Roast for 25 to 30 minutes, flipping once, until deep golden. They crisp up as they cool.
Simmer the brown rice alone in plenty of water for 10 minutes. Add the lentils and half the cumin and simmer for about 22 minutes more, until both are tender. Drain and season with a pinch of salt.
Cook the pasta in boiling salted water until just al dente, then drain.

For the sauce, warm the rest of the oil and half the garlic (finely chopped) over low heat for 1 minute. Stir in the tomato paste, the crushed tomato, the rest of the cumin, the coriander, cinnamon and salt. Simmer for 12 minutes until thick, then stir in the chickpeas to warm through.
Crush the remaining garlic and stir it into the vinegar with a splash of water. This is the daqqa.

Pile the lentils and rice into bowls, top with the pasta, the saucy chickpeas and the crispy onions. Spoon over the garlic vinegar, scatter with parsley and add a spoonful of shatta at the table. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the onions in a separate container.
tip: Cook the lentil and rice base on Sunday and keep it in the fridge, then koshari is a 25-minute job. Re-crisp the leftover onions in a dry pan before you eat them.

name: Alexandrian grilled sardines with cumin and lemon, tahini sauce and baladi salad
inspiredBy: the grilled sardines of Alexandria's fish markets, rubbed with cumin and garlic
about: Fresh sardines rubbed with garlic, cumin and lemon, grilled until the skin blisters, with a lemony tahini sauce, a crunchy tomato, cucumber, carrot and parsley salad and warm bread. The sardines bring **omega-3, vitamin D, B12 and calcium**.
steps: Mash half the garlic with the salt, then stir in the cumin, paprika, chili, half the oil and half the lemon juice. Rub this all over the sardines, inside and out, and leave them for 15 minutes.
Heat the broiler (or a grill pan or barbecue) as hot as it goes. Cook the sardines for 3 to 4 minutes on each side, until the skin is blistered and the flesh flakes off the bone.
Make the tahini sauce. Mash the rest of the garlic, stir in the tahini and half the remaining lemon juice, and thin with water until it pours like cream.
Toss the tomato, cucumber, carrot, onion and parsley with the rest of the lemon juice and oil and a pinch of salt.
Serve the sardines hot with the salad, the tahini sauce and warm bread.
tip: Ask the fishmonger to gut and scale the sardines. If you cannot find fresh ones, mackerel fillets work the same way.

name: Bamia bil lahma, okra and beef in garlicky tomato, with brown rice
inspiredBy: Egyptian bamia, the okra and meat stew every Cairo family makes, with a garlic and coriander taqliya
about: Tender okra and small chunks of beef simmered in a thick tomato sauce, finished with a sizzle of garlic and coriander, over brown rice. Okra is **rich in fibre, folate and vitamin K**, and the garlic and tomato make it taste like Friday lunch.
steps: Brown the beef in half the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat, about 5 minutes. Add the onion and cook until golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the tomato paste, the crushed tomato, the bay leaf, the pepper, half the salt and 250 ml of water. Cover and simmer gently for about 55 minutes, until the beef is nearly tender.
Start the rice in a separate pot with twice its volume of water about 35 minutes before the end, and cook until fluffy.
Add the okra whole, trimming only the stems, and simmer for another 15 minutes, until tender. Do not stir too much, it will turn slimy. Shake the pot instead.
Fry the sliced garlic with the ground coriander in the rest of the oil until golden, about 1 minute, then tip the sizzling taqliya into the pot with the lemon juice.
Serve over the rice, scattered with parsley. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: A pressure cooker cuts the beef to about 20 minutes, which makes this a weeknight dish. Cut the okra without piercing the pods and do not soak it, so it stays firm.
ingredients: small whole pods, frozen is fine

name: Sudanese chicken and peanut mullah with spinach, sorghum asida and rocket
inspiredBy: Sudanese mullah dakwa, the peanut and tomato stew, with asida made from sorghum
about: Chicken simmered with onion, tomato, ginger and ground roasted peanuts into a thick, rich stew with spinach folded in, mounded around a soft sorghum asida with a peppery rocket salad. The chicken, peanuts and spinach bring **protein, vitamin E, magnesium and folate**.
steps: Grind the peanuts with a splash of water in a mortar or small blender until they make a coarse paste. This is the dakwa.

Brown the chicken in the olive oil for 4 to 5 minutes. Lift it out. In the same pot, cook the onion until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic, baharat, cumin, ginger and chili and stir for 1 minute.
Stir in the tomato paste, then the crushed tomato and salt. Simmer for 5 minutes, then return the chicken with 300 ml of water. Cover and simmer for 20 minutes.

Stir a ladle of the sauce into the peanut paste to loosen it, then stir it all into the pot. Simmer uncovered for 10 minutes more, until thick and the oil shines at the edges. Fold in the spinach for the last 2 minutes and add the lemon juice.

Meanwhile, make the asida for tonight only. Whisk all the sorghum flour with twice its weight of cold water until smooth. Bring another twice its weight of salted water to a boil, pour in the paste while whisking, then switch to a wooden spoon and beat hard over low heat for 6 to 8 minutes, until stiff, smooth and glossy. Shape into a mound in a bowl and make a well.

Spoon the mullah into the well and serve the rocket dressed with a squeeze of lemon alongside. Asida is best fresh, so pack the second portion of mullah, with its rocket in a separate box, for tomorrow's lunch with warm pita or rice.
tip: A tablespoon of natural peanut butter stands in for the ground peanuts. Ghee is the traditional fat in Sudan and is delicious here.
ingredients: baladi bread or whole-wheat pita, for tomorrow's portion

name: Alexandrian sayadeya, spiced mackerel over caramelized onion and cumin brown rice
inspiredBy: Alexandria's sayadeya, the fisherman's rice, made with brown rice and baked mackerel instead of fried fish
about: Deeply caramelized onions and cumin cooked into brown rice, topped with spice-rubbed mackerel, sweet browned onions and a few toasted almonds, with a bright tomato and parsley relish. It is Alexandria's weekend dish. The mackerel brings **omega-3 and B12**, and the almonds add vitamin E.
steps: Cook the onions in half the oil in a wide, heavy pot over medium-low heat, stirring often, for 25 to 30 minutes, until deep brown and sweet. Add a splash of water if they start to catch. Set a third of them aside for the top.

Add half the garlic and most of the cumin to the pot, then the rice. Stir for 1 minute, then add about 2.2 times the rice's volume of boiling water and half the salt. Cover and cook on low for 35 to 40 minutes, until the rice is tender. Rest, covered, for 5 minutes.
Heat the oven to 230°C (450°F). Mash the rest of the garlic with the remaining cumin, the chili, a little of the lemon juice and the rest of the oil, and rub it all over the mackerel.
Roast the mackerel skin-side up for 10 to 12 minutes, until the skin crackles and the flesh flakes.
Toss the tomato with the parsley, the rest of the lemon juice and a pinch of salt.
Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes.

Spoon the rice onto plates, top with the mackerel, the reserved onions and the almonds, and serve the relish beside it. Keep the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the fish, rice and relish in separate containers. Reheat the rice with a splash of water. The fish is good cold or warm.
tip: Make the onions the day before, they are the slow part, and the whole dinner comes together in 45 minutes. Mullet or sea bass is what Alexandrians use, and either works here too.

name: Kebda Iskandarani, chicken liver with garlic, cumin and sweet pepper in baladi bread
inspiredBy: Alexandria's street-corner liver, a favourite sandwich in Egypt's port city, made with chicken liver
about: Quick-seared chicken liver with plenty of garlic, cumin and red pepper, finished with lemon, stuffed in warm bread with tomato and a garlicky yogurt sauce, with roasted sweet potato wedges and crisp chickpeas on the side. Liver is one of the richest foods for **iron, B12 and vitamin A**, and a small portion once a week is plenty. Skip it if you are pregnant or planning to be.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the sweet potato wedges and the chickpeas with a third of the oil, half the cumin and half the salt on a tray and roast for 30 minutes, turning once, until the wedges are golden and soft and the chickpeas are a little crisp.
Stir a little crushed garlic and a pinch of salt into the yogurt and set aside. Crush the rest of the garlic with the remaining salt and cumin.

Pat the liver dry. Heat the rest of the oil in a wide pan until very hot. Add the liver in one layer, then the red pepper and the garlic mix, and cook, tossing, for about 4 minutes in all, until the liver is browned and no pink remains. Overcooked liver goes dry, so do not go much past that.
Squeeze over the lemon juice and stir in the parsley.

Split the warm bread, spread a spoonful of the garlic yogurt inside and tuck in the tomato and liver. Serve the rest of the yogurt as a dip for the wedges and chickpeas, with the shatta for those who want it.
tip: Soaking the liver in milk or lemon water for 15 minutes mellows the flavour if you are new to liver. In Alexandria it is often served with tahini too.

name: Hummus el-sham, warm cumin chickpeas with lemon
inspiredBy: hummus el-sham, the warm chickpeas sold in paper cups on Cairo street corners
about: Chickpeas warmed with cumin, olive oil and a squeeze of lemon, like the cups sold at Cairo street corners. A bowl brings **plant protein and fibre**.
steps: Warm the chickpeas with the olive oil, cumin and a splash of the tin's liquid in a small pan or the microwave for 2 to 3 minutes.
Add the lemon juice, salt and pepper, and eat warm.

name: Termis (lupini beans) with lemon and cumin
inspiredBy: termis, the lupini beans sold from Egyptian street carts
about: Firm, salty lupini beans tossed with lemon and cumin, a famous Egyptian street snack. They bring **plant protein and fibre** for very few calories.
steps: Rinse the lupini and toss with the lemon, cumin and salt.
Squeeze each bean out of its skin with your fingers and eat the soft inside, or eat them whole.

name: Sardines with tomato and shatta on baladi bread
inspiredBy: sardin ala el-eish, tinned sardines mashed onto warm bread with a kick of shatta, a quick Cairo bite
about: Tinned sardines mashed with lemon and a spoonful of shatta, piled onto warm bread and topped with sliced tomato. The soft sardine bones bring **calcium and omega-3**.
steps: Warm the bread in a dry pan or the toaster.
Mash the sardines with the lemon, shatta and pepper, pile onto the bread and lay the tomato on top.
ingredients: tinned in water or brine, drained

name: Carrot, orange and almond smoothie
inspiredBy: carrot and orange juice from Cairo juice bars, thickened with almonds as in a koktail
about: Carrots and an orange blended into a sweet, golden drink with a few almonds for body, like the corner juice stands in Cairo. The carrots bring **a full day of vitamin A**, and the almonds and orange bring vitamin E and vitamin C. Keep the pulp in for fibre.
steps: Soak the almonds in warm water for 10 minutes, then drain. Grate the carrots.
Blend the carrots, orange, almonds and about 100 ml of cold water for 2 minutes, until as smooth as it will go.
Add the lemon juice, taste, and serve over ice. Add a little more water if it is too thick.

name: Roasted sweet potato with cinnamon and a squeeze of lemon
inspiredBy: batata, the roasted sweet potato sold from carts on winter streets in Cairo
about: A hot roasted sweet potato with a pinch of cinnamon and a squeeze of lemon, like the carts on Cairo corners in winter. It brings **vitamin A and fibre**.
steps: Prick the sweet potato and microwave it for 8 minutes, or roast at 200°C (400°F) for about 45 minutes for the best flavour, until it is soft and collapses when squeezed.
Split it open and sprinkle with the cinnamon, lemon juice and salt.
tip: Roast it on Tuesday next to the koshari onions, since the oven is already hot, and rewarm it on Wednesday.

name: Zabadi with chopped dates and cinnamon
inspiredBy: plain yogurt with dates, the way a Nile Valley kitchen would sweeten it
about: Plain yogurt with chopped dates and cinnamon, sweetened by the fruit. The yogurt brings **protein and calcium**.
steps: Stir the chopped date into the yogurt, then sprinkle with the cinnamon.
ingredients: ½ medjool or 2 small dates, chopped

name: Dates stuffed with almonds
inspiredBy: the almond-stuffed dates of Egyptian and Sudanese tea tables
about: Soft dates stuffed with whole almonds, served with tea in many Nile Valley homes. The almonds bring **vitamin E and magnesium**.
steps: Slit the dates and remove the pits. Tuck an almond into each date, and eat the rest of the almonds alongside.

name: Dates with tahini
inspiredBy: dates and tahini, a sweet, nutty pairing from the Egyptian breakfast table
