Warm the oil in the same pot. Add the mustard seeds, and when they pop, add the urad dal and the peanuts. Stir for about a minute, until the dal turns golden and the peanuts smell roasted. This is the tempering (thalippu), and the urad dal is what gives upma its nutty crunch.

Add the curry leaves (stand back, they spit), the green chili, ginger and two thirds of the onion. Cook until the onion is soft and glassy, about 4 minutes. Spoon a quarter of this mixture into a small bowl for the eggs.

Stir the green beans into the pot for 1 minute. Add the toasted millet, half the salt and a little over twice as much water as millet. Bring to a boil, then cover and cook on low until the water is absorbed and the millet is tender, about 15 minutes.

While the millet cooks, make the podimas. Warm a small non-stick pan, add the spoonful of onion mixture and the rest of the raw onion and cook for a minute. Beat in the eggs with the rest of the salt and stir gently until just set and still glossy, about 2 minutes.
Rest the upma covered for 5 minutes, then fluff with a fork. Serve with the egg podimas and a bowl of curd.
tip: Make the upma the night before and reheat it with a splash of water while the eggs cook, or use a pressure cooker and have it ready in 10 minutes.

name: Lemon foxtail millet with peanuts and chickpeas, and cucumber pachadi
inspiredBy: Karnataka chitranna (lemon rice) made with foxtail millet, with chickpeas as in a Tamil sundal
about: Fluffy foxtail millet tossed with mustard seed, urad dal, peanuts, ginger and a good squeeze of lemon, with chickpeas folded in and a cooling cucumber pachadi on the side. It is a lunchbox favourite across Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. The chickpeas and curd make it a **filling, protein-rich** lunch.
steps: Rinse the millet, drain it and cook it in a little over twice its volume of water with a pinch of the salt, covered, until tender and fluffy, about 15 minutes. Spread it on a plate for a few minutes so the grains stay separate.

Warm the oil in a wide pan. Add the mustard seeds, and when they pop, add the urad dal, the peanuts and the dried chili and fry until the dal is golden. This is the tempering (thalippu), and it is what makes lemon millet taste like lemon millet. Spoon a little of the tempering into a small cup and keep it for the pachadi.
Add the curry leaves (stand back, they spit), the ginger and turmeric to the pan and stir for 30 seconds. Add the chickpeas and warm them through for 2 minutes.
Fold in the millet and the rest of the salt, then take the pan off the heat and stir in the lemon juice. Adding the lemon off the heat keeps it fresh and bright.
Squeeze the grated cucumber dry and stir it into the curd with a pinch of salt, then stir in the reserved tempering. Serve the pachadi alongside the millet.

name: Moong dal and cabbage kootu with carrot poriyal and brown rice
inspiredBy: Tamil muttaikose kootu and carrot poriyal, the classic home lunch plate
about: A gentle, coconut-scented kootu of split moong dal and soft cabbage, alongside a sweet carrot poriyal tempered with mustard and urad dal, with brown rice and a bowl of curd. It is the sort of plate you would be served at a Tamil home lunch. The moong brings **protein, folate and iron**, and the carrot brings **vitamin A**.
steps: Rinse the brown rice and cook it in plenty of boiling water until tender, about 30 minutes, then drain.
Rinse the moong dal and simmer it with the turmeric, half the salt and about 3 cups of water until soft but not mushy, about 15 minutes.

Stir the cabbage into the dal and cook until it is soft and sweet, about 6 minutes. Crush half the coconut with the cumin and one of the dried chilies in a mortar into a rough paste, stir it in and simmer for 2 minutes. This is the kootu.

Now the tempering (thalippu). Warm the oil in a small pan, add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then add the urad dal, the other dried chili and the curry leaves (stand back, they spit) and fry until the dal is golden. Pour half over the kootu.

Stir the grated carrot into the rest of the tempering with the remaining salt and a splash of water. Cover and cook for 5 to 6 minutes, until just tender, then uncover and stir in the rest of the coconut. This dry stir-fry is the poriyal.
Serve the kootu and the poriyal over the rice with the curd on the side.
tip: Use bottle gourd, ash gourd or zucchini in place of the cabbage for a different kootu.

name: Pepper rasam cup
inspiredBy: Tamil milagu rasam (pepper rasam)
about: A thin, tangy, peppery soup of tomato, tamarind, garlic and a little dal, with a mustard, dried chili and curry leaf tempering. Rasam is the South Indian cure for everything, and a hot cup in the afternoon is lovely. It has **vitamin C and lycopene** from the tomato.
steps: Mash the cooked dhal with a splash of hot water until it is smooth and thin.

Put the tomato, tamarind, half the garlic, half the pepper, half the cumin, the salt and 1 cup of water in a small pot. Simmer for 8 minutes, until the tomato has collapsed. Stir in the dhal and simmer 2 minutes.

Now the tempering. Warm the oil in a small pan, add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then the rest of the cumin, pepper and garlic, the dried chili, the hing and the curry leaves (stand back, they spit), and pour it over the rasam. Sip it hot.
ingredients: two spoonfuls of leftover cooked dhal, or red lentils cooked soft
a piece of whole dried red chili

name: Moong kosambari
inspiredBy: Karnataka hesaru bele kosambari
about: A cool, crunchy Karnataka salad of soaked split moong dal, cucumber and coconut with lemon and a mustard seed tempering. It is a temple and festival favourite and it is light, with **protein and fibre**.
steps: Toss the soaked moong dal with the cucumber, coconut and finely chopped green chili in a bowl.
Warm the oil in a small pan, add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then add the curry leaves for a few seconds and pour the sizzling oil over the salad.
Add the salt and lemon juice, toss and eat within the hour while the dal is still crunchy.
ingredients: moong dal, soaked in water for 1 to 2 hours and drained

name: Boiled peanut sundal
inspiredBy: Tamil verkadalai sundal
about: Fresh peanuts simmered until tender and tossed with mustard seed, curry leaf, green chili and fresh coconut, a favourite street snack on the Tamil coast. It is hearty, with **protein and magnesium**.
steps: Soak the peanuts in cold water for 4 hours, then drain. Cover them with fresh water, add a pinch of the salt and simmer until tender, about 35 minutes. Drain them.
Warm the oil in a pan, add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then the curry leaves and chopped green chili for a few seconds.
Add the peanuts and the rest of the salt and toss for 2 minutes. Off the heat, stir in the coconut and lemon juice.

name: Papaya with lemon
about: Ripe papaya in bite-sized chunks with a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of black pepper, a soft, fragrant fruit snack. The papaya brings **vitamin C and vitamin A**.
steps: Scoop out the seeds and cut the papaya into chunks.
Squeeze the lemon over the top and add a pinch of freshly ground pepper.

name: Boiled egg with lunu miris
inspiredBy: Sri Lankan lunu miris
about: A hard-boiled egg halved and topped with lunu miris, the Sri Lankan relish of onion pounded with chili, lemon and salt. It is hot, sour and savoury, and it is a very easy snack. The egg brings **protein and choline**.
steps: Hard-boil the egg for 9 minutes, cool it in cold water, peel and halve it.
Pound the onion with the chili powder, lemon juice and salt into a wet red relish and spoon it over the egg.

name: Papaya with soaked almonds and lemon
about: Ripe papaya in bite-sized chunks with a few soaked almonds, a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of black pepper. It is soft, sweet and a little crunchy, and it gives you **vitamin C, vitamin A and vitamin E**.
steps: Scoop out the seeds and cut the papaya into chunks. Drain the soaked almonds.
Squeeze the lemon over the papaya, scatter the almonds on top and add a pinch of freshly ground pepper.
ingredients: soaked in water for a few hours or overnight

name: Badam lassi
inspiredBy: South Indian badam paal, as a lassi
about: Cold yogurt blended with soaked almonds, a pinch of cardamom and a splash of water into a thick, cooling drink, a South Indian take on badam milk. The almonds bring **vitamin E and magnesium**, and the yogurt brings calcium.
steps: Slip the skins off the soaked almonds so the lassi blends smooth. Put the curd, the almonds, the cardamom and about a quarter cup of cold water in a blender.
Blend until completely smooth and serve over ice.
tip: Blend in a little ripe papaya or a pinch of jaggery for a sweeter drink.
ingredients: soaked in water for a few hours or overnight and drained

name: South African oats with apricots, almonds and cinnamon
inspiredBy: South African oats porridge, with dried apricots and cinnamon
about: Creamy oats cooked in milk with chopped dried apricots and a good pinch of cinnamon, topped with toasted almonds. It is warm, gently sweet and ready in about 10 minutes. The almonds bring **vitamin E and magnesium**, and the milk adds calcium and protein.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan over medium heat until golden and nutty, about 3 minutes. Chop them roughly.
Put the oats, milk, apricots, cinnamon and salt in a small pot.
Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat, stirring often, until the oats are thick and creamy, about 6 minutes. Loosen with a splash of water if it gets too thick.
Spoon into a bowl and scatter the almonds over the top.
tip: Chop the apricots small so they melt into the porridge and sweeten it, with no sugar needed. Leave out the apricots and stir in a sliced ripe pear if you have no dried fruit.

name: Eggs in chakalaka with beans
inspiredBy: South African chakalaka, the spicy vegetable relish served at every braai, cooked into a breakfast skillet with beans and eggs
about: Soft eggs set in a spicy tomato, pepper and carrot chakalaka with a few beans and a handful of spinach, the way South Africans love their baked beans and eggs. It is hearty, bright and a little hot. The eggs and beans bring **protein, choline and folate**.
steps: Warm the oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Cook the onion, green pepper and carrot until soft and starting to colour, about 6 minutes.
Stir in the garlic, chakalaka spice and cayenne and cook for 1 minute, until it smells toasty.
Add the tomato, beans and salt and simmer, stirring, until the tomato is jammy, about 6 minutes. Stir in the spinach until just wilted.
Make two wells in the chakalaka and crack an egg into each. Cover and cook gently until the whites are just set and the yolks are still soft, 4 to 5 minutes.
Toast the bread and serve it alongside for scooping up the eggs and the sauce.
tip: Cook the chakalaka (steps 1 to 3) the evening before, while the bobotie bakes or the umngqusho simmers. Reheat it in the morning, crack in the eggs and breakfast takes 6 minutes.
ingredients: sugar beans or pinto beans, drained

name: Mabele sorghum porridge with amasi, guava, peanuts and sunflower seeds
inspiredBy: Mabele, the sorghum porridge of Botswana, Lesotho and South Africa, eaten soft with amasi (fermented milk), made here with whole sorghum cooked soft
about: A soft, slightly nutty sorghum porridge (mabele) topped with cold, tangy amasi, ripe guava and toasted peanuts and sunflower seeds. The sorghum, peanuts and seeds bring **iron, magnesium and vitamin E**, and the amasi adds calcium and protein.
steps: The night before, rinse the sorghum and soak it in plenty of cold water. Make enough for two mornings.

In the evening, drain the sorghum and put it in a pot with about three times as much fresh water and the salt. Bring to a boil, then simmer partly covered, stirring now and then, until the grains are tender and the porridge is thick, about 50 minutes. Top up with a splash of water if it gets dry. A pressure cooker does it in about 20 minutes.

Beat the porridge hard with a wooden spoon and mash some of the grains against the side of the pot, until it is soft and spoonable. This makes two portions, so cool both, cover and keep them in the fridge.

Next morning, toast the peanuts and sunflower seeds in a dry pan for 3 minutes. Warm one portion with a splash of water, spoon it into a bowl and pour the amasi over it. Top with the guava and the toasted nuts and seeds.
The next day, warm the second portion and top it the same way.
tip: Cook it in the evening while dinner simmers, so breakfast is only a reheat. If you cannot find amasi, kefir or buttermilk is just as tangy. Use a ripe peach or a few strawberries when guava is not in season.
ingredients: plain kefir or buttermilk, for the amasi

name: Pilchards in tomato with soft pap and tomato and onion sambal
inspiredBy: South African pilchards and pap, the classic tinned fish lunch, with a fresh tomato and onion sambal
about: Canned pilchards warmed with onion, garlic and a handful of morogo-style greens, spooned over soft maize pap with a sharp tomato and onion sambal on the side. It is cheap, fast and a proper South African lunch. The pilchards bring **omega-3, vitamin B12 and calcium** from their soft bones.
steps: Make the sambal first so the flavours meet. Slice half the onion very thin and chop half the tomato. Toss them with the lemon juice, a pinch of cayenne, a pinch of salt and the cilantro, and leave it to sit.

Bring a pot of water to a boil, about five times the weight of the meal for a soft, spoonable pap, with a pinch of salt. Whisk in the cornmeal in a slow stream so there are no lumps. Turn the heat to low, cover and cook, stirring often, until the pap is thick and soft, about 15 minutes.
While the pap cooks, warm the oil in a small pan. Cook the rest of the onion and the garlic until soft, about 4 minutes. Add the remaining tomato and cook until saucy, about 3 minutes.
Tip in the pilchards with their sauce and break them up gently. Add the spinach and warm everything through until the spinach has just wilted, about 3 minutes.
Spoon the pap onto a plate, top with the pilchards and serve the sambal alongside.
tip: Use plain white cornmeal (whole-grain if you can find it), not masa harina or precooked arepa flour. Sardines in tomato sauce work if you cannot find pilchards.
ingredients: pilchards or sardines, with their tomato sauce
split between the sambal and the pan
half sliced thin for the sambal

name: Bobotie-inspired lentil and beef bake with turmeric rice and carrot sambal
inspiredBy: Cape Malay bobotie, spiced mince baked under an egg custard, with lentils sharing the work and brown rice for the usual yellow rice
about: Gently spiced beef and lentils with apricots and chutney, baked under a golden egg and milk custard, with turmeric brown rice and a bright carrot sambal. It is sweet, savoury and comforting, and it is even better the next day. The beef and lentils together bring **iron, zinc and plenty of protein**.
steps: Heat the oven to 180C (350F). Rinse the rice and put it in a pot with plenty of water and half the turmeric. Simmer, covered, until tender, about 35 minutes, then drain. Make enough for two portions.
At the same time, simmer the lentils in plenty of water until just tender, about 25 minutes, and drain.
Warm the oil in a large pan. Cook the onion until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic, Cape Malay masala, cinnamon and the rest of the turmeric and cook for 1 minute, until fragrant.
Add the beef and break it up as it browns, about 6 minutes. Stir in the lentils, chutney, apricots, half the lemon juice, salt and a splash of water. Simmer for 5 minutes, until moist but not wet.

Press the mixture into a baking dish and tuck the bay leaves on top. Beat the eggs with the milk and a pinch of salt and pour this over. Bake until the custard is set and lightly golden, about 25 minutes.
While it bakes, toss the grated carrot with the remaining lemon juice and a pinch of salt for the sambal.
Serve a portion of bobotie with the rice and the carrot sambal. This makes two portions, so pack the second for tomorrow's lunch. It reheats well, or eat it cold.
tip: Use lean ground lamb if you like, which is also very Cape. For extra tang, serve a spoonful of chutney on the side.

name: Cape Malay-style mackerel and butternut curry with spinach
inspiredBy: Cape Malay fish curry, with tamarind for the sour note and butternut for sweetness
about: Chunks of mackerel simmered gently in a tomato and tamarind curry with sweet butternut and spinach, finished with lemon and cilantro. It is fragrant rather than fiery, with the sweet and sour balance the Cape does so well. The butternut adds **vitamin A**, and mackerel is a rich source of **omega-3, vitamin B12 and vitamin D**.
steps: Peel the butternut and cut it into 2 cm chunks. Cut the mackerel into big chunks, leaving the skin on, and sprinkle with half the salt and a little of the turmeric.
Warm the oil in a wide pot over medium heat. Cook the onion until soft and golden, about 8 minutes.
Add the garlic, Cape Malay masala and the rest of the turmeric. Stir for 1 minute until it smells wonderful.
Add the tomato, tamarind, chutney and a mug of water, then add the butternut. Cover and simmer until it is nearly tender, about 12 minutes.

Nestle the mackerel into the sauce, cover and cook gently until it flakes, 6 to 8 minutes. Do not stir hard or the fish will break up. Fold in the spinach for the last 2 minutes, just until it wilts, then add the lemon juice, cilantro and the rest of the salt.
This makes two portions. Pack the second for tomorrow's lunch and reheat it gently.
tip: Serve with rice or a roti for a bigger plate. Any oily fish works, such as sardines or fresh snoek if you have it.
ingredients: fillets with skin, cut in chunks

name: Zimbabwean beef stew with peanut greens and sadza
inspiredBy: Zimbabwean sadza ne nyama with muriwo une dovi, greens cooked in ground peanuts (a peanut butter sauce)
about: Slow-simmered beef in a tomato and onion gravy, with collard greens cooked in crushed roasted peanuts, and a modest portion of sadza to scoop it all up. It is the everyday Zimbabwean plate, and the greens make it so much more than meat and starch. Beef and greens together bring **iron, zinc and B12**, and the collards add calcium.
steps: Warm half the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat. Brown the beef in batches until deeply browned, about 8 minutes, and set aside.
In the same pot, cook two thirds of the onion until soft. Add the garlic, black pepper, bay leaves and cayenne, then the tomato, and cook until it breaks down into a sauce, about 6 minutes.

Return the beef to the pot with enough water to just cover it. Cover and simmer very gently until the beef is tender and the gravy is thick, about 90 minutes, or 35 minutes in a pressure cooker. Season with the salt near the end. This makes two portions.

For the greens, soften the rest of the onion in the remaining oil in a wide pan. Add the collards with a splash of water and cook, covered, for 6 minutes, then add the spinach and cook until both are silky and tender, about 4 more minutes. Stir in the crushed peanuts and a spoonful of the stew gravy and cook for 2 more minutes, until glossy and not wet.

For the sadza, bring water to a boil, about three times the weight of the meal. Stir a third of the meal with a splash of cold water to a slurry, whisk it into the boiling water and simmer for 5 minutes. Add the rest in handfuls, beating hard with a wooden spoon, then cover and cook on low for 5 minutes. Beat again until stiff and smooth.
Serve the sadza with the beef and the greens. Pack the second portion of stew and greens for tomorrow's lunch, and make a fresh small pot of sadza then, or reheat the leftover with a splash of water.
tip: A pressure cooker makes this a weeknight dish: 35 minutes for the beef. A spoonful of smooth peanut butter can stand in for the crushed peanuts. Collards stand in for the rape greens (kale-like) Zimbabweans use. Kale or chard work too, and amaranth leaves (morogo) are the traditional choice if you can find them.
ingredients: like Zimbabwean rape greens, ribs removed and sliced thin
whole-grain white mealie meal, for the sadza

name: Chakalaka and beans with boerewors-style patties and sweet potato
inspiredBy: South African chakalaka and beans, with lean patties seasoned like boerewors (coriander, clove and nutmeg) instead of the fatty sausage
about: A thick, spicy vegetable and bean stew, chakalaka, with juicy herb-and-spice pork patties seasoned like boerewors, and roasted sweet potato wedges to catch the sauce. It is the comfort food of any South African table. The beans and vegetables bring **fibre, folate and vitamin C**, and the sweet potato adds vitamin A.
steps: Cut the sweet potato into wedges and roast on a tray at 220C (425F) until soft and browned at the edges, about 25 minutes, turning once.
Mix the pork with the grated onion, boerewors spice, lemon juice and half the salt. The grated onion keeps lean pork juicy. Shape into patties and let them rest for 10 minutes.
Warm the oil in a wide pan. Cook the diced onion, green pepper and carrot until soft, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic, chakalaka spice and cayenne and cook for 1 minute.
Add the tomato and simmer until thick, about 10 minutes. Stir in the beans and the rest of the salt and cook until the chakalaka is thick and jammy, about 8 minutes.
Pan-fry the patties in a non-stick pan over medium heat, using a little of the oil, until well browned and cooked through, about 4 minutes per side.
Stir the cilantro into the chakalaka. Serve the patties on the beans with the sweet potato wedges alongside.
This makes two portions. Pack the second for tomorrow's lunch. The patties are good cold or reheated in a pan.
tip: Ground pork is usually 80/20. Ask for a lean grind, or use lean ground beef or lamb. Cook the chakalaka a day ahead: it only improves.
ingredients: 30 g grated for the patties, the rest diced
chopped, or use a can of crushed
pinto beans in place of sugar beans, drained

name: Umngqusho, samp and beans with lamb and greens
inspiredBy: Xhosa umngqusho, the slow-cooked samp and sugar bean dish, with a little lamb for flavour and greens folded in
about: Sugar beans and a little samp (dried hominy) simmered with lamb, onion, garlic and a little butter, finished with tomato, collard greens and cilantro. It is slow, filling food from the Eastern Cape. Beans and samp together bring **fibre, iron and folate**, the collards add calcium and the lamb adds zinc and B12.
steps: The night before, soak the samp in plenty of cold water. Drain it in the morning.

Melt the butter with the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat. Brown the lamb for about 6 minutes, then add the onion and cook until soft, about 6 minutes. Stir in the garlic, bay leaves, black pepper and cayenne.

Add the drained samp and enough water to cover by two finger widths. Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer gently, stirring now and then and topping up the water, until the samp is very tender and creamy, about 2 hours, or 45 minutes in a pressure cooker.
With 30 minutes left, stir in the beans and tomato and cook uncovered, mashing a few beans against the side of the pot so they melt into the samp.
Fold in the collards and cook for 8 minutes, until silky and tender. Stir in the cilantro and the salt.
This makes two portions. Pack the second for tomorrow's lunch. The pot keeps 4 days in the fridge, and freezes well.
tip: Real samp and sugar beans from a South African shop swap in by weight. Borlotti is the closest canned bean. Canned hominy, rinsed, also works: add it with the beans and the pot is ready in 40 minutes. Short on time? A pressure cooker makes dried samp a weeknight option.
ingredients: dried hominy, in place of samp, soaked overnight
pinto beans in place of sugar beans, canned, drained

name: Peri-peri chicken and livers with roasted butternut and spinach salad
inspiredBy: Mozambican and Portuguese frango piri-piri, with the roasted butternut salad you find at a South African braai
about: Chicken thighs and livers marinated in peri-peri, lemon and garlic and roasted until sticky and browned, with sweet roasted butternut, spinach, sliced onion and toasted pumpkin seeds. It is bold, smoky and bright, cooled with a lemony amasi drizzle, and the leftovers make a good cold plate tomorrow. The livers bring **iron, folate and choline**, the butternut and spinach add vitamin A and K, and the pumpkin seeds add zinc.
steps: Stir together the peri-peri sauce, half the lemon juice, the garlic, smoked paprika, half the oil and half the salt. Rub it all over the chicken thighs, and toss the trimmed livers in a spoonful of it too. Marinate the thighs for at least 30 minutes, or overnight, and keep the livers in the fridge until you need them.
Heat the oven to 220C (425F). Toss the butternut with the rest of the oil and salt on one tray. Put the chicken on another tray.

Roast the butternut until golden at the edges, about 30 minutes, turning once. Roast the chicken until it is browned and sticky at the edges and the juices run clear, 25 to 30 minutes, adding the livers to the tray for the last 8 minutes, until browned outside and just cooked through.
Toast the pumpkin seeds in a dry pan until they pop, about 3 minutes.

Toss the sliced onion with a squeeze of the lemon juice and a pinch of salt and leave it for 5 minutes to soften. Stir the rest of the lemon juice into the kefir with the cilantro to make a cooling amasi drizzle.
Pile the spinach on a plate, top with the warm butternut, the onion and the seeds. Serve the chicken and livers alongside, spoon the pan juices over them and drizzle with the amasi.
This makes two portions. Pack the second for tomorrow's lunch, with the spinach, seeds and amasi drizzle kept separate until you eat.
tip: Livers go grainy when reheated, so eat the leftover livers cold, sliced over the salad. Not a liver fan? Leave them out and add a little more chicken. Marinate overnight for the best flavour. Serve extra peri-peri at the table for people who like it hot, and use a mild sauce for kids.
ingredients: sliced thin, red if you have it
plain kefir or buttermilk, for the drizzle

name: Braaied mackerel with chutney glaze, sweet potato, greens and bean salad
inspiredBy: South African braaied snoek, basted with sweet chutney, butter and lemon, with mackerel standing in for snoek
about: Mackerel fillets brushed with a sticky chutney, lemon and garlic glaze and grilled hot, with sweet potatoes baked in foil, garlicky greens and a tangy bean and tomato salad. It is a Sunday braai at its best, and works on a grill or under the broiler. Mackerel gives you a big dose of **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**.
steps: Heat the grill (braai or broiler) until very hot. Wrap the sweet potatoes in foil with a pinch of salt and cook on the coals or at 200C (400F) until tender, about 40 minutes. A few minutes in the microwave first speeds it up.
Warm the butter, chutney, a spoonful of the lemon juice, half the garlic and the cayenne in a small pan until melted and runny, about 2 minutes.
Toss the beans, tomato, onion, oil, cilantro and half the lemon juice with a pinch of salt and let the salad sit while the fish cooks.
Warm a little of the oil in a pan and cook the collards with the rest of the garlic and a splash of water, covered, until silky and tender, about 8 minutes. Keep warm.

Pat the mackerel dry and season it with salt and pepper. Brush it with the glaze. Grill skin side down on a lightly oiled grid for about 4 minutes, brush again, then flip and cook 2 to 3 minutes more, until it flakes. Under a broiler, cook skin side up for 6 to 7 minutes and skip the flip.
Squeeze the rest of the lemon juice over the fish and serve it with the sweet potatoes, the garlicky collards and the bean salad.
tip: Fresh snoek is the real thing if you can get it. Mackerel is richer and easier to find. Cook it fresh on the day, not as a leftover.
ingredients: a spoonful for the glaze, the rest for the salad and fish
minced, half for the glaze and half for the greens
pinto beans in place of sugar beans, drained

name: Guava with roasted peanuts
about: Sweet and slightly tart guava with a handful of roasted peanuts, the kind of snack you would grab from a South African fruit stall. Guava has more **vitamin C** than an orange, and the peanuts add protein and vitamin E.
steps: Cut the guava into wedges. The seeds are soft, so you can eat them.
Eat with the peanuts, in alternating bites.

name: Biltong with almonds
inspiredBy: South African biltong, the air-dried spiced beef eaten at every braai
about: Thin strips of dried, spiced beef with a handful of almonds, a salty and crunchy pairing. Biltong packs a lot of **protein and iron** into a small snack, and the almonds add vitamin E.
steps: Slice the biltong into thin strips if it is in a piece.
Eat a strip of biltong with a few almonds, or just alternate bites.
tip: Buy biltong at a South African shop or online. For jerky, pick the plainest, least sweet one, never teriyaki.

name: Amasi with mango
about: Cold, thick amasi (fermented milk) with sweet ripe mango. It brings **calcium and protein**, with vitamin A and vitamin C from the mango.
steps: Spoon the kefir into a bowl.
Top with the diced mango and eat it cold.
ingredients: plain kefir or buttermilk, for the amasi

name: Amasi with guava
about: Cold, tangy amasi (fermented milk) with soft, fragrant guava. It brings **calcium and protein**, and the guava adds more vitamin C than an orange.
steps: Spoon the kefir into a bowl.
Top with the diced guava and eat it cold.
ingredients: plain kefir or buttermilk, for the amasi

name: Dried apricots with almonds
about: Chewy Cape-style dried apricots with a handful of almonds, a snack that keeps in the bag all day. The apricots bring vitamin A and potassium, and the almonds add **vitamin E and magnesium**.
steps: Put the apricots and almonds in a small bowl.
Eat them together so the sweet apricot balances the crunch.

name: Mielie with butter, lemon and chili
about: A braaied or boiled cob of sweet corn with a little butter, a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of chili, the way it is sold at roadside stalls. Roadside mielies are starchier; sweet corn is the closest cob here. It is a **whole-food starch** with fibre and folate.
steps: Bring a pot of salted water to a boil, or heat a grill until hot.
Boil the cob until the kernels are tender, about 8 minutes, or grill it, turning often, until it is charred in spots, about 12 minutes.
Rub the hot cob with the butter, squeeze over the lemon and finish with a pinch of cayenne.
ingredients: kernels cut from one large cob

name: Mango with lemon and chili
about: Ripe mango strips with a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of chili, a bright, sweet and spicy street-stall snack. It brings **vitamin C and vitamin A**.
steps: Cut the mango into strips.
Squeeze the lemon over it and dust with a pinch of cayenne.

name: Pilchards on toast with tomato
inspiredBy: South African pilchards on toast, a classic tinned-fish snack
about: Tinned pilchards mashed onto warm whole-wheat toast with sliced tomato, a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of chili, an old South African favourite. It is a quick hit of **omega-3, calcium and vitamin B12**, since the soft bones are edible.
steps: Toast the bread until golden and crisp.
Mash the pilchards lightly with a fork, bones and all, then spread them over the toast.
Top with the tomato, a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of cayenne.
tip: The rest of the tin keeps 2 days, covered, in the fridge.
ingredients: pilchards or sardines, with their sauce

name: Peri-peri pumpkin seeds
about: Pumpkin seeds toasted with smoked paprika, cayenne and a squeeze of lemon, a crunchy bag-of-the-day snack. They are one of the best food sources of **magnesium and zinc**.
steps: Toast the pumpkin seeds in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring, until they puff and pop, about 4 minutes.
Take the pan off the heat and stir in the smoked paprika, cayenne, salt and lemon juice. It sizzles and coats the seeds. Cool a minute before eating.

name: Dried apricots with toasted pumpkin seeds
about: Chewy dried apricots with a handful of toasted pumpkin seeds, a sweet and crunchy bag-of-the-day snack. The apricots bring vitamin A and potassium, and the seeds add **zinc and magnesium**.
steps: Toast the pumpkin seeds in a dry pan until they pop, about 3 minutes.
Eat them with the apricots, a few of each in every bite.

name: Mango with dried apricots
about: Fresh ripe mango with a few chewy dried apricots, a double dose of sweet and tangy fruit. It brings **vitamin A and vitamin C** and a good amount of potassium.
steps: Dice the mango into a bowl.
Chop the apricots small and scatter them over the mango.

name: Mango with toasted pumpkin seeds
about: Ripe mango with a handful of toasted pumpkin seeds, sweet and nutty. The mango brings **vitamin C and vitamin A**, and the seeds add zinc and magnesium.
steps: Toast the pumpkin seeds in a dry pan until they pop, about 3 minutes.
Dice the mango and scatter the seeds over it.

name: Jok moo, Thai pork and ginger rice porridge with a soft egg
inspiredBy: Central Thai jok moo, made from cooked brown rice
about: A silky rice porridge with tender minced pork, ginger, a soft egg and gai lan, topped with crisp shallot, scallion and cilantro. It's a classic Bangkok breakfast, made from the brown rice you cooked on the weekend. The pork and egg bring **protein and choline**, and the dried shrimp add a little calcium and iodine.
steps: Soak the dried shrimp in warm water for 10 minutes, then chop them finely. Stir the pork with the fish sauce, half the ginger and a pinch of white pepper for about a minute, until it turns tacky, then roll it into marble-sized balls with wet hands.
Fry the shallot rings in the oil over medium heat until golden and crisp, about 4 minutes. Lift them out onto a paper towel.

Put the rice, the shrimp, the rest of the ginger and about 3 times as much water as rice by volume in a pot. Bring to a boil, then simmer gently, stirring now and then, for 25 to 30 minutes, until the grains have broken down. Mash about a third of the rice against the side of the pot so the porridge turns silky.

Turn the heat down until the porridge is barely simmering and drop in the pork balls. Cook for 5 minutes, until cooked through, then stir in the gai lan and the salt for 1 minute, until the greens are bright.
Ladle into a bowl and crack the egg into the middle. Spoon some of the hot porridge over it and leave it for a minute, until the white turns milky and the yolk stays soft.
Top with the crisp shallot, scallion and cilantro.
tip: On weekdays, make the porridge base (the rice, shrimp and ginger) the night before, and roll the pork balls and fry the shallots then too. In the morning, reheat the base with a splash of water and add the pork, greens and egg, which takes about 15 minutes. A few chili slices at the table is how most Thai cooks finish it.

name: Khai jiao, Thai pork omelette with tomato and brown rice
inspiredBy: Central Thai khai jiao moo sap, the street omelette
about: A golden omelette with a little minced pork, crisp at the edges and seasoned with fish sauce and lime, over brown rice with juicy tomato wedges and cilantro. It's the breakfast and quick lunch of every Thai street corner. The eggs and pork bring **protein and choline**, and the tomato adds vitamin C.
steps: Warm the rice if it's cold. Cut the tomato into wedges and put them on a plate with the rice and cilantro.
Beat the eggs in a bowl with the fish sauce, salt, lime juice and scallion until the mixture is frothy.
Heat the oil in a non-stick wok over medium-high heat. Add the pork and cook for 2 minutes, breaking it up, until it's no longer pink. Tip the pork into the beaten egg and leave the oil in the wok.
Turn the heat to high. When a drop of egg sizzles right away, pour in the egg and leave it alone for 1 minute, until the edges bubble and turn golden and crisp.
Flip the omelette, cook for another minute, then slide it onto the rice and serve with the tomato.
tip: A drizzle of sriracha on the omelette is how most people eat it.

name: Xôi black rice with mung beans, dried shrimp and peanut
inspiredBy: Vietnamese xôi đậu xanh, with black sticky rice for the fibre and a little coconut milk
about: Chewy black glutinous rice with soft, smooth mashed mung beans, a jammy egg, crisp fried shallot and a savoury sprinkle of crushed peanuts and dried shrimp, with a little coconut milk drizzled over. It's a slow weekend breakfast that makes two bowls, so Sunday morning is a reheat. Black rice and mung beans bring **fibre and plant protein**, and the egg and warm soy milk add **choline, calcium and vitamin D**.
steps: Rinse the black glutinous rice for both servings (nếp cẩm, also sold as Thai black sticky rice, which roughly triples as it cooks) along with the mung beans, and soak them in separate bowls for at least 1 hour, or Friday night if you like. Plain black rice is not sticky enough for xôi.
Drain the rice and cook it in a small pot with 1½ times its volume of water, covered, over low heat for 35 to 40 minutes, until chewy and tender. Rest it with the lid on for 10 minutes.
While the rice cooks, rinse the peeled split mung beans and simmer them in plain water for 15 to 20 minutes, with no soaking, until they fall apart. Drain, add the salt and mash until smooth.

Soak the dried shrimp in warm water for 10 minutes, then chop finely. Toast the shrimp and peanuts together in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until fragrant, and crush them lightly. Toss the carrot and cucumber sticks with the lime juice, palm sugar and a pinch of salt and leave them for 15 minutes, until they turn tangy.

Boil one egg for 7 minutes, until the white is set and the yolk is still a little soft, then cool it under cold water, peel and halve it. Fry the shallot rings in the oil until golden and crisp, about 4 minutes, and drain them on a paper towel.

Pile the rice into bowls, spoon the mung beans over it and top with the egg, the shrimp and peanut mix, the shallot and the scallion. Drizzle with the coconut milk and serve with the pickled carrot and cucumber, and a cup of warm soy milk.
Keep the second portion of rice and mung beans in the fridge. On Sunday, boil a fresh egg while the rice reheats with a splash of water, covered, until steaming.
tip: Add a few slices of Chinese sausage or a spoon of pork floss if you have it, as many xôi stalls do.
ingredients: black glutinous rice (nếp cẩm), cooked weight, see step 2

name: Gỏi cuốn, shrimp summer rolls with a peanut dip
inspiredBy: Southern Vietnamese gỏi cuốn, the fresh rolls eaten with a peanut dip
about: Cool, chewy rice paper rolls packed with shrimp, seared tofu, thin rice noodles, crisp lettuce, carrot, mint and cilantro, with a smooth peanut and lime dip. Nothing here is cooked beyond the shrimp and tofu, so it's a fresh, light lunch. The shrimp and tofu bring **protein and calcium**, and the herbs add vitamin K.
steps: Soak the snapped noodles in a bowl of hot water for 10 minutes, until tender. Drain well and snip them into shorter lengths.

Poach the shrimp in simmering water for 2 to 3 minutes, until pink and curled. Drain, cool and cut each one in half lengthwise. Pat the tofu dry and sear the strips in a dry non-stick pan over medium-high heat for about 2 minutes per side, until golden. Let them cool.

Make the dip: grind the peanuts with the garlic to a rough paste in a mortar or small food processor. Stir in the lime juice, fish sauce, palm sugar, the spoonful of coconut milk and a tablespoon of warm water until smooth and spoonable.

Dip one sheet of rice paper in warm water for 10 seconds, until just pliable, and lay it on a damp towel. Lay a few shrimp halves along the lower edge, then a bed of lettuce, herbs, carrot, tofu and noodles. Fold in the sides and roll it up snugly.
Repeat with the rest to make about 5 rolls and serve with the dip. If you're taking them to work, wrap them in a damp paper towel and then in plastic so they don't dry out or stick.
tip: Swap the shrimp for extra tofu.
ingredients: thin; snapped and soaked in hot water
calcium-set, check the label, cut into strips
ground to a paste with the garlic, for the dip

name: Đậu phụ sốt cà chua, tofu simmered in tomato with brown rice
inspiredBy: Northern Vietnamese đậu phụ sốt cà chua
about: Golden pan-fried tofu simmered in a sweet, tangy tomato sauce with a little pork, shallot and cilantro, a staple of the northern Vietnamese family table. It's a quick, cheap lunch that tastes better than it sounds. The calcium-set tofu brings **a big share of your day's calcium**, and the tomatoes add vitamin C.
steps: Pat the tofu dry. Heat half the oil in a non-stick pan over medium-high heat and fry the slices for 2 to 3 minutes per side, until golden. Lift them out.
Add the rest of the oil to the pan with the shallot and garlic and cook for 1 minute. Add the pork and cook for 2 minutes, breaking it up, until no longer pink.
Add the tomato wedges and cook, stirring, for 4 to 5 minutes, until they collapse into a thick sauce. Stir in the fish sauce, the salt and a splash of water.
Slide the tofu back into the sauce and simmer for 3 minutes, so it soaks up the flavour. The sauce should be tangy, savoury and a little sweet from the tomatoes.
Scatter on the scallion and cilantro. Serve over the brown rice with the cucumber slices on the side.
tip: A pinch of black pepper over the top is the traditional finish.
ingredients: calcium-set, check the label, cut into thick slices

name: Thai red curry with chicken, tofu and gai lan
inspiredBy: Central Thai kaeng phet gai, with a quick fresh paste and extra vegetables
about: A fragrant red curry with a quick fresh paste of lemongrass, galangal, garlic, chili and shrimp paste, spiced with toasted coriander and cumin, and stirred through with chicken, tofu and gai lan in a little coconut milk with Thai basil on top. It makes two servings, so tomorrow's lunch is done. The coconut milk is just enough for flavour and richness, and the calcium-set tofu and gai lan make it **a good source of calcium**.
steps: Toast the coriander seed and cumin in a dry pan for 1 minute, until fragrant. Slice the lemongrass and galangal as finely as you can, tear the lime leaves, and blitz them with the garlic, chilies, shrimp paste, the toasted spices, the white pepper and 2 tablespoons of water in a mini chopper (or pound in a mortar) into a rough, fragrant paste.
Spoon the thick cream off the top of the coconut milk into a wide pot over medium heat and fry the paste for 2 minutes, until it smells wonderful and the oil starts to separate.
Pour in the rest of the coconut milk and about ½ cup (125 ml) of water for each serving. Add the tofu and the gai lan stems and simmer gently for 8 minutes.
Add the sliced chicken and simmer for 6 to 7 minutes, until it's just cooked through, then add the gai lan leaves for the last minute.
Stir in the fish sauce and palm sugar. Taste: it should be salty, a little sweet and properly hot. Take it off the heat and tear in the Thai basil.
Serve over the brown rice. Pack the second portion, with its rice, for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Swap the chicken for shrimp or extra tofu if you like. A spoon of ready-made red curry paste makes it a 20-minute dinner.
ingredients: stems and leaves, cut into 4 cm pieces
calcium-set, check the label, cut into cubes

name: Steamed salmon with lime, garlic and chili, with garlicky water spinach
inspiredBy: Central Thai pla neung manao, usually made with sea bass, here with salmon for its omega-3 fats
about: Salmon steamed gently over lemongrass and finished with a sharp, fiery sauce of lime, garlic, chili and cilantro, with garlicky water spinach and brown rice. It's all about the sauce, the sour, salty, sweet and hot every Thai table has. The salmon brings **omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the water spinach adds vitamin A and vitamin K.
steps: Bruise the lemongrass with the back of a knife and lay it in a steamer basket, or on a rack in a wide pot over 2 cm of water. Lay the salmon on top.
Cover and steam over a steady simmer for 8 to 10 minutes, until the salmon is just opaque and flakes at the thickest part.
While it steams, pound or finely chop half the garlic with the chili and the cilantro stems. Stir in the lime juice, fish sauce, palm sugar and 2 tablespoons of water until the sugar dissolves.

Heat the oil in a wok over high heat, fry the rest of the garlic for 20 seconds, then add the water spinach stems and stir-fry for 1 minute. Add the leaves and a splash of water for 1 to 2 minutes, until the leaves are wilted but the stems still snap.
Lift the salmon onto a plate, spoon the sauce over it and scatter on the cilantro leaves. Serve with the water spinach and the brown rice.
tip: The sauce is also excellent on steamed sea bass or cod, or spooned over tofu.
ingredients: divided between the sauce and the greens

name: Larb neua, Isaan beef herb salad in lettuce cups
inspiredBy: Isaan larb neua, with brown rice standing in for sticky rice
about: Minced lean beef cooked with only a splash of water, then tossed warm with lime, fish sauce, chili, toasted rice powder, shallot and handfuls of mint and cilantro. You scoop it into lettuce cups with raw yardlong beans and cucumber, so there's crunch in every bite. The beef brings **iron and zinc**, and the lime and the generous herbs add vitamin C and vitamin K.
steps: Spread about 2 tablespoons of the cooked brown rice in a dry pan over medium heat and stir for 8 to 10 minutes, until it's dry, golden and crunchy. Grind it to a coarse powder in a mortar or spice grinder.

Put the beef in a wide pan with a few tablespoons of water. Cook over medium heat, breaking it up with a spoon, for 6 to 7 minutes, until browned and cooked through and the pan is almost dry. Take it off the heat and let it cool for 2 minutes.
Toss the warm beef with the lime juice, fish sauce, chili flakes and half the rice powder. It should be sour first, then salty, then hot.
Stir in the shallot, scallion, mint and cilantro just before serving, so the herbs stay bright.
Spoon into lettuce cups and serve with the raw yardlong beans, cucumber and the rest of the brown rice. Scatter on the rest of the rice powder.
Pack the second portion without the herbs and lettuce, and stir in fresh herbs tomorrow.
tip: Use minced chicken or pork for larb gai or larb moo. Isaan cooks often add a spoon of roasted chili flakes at the table.
ingredients: lean beef chuck, finely chopped or pulsed in a food processor
from your batch, with a spoonful toasted for the powder; the stand-in for sticky rice

name: Cá thu kho tộ, caramel braised mackerel with greens
inspiredBy: Southern Vietnamese cá kho tộ, normally catfish in a clay pot, here with mackerel and less sugar
about: Chunks of mackerel simmered in a clay-pot style sauce of caramel, fish sauce, garlic, ginger and black pepper, with boiled water spinach and rice. It's sweet, salty and peppery, and the sauce is made for spooning over rice. The mackerel brings **omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the water spinach adds vitamin A and vitamin K.
steps: Toss the fish with half the garlic, the shallot and a few grinds of black pepper and leave it for 10 minutes.

Make the caramel: put the palm sugar and a tablespoon of water in a small heavy pot over medium heat. Don't stir, just swirl the pot, for 3 to 4 minutes, until it turns a deep amber. Stand back and pour in about 100 ml (⅓ cup) of water, which will spit, and stir until the caramel dissolves.
Stir in the oil, the rest of the garlic, the ginger, the fish sauce and the chili, then slide in the fish and spoon the sauce over it.
Simmer gently, partly covered, for 10 minutes, turning the fish once, then uncover for the last 5 minutes so the sauce reduces to a glaze and the fish is cooked through and tender.
While it simmers, boil the water spinach for 1 to 2 minutes, until tender but still bright. Drain well.
Serve the fish and its sauce with the water spinach and brown rice, scattered with the scallion. Spoon a little of the sauce over the greens.
tip: Catfish or tilapia make the more traditional version.
ingredients: cut into 4 cm steaks or chunks

name: Thịt nướng sả, lemongrass pork on brown rice with pickles and nước chấm
inspiredBy: Southern Vietnamese cơm tấm thịt nướng, with whole brown rice in place of broken rice
about: Thin slices of pork marinated in lemongrass, shallot and garlic and seared until the edges caramelize, on brown rice with quick-pickled carrot, cucumber, blanched water spinach and a spoonful of scallion oil. A small bowl of sweet, sour, salty nước chấm goes over the top. It's the classic Saigon rice plate, with less sugar and whole grain rice, and the pork brings **thiamin (B1)** while the pickles keep it fresh.
steps: Slice the pork 4 mm thick. Mix it with the lemongrass, shallot, half the garlic, half the fish sauce, 4 g (about 1 tsp) of the palm sugar and a teaspoon of the oil. Leave it to marinate for at least 30 minutes, or overnight in the fridge.
Toss the carrot with a third of the lime juice, a pinch of the sugar and a tablespoon of water. Leave it for 15 minutes to turn tangy and crisp.

Make the nước chấm: whisk the rest of the lime juice, the rest of the fish sauce, about 3 g (¾ tsp) of the sugar, the rest of the garlic, the chili and 3 tablespoons of warm water until the sugar dissolves.
Make the scallion oil (mỡ hành): put the sliced scallion in a small bowl. Heat the rest of the oil until it shimmers, pour it over the scallion and let it sizzle.

Heat a cast iron or non-stick pan over high heat, or fire up the grill. Cook the pork in batches for about 2 minutes per side, until the edges are browned and sticky. Blanch the water spinach for 1 minute and drain.
Plate the rice with the pork, water spinach, pickled carrot and cucumber slices. Spoon the scallion oil over the rice and about 2 tablespoons of nước chấm over the plate, rather than drenching it.

For the second portion, keep the pork, pickles and sauce in the fridge. Blanch both portions of water spinach tonight. In the morning, reheat the pork in a hot pan and pack it with the rice, greens and pickles.
tip: The marinated pork freezes well raw, so you can make a double batch.
ingredients: sliced across the grain, 4 mm thick
divided between the marinade and the sauce
divided between the marinade, the pickle and the sauce
divided between the pork and the scallion oil
divided between the pickle and the sauce

name: Phở bò with a slow broth, bean sprouts and a herb plate
inspiredBy: Vietnamese phở bò, Saigon style, with a lean cut of beef and a generous herb plate
about: Lean beef chuck simmered for a couple of hours with charred shallot and ginger, star anise, cinnamon and coriander seed until the broth is clear and fragrant, then ladled over rice noodles with a plate of bean sprouts, Thai basil, cilantro, lime and chili. It's the weekend project that makes the house smell wonderful and gives you two bowls. The beef brings **iron and zinc**, and the herb plate brings vitamin C.
steps: Char the shallots and ginger, cut side down, in a dry pan or under the broiler for 8 to 10 minutes, until blackened in spots. Rinse off any burnt bits.

Put the beef (and a few beef bones from the butcher, if you want a richer broth) in a big pot, cover with cold water, bring to a boil for 5 minutes and pour off the grey water. Rinse the beef and the pot, then cover the beef with about 1½ litres (6 cups) of fresh water for two servings.

Add the charred shallots and ginger, the star anise, cinnamon and coriander seed. Bring to a boil, skim off any foam, then simmer gently, partly covered, for 1½ to 2 hours, until the beef is very tender.
Lift out the beef, let it cool a little and slice it thinly against the grain. Strain the broth, stir in the fish sauce and taste. It should be savoury and fragrant, not too salty.
Cook the noodles in boiling water as the package says, usually 4 to 5 minutes. Rinse and divide into big bowls.
Top the noodles with the beef and ladle over the boiling broth. Scatter on the scallion and cilantro.
Serve with a plate of bean sprouts, basil, lime wedges and chili for everyone to add as they like.
For tomorrow's bowl, keep the broth and sliced beef in the fridge, cook fresh noodles and bring the broth to a rolling boil.
tip: In a pressure cooker the broth takes 45 minutes. Without bones the broth is lighter and cleaner, which is how a lean phở is meant to taste.
ingredients: lean beef chuck or brisket, in one or two big pieces
about a 5 cm piece, unpeeled, halved lengthwise
a small cinnamon stick, or ¼ tsp ground in a tea ball

name: Lemongrass grilled mackerel with som tam
inspiredBy: Isaan pla ping and som tam Thai, with mackerel for the usual river fish and brown rice for sticky rice
about: A whole mackerel stuffed with lemongrass and grilled until the skin blisters, served with a pounded green papaya salad of lime, chili, garlic, tomato, beans, carrot, dried shrimp and peanuts. It's the Isaan way to eat a grilled fish, with a fiery, sour salad on the side. The mackerel brings **omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the papaya salad adds vitamin C.
steps: Pat the mackerel dry and cut three slashes on each side. Stuff the cavity with the bruised lemongrass and one smashed garlic clove, and brush the skin with a little of the fish sauce. If you only find fillets, sandwich the lemongrass between two fillets and tie them with kitchen string.
Broil on a rack set close to the heat, or grill, for 7 to 8 minutes per side, until the skin is blistered and the flesh flakes easily at the thickest part. Mackerel is oily, so it needs no extra oil.

Make the som tam: soak the dried shrimp in warm water for 10 minutes. In a big bowl or mortar, pound the rest of the garlic, the chili and the shrimp to a rough paste. Add the yardlong beans and bruise them gently so they crack but keep their snap.

Add the tomato, papaya and carrot with the lime juice, the rest of the fish sauce and the palm sugar and toss, pounding lightly, until the sugar dissolves and the papaya just softens. Taste: it should be hot, sour, salty and a little sweet.
Scatter the peanuts over the salad. Serve the fish on a plate with the salad and the rice, and spoon some of the salad juices over the fish.
tip: Use sea bass or trout if you can't find mackerel. If green papaya is hard to find, shredded kohlrabi or cabbage works well.
ingredients: whole, gutted fish, listed as the edible weight, so buy one of about 300 g
from your batch, the stand-in for sticky rice

name: Pad kra pao gai, Thai basil chicken with a crispy fried egg
inspiredBy: Thai pad kra pao gai, with Thai basil in place of the usual holy basil
about: Minced chicken stir-fried hard and fast with a lot of garlic, chili, yardlong beans and a big handful of Thai basil, served over brown rice with a crispy fried egg on top. It's the dish Thai people order when they can't decide, and it takes 20 minutes. The chicken and egg bring **protein and choline**, and the Thai basil adds vitamin K.
steps: Pound or chop the garlic and chili into a rough, chunky paste. Stir the fish sauce, palm sugar and 2 tablespoons of water together in a small bowl.
Heat half the oil in a wok over high heat until it shimmers. Fry the garlic and chili paste for 20 seconds, until fragrant. Don't let the garlic brown.

Add the chicken and stir-fry hard for 2 minutes, breaking it up. Add the yardlong beans, the sauce and a splash of water, and cook for 2 minutes more, until the beans are bright and the chicken is cooked through but still moist.
Turn off the heat and stir in the Thai basil until it just wilts.
Heat the rest of the oil in a small non-stick pan until very hot. Crack in the egg and fry it for 1 to 2 minutes, until the white is crisp at the edges and the yolk is still runny.
Serve the chicken over the brown rice with the fried egg on top.
tip: Cut back to one chili if you want it mild. Holy basil is the traditional herb if you can find it at an Asian market.
ingredients: divided between the stir-fry and the egg

name: Warm ginger soy milk
inspiredBy: Thai nam tao hu and Vietnamese sữa đậu nành
about: Fortified soy milk warmed with ginger and a little palm sugar, the way it's sold at breakfast stalls in Bangkok and Hanoi. It's a calming snack with **calcium and vitamin D**, if you pick a fortified one.
steps: Warm the soy milk with the ginger and sugar in a small pot over low heat for 5 minutes, without boiling.
Strain out the ginger, if you like, and sip warm.

name: Papaya with lime and roasted peanuts
about: Soft, sweet ripe papaya with a handful of crunchy roasted peanuts and a squeeze of lime. The peanuts bring **vitamin E and protein**, and the papaya brings vitamin C and folate.
steps: Scoop the papaya out of its skin, cut it into chunks and squeeze the lime over it.
Eat it with the peanuts alongside.

name: Papaya with lime and chili salt
about: Soft ripe papaya with a squeeze of lime and a pinch of chili salt. It's sweet, sour, salty and hot, and brings **vitamin C and vitamin A**.
steps: Scoop the papaya out of its skin and cut it into chunks.
Mix the chili flakes and salt, squeeze the lime over the papaya and dip each piece in the mix.

name: Guava with chili salt
inspiredBy: Thai prik kleua, the chili salt that comes with street fruit
about: Crisp, fragrant guava dipped in the salty, hot mix that Thai street vendors sell with every fruit. A single guava has **more than a day's vitamin C** and plenty of fibre.
steps: Stir the salt and chili flakes together on a small plate.
Cut the guava into wedges, squeeze the lime over them and dip each one in the chili salt.

name: Guava with lime and salt
about: Crisp guava wedges with a squeeze of lime and a pinch of salt, a simple Vietnamese fruit snack. It's one of the best **vitamin C and fibre** snacks there is.
steps: Cut the guava into wedges.
Squeeze the lime over them and add a tiny pinch of salt.

name: Pineapple with lime and salt
about: Sweet pineapple chunks with a squeeze of lime and a tiny pinch of salt, which makes the sweetness taste brighter. The pineapple brings **vitamin C and manganese**.
steps: Cut the pineapple into chunks.
Squeeze the lime over them and add a tiny pinch of salt.

name: Pineapple with chili salt
about: Sweet, tangy pineapple with the little sprinkle of salt and chili that makes it taste like a street stall. It's high in **vitamin C and manganese**.
steps: Cut the pineapple into spears.
Mix the salt and chili flakes and sprinkle a little over the fruit.

name: Pineapple with mint and lime
about: Juicy pineapple chunks tossed with torn mint and a squeeze of lime. The mint makes it taste cool and fresh, and the pineapple brings **vitamin C and manganese**.
steps: Cut the pineapple into chunks.
Toss with the torn mint and lime juice.

name: Tào phớ, soft tofu with ginger syrup
inspiredBy: Vietnamese tào phớ, usually made with silken soy pudding
about: Warm, silky tofu in a light ginger syrup, a popular snack across Vietnam. The calcium-set silken tofu brings **calcium and plant protein**, and the ginger is warming.
steps: Simmer the ginger, palm sugar and about 50 ml of water in a small pot for 6 to 8 minutes, until it's a light syrup that coats a spoon.
Slide the silken tofu into a bowl and warm it for about 45 seconds in the microwave, or lower it into barely simmering water for 2 minutes. Don't stir it.
Spoon the ginger syrup over the tofu.
ingredients: calcium-set silken tofu, check the label

name: Chè đậu xanh, warm mung beans with coconut milk
inspiredBy: Vietnamese chè đậu xanh
about: A small bowl of soft, smooth mung beans simmered with ginger and a little coconut milk, a comforting Vietnamese sweet soup. You make two bowls at once, so the second is ready for another day. It brings **fibre, iron and folate**.
steps: Rinse about ¼ cup (50 g) of peeled split mung beans and simmer them with the ginger in about 6 times their volume of water for 15 to 20 minutes, with no soaking, until they fall apart.
Stir in the palm sugar and the coconut milk and warm through for 1 minute.
Serve one bowl warm. Keep the other in the fridge for up to 4 days and reheat with a splash of water.

name: Carrot and cucumber sticks with a peanut lime dip
about: Crunchy carrot and cucumber sticks with a smooth dip of peanut, garlic, lime and a spoonful of coconut milk, the same dip as the gỏi cuốn. It's a light snack with **fibre and vitamin A**.
steps: Cut the cucumber and carrot into sticks.
Grind the peanuts with the garlic to a paste, then stir in the lime juice, palm sugar, fish sauce, coconut milk and a spoonful of water, and use it for dunking.
ingredients: ground to a paste with the garlic

name: Guava with mint and lime
about: Crisp guava wedges tossed with torn mint and a squeeze of lime. The mint makes it taste cool and fresh, and the guava brings **vitamin C and plenty of fibre**.
steps: Cut the guava into wedges.
Toss with the torn mint and lime juice.

name: Overnight oats with soy beverage, ground flax, walnuts and figs
inspiredBy: Greek and Levantine fig and walnut breakfasts, as an overnight jar
about: Rolled oats soaked overnight in cinnamon soy beverage with chopped dried figs, ground flax and wheat germ, then topped with toasted walnuts for crunch. The figs melt into the oats and sweeten them, so you need no sugar. The fortified soy beverage brings **vitamin B12 and calcium**, and the flax and walnuts bring plant omega-3. Wheat germ adds **vitamin E and choline**.
steps: The night before, chop the figs and stir them into a jar with the oats, ground flax, wheat germ, cinnamon, salt and about ¾ cup of the soy beverage. It should look a little runny, since the oats, flax and wheat germ drink it up.
Cover and refrigerate overnight so the oats turn thick and creamy.
In the morning, give it a stir. It should be thick and spoonable, and a splash more soy beverage loosens it if it has gone stiff.
Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 3 minutes, until you can smell them, then chop roughly.
Top the oats with the walnuts and drink the rest of the soy beverage alongside.
tip: Toast a week of walnuts on Sunday and keep them in a jar. Mix two oat jars at once, they keep for 3 days in the fridge.
ingredients: fortified with B12 and calcium (check the carton); about ¾ cup in the jar, the rest to drink alongside

name: Ful medames with lemon, tomato and parsley
inspiredBy: Egyptian ful medames and the Lebanese ful that mixes in a few chickpeas
about: Warm, garlicky fava beans and a few chickpeas mashed roughly with cumin and lemon, then topped with chopped tomato, onion and parsley and a good drizzle of olive oil, the way it is eaten in Cairo. You scoop it up with warm pita. The beans bring **iron and folate**, and the tomato and lemon help you absorb that iron.
steps: Mash the garlic with the salt into a paste. Warm the fava beans and chickpeas in a small pot with a splash of their liquid, the garlic and the cumin, stirring now and then, until steaming hot, about 5 minutes.
Mash roughly with a fork, leaving some whole beans for texture. Stir in the lemon juice and half the olive oil.
Spoon the beans into a shallow bowl. Drizzle with the rest of the olive oil, then pile on the tomato, onion and parsley and dust with Aleppo pepper.
Warm the pita in a dry pan or the toaster and tear it up to scoop.
tip: A pinch of chili flakes or a few chopped pickles on top is very welcome.
ingredients: from a tin, with a little of the liquid

name: Chickpea fatteh with garlicky soy yogurt, tahini and toasted walnuts
inspiredBy: Lebanese and Syrian fattet hummus, with plain soy yogurt in place of the usual dairy yogurt
about: Warm chickpeas piled over crisp toasted pita, drenched in a cool, garlicky sauce of plain soy yogurt, tahini and lemon, and finished with sizzled walnuts and parsley. It is the traditional yogurt fatteh made plant-based, with hemp hearts blended into the sauce. The chickpeas and soy yogurt bring **protein and calcium**, the walnuts and hemp bring plant omega-3, and the glass of fortified soy beverage alongside adds **vitamin B12**.
steps: Tear the pita into bite-size pieces and toast them in a dry pan or a hot oven until golden and crisp, about 5 minutes.
Warm the chickpeas in a small pot with the cumin and a splash of water until steaming, about 5 minutes.
Mash the garlic with the salt, then blend or whisk it with the soy yogurt, tahini, hemp hearts and lemon juice until smooth. Thin with a spoonful of cold water if it is stiff.
Sizzle the walnuts in the olive oil for 1 to 2 minutes, until they smell toasty. Watch them, they scorch quickly.

Layer the pita in a bowl, spoon the chickpeas and a splash of the warm cooking water over it, pour on the yogurt sauce and finish with the hot walnuts and oil, the parsley, sumac and Aleppo pepper. Warm the soy beverage with a pinch of cinnamon and drink it alongside.
tip: On a weekday, toast the pita and make the sauce the night before. In the morning it takes 10 minutes.
ingredients: fortified with B12 and calcium (check the carton), a glass, warmed, to drink alongside

name: Hummus bowl with roasted baharat tofu and seitan, cauliflower and tomato
inspiredBy: Lebanese hummus plates, with spiced roasted tofu and seitan where the meat would go
about: Thick, lemony hummus spread in a bowl and topped with crisp-edged tofu and seitan roasted with baharat, roasted cauliflower, a chopped cucumber and tomato salad and toasted almonds. Think of the hummus plates in Beirut, with tofu and seitan where the spiced meat would be. The calcium-set tofu and chickpeas bring **protein, iron and calcium**, and the cauliflower adds choline.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C. Pat the tofu dry, cut it and the seitan into cubes and toss with half the canola oil, the baharat and a pinch of salt. Toss the cauliflower florets with the rest of the canola oil and a pinch of salt. Roast both on a tray for 20 minutes, turning once, until the tofu and seitan edges are crisp and the cauliflower is browned.

Warm the chickpeas in a small pot with a splash of water for 3 minutes. Blend them with the tahini, half the lemon juice, the garlic, cumin and a few spoonfuls of ice water, in a mini processor if you have one, for a full 2 minutes until very smooth and creamy.
Chop the cucumber, tomato and parsley and toss with the rest of the lemon juice and a pinch of salt. Toast the almonds in a dry pan for 3 minutes.
Spread the hummus in a wide bowl, make a dip in the middle and drizzle in the olive oil.
Pile the tofu, seitan, cauliflower and salad on top, scatter over the almonds and dust with za'atar. Warm pita on the side is welcome.
tip: Monday's lunch is easiest made on Sunday: roast the tofu, seitan and cauliflower and blend the hummus, then pack them separately. A double batch of hummus blends smoother and keeps 4 days in the fridge.

name: Horiatiki with marinated tofu "feta" and white beans
inspiredBy: Greek horiatiki, as it is eaten on fasting days, with tofu in place of feta
about: A Greek village salad of ripe tomato, cucumber, pepper, olives and capers under a slab of lemony oregano tofu, with white beans and pita to make it a meal. It is the kind of thing Greek cooks put together on fasting days, when there is no cheese. The tofu brings **calcium and protein**, and the white beans bring iron and fibre.
steps: Press the tofu between towels for 10 minutes, then lay the slab in a shallow dish and spoon over half the lemon juice, half the vinegar, half the oregano and a good pinch of salt. Marinate for at least 30 minutes, or leave it in the fridge in the morning or overnight.
Cut the tomato into wedges, the cucumber into thick half-moons and the pepper into rings, and slice the onion thinly.
Toss the vegetables with the white beans, olives, capers, the rest of the lemon juice and vinegar and most of the olive oil.
Spoon the salad onto a plate and set the tofu on top like a slab of feta. Drizzle with the last of the oil, the marinade and the rest of the oregano.
Toast the pita and tear it up to mop the juices.
tip: Marinate the tofu the night before or in the morning, it tastes much better after a few hours. Crumble it with your hands if you want it to look more like feta.
ingredients: pressed, cut in a thick slab

name: Mujaddara hamra with caramelized onions and lemony cabbage salad
inspiredBy: Lebanese mujaddara hamra, the bulgur version, with malfouf salad
about: Brown lentils and bulgur cooked together with cumin, topped with deep golden onions, and served with a crunchy lemon, garlic and mint cabbage and carrot salad. It is the Lebanese Lenten classic, plain food done properly. The lentils and bulgur together bring **protein, iron and fibre**, and the lemony salad helps you absorb the iron.
steps: Rinse the lentils, cover with plenty of water and simmer for 12 to 15 minutes, until nearly tender but still holding their shape. Drain, saving the cooking water.

While the lentils simmer, slice the onions thin. Cook them in the canola oil over medium heat, stirring every few minutes and adding a splash of water if they catch, for 25 minutes, until deep golden and sweet. Take out a third and keep it for the top.
Stir the cumin and baharat into the onions left in the pot for 30 seconds, then add the bulgur, the lentils, the salt and enough of the lentil water to cover by about 2 cm.
Cover and simmer gently for 15 minutes, until the water is gone. Rest off the heat for 10 minutes, then fluff with a fork.
Shred the cabbage finely and grate the carrot. Mash the garlic with a pinch of salt and toss it with the cabbage, carrot, lemon juice, olive oil and torn mint.
Serve the mujaddara topped with the reserved onions, with the cabbage salad on the side. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Keep the cabbage salad in a separate container so it stays crunchy for tomorrow.

name: Gigantes plaki, giant white beans baked in tomato, dill and parsley
inspiredBy: Greek gigantes plaki, made with canned beans so it works on a weeknight
about: Creamy white beans baked in a sweet-sharp tomato sauce with celery, carrot and dill until the edges blister. It is Greek Lenten cooking at its best, and it tastes even better the next day. The beans bring **iron, calcium and fibre**, and a squeeze of lemon at the end helps you absorb the iron.
steps: Heat the oven to 200 C. Warm the olive oil in a wide ovenproof pan and cook the chopped onion, celery and diced carrot for 8 minutes, until soft.
Stir in the garlic, paprika and oregano for 30 seconds, then add the crushed tomato, bay leaf, salt and a splash of water. Simmer for 10 minutes, until the sauce thickens.
Fold in the white beans, half the dill and half the parsley, and slide the pan into the oven for 20 to 25 minutes, until the sauce is bubbling and the edges are browned.
Finish with the lemon juice and the rest of the herbs. Serve with crusty bread or warm pita if you like. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Cannellini work well here, and canned giant beans from a Greek grocer are even better. If you cook dried giant beans, soak them overnight and simmer them for about an hour before they go into the sauce.

name: Seitan, mushroom and cauliflower shawarma plate with garlic sauce and pickled carrot
inspiredBy: Lebanese shawarma, with seitan, mushrooms and cauliflower for the meat and a tofu garlic sauce for the toum
about: Baharat-spiced seitan, mushrooms and cauliflower roasted on one tray until the edges crisp, piled on a plate with a fluffy tofu garlic sauce, tomato, parsley and tangy pickled carrot, with warm pita on the side to scoop. It has the smoky, garlicky shawarma-stand flavour without the spit. The seitan and tofu together bring **protein, selenium and calcium**, and the vitamin D mushrooms add **vitamin D**.
steps: Heat the oven to 230 C. Cut the seitan into thin strips. Toss them with the baharat, paprika, cumin, half the lemon juice, half the garlic (mashed), half the canola oil and a good pinch of salt. Let them sit while the oven heats.
Meanwhile, toss the carrot ribbons with the vinegar and a pinch of salt and leave them to pickle.
Blend the tofu with the rest of the garlic, the rest of the lemon juice, a pinch of salt and a splash of cold water until fluffy and white, like toum.

Spread the seitan, mushrooms and cauliflower on one big tray (two if they crowd), drizzle the mushrooms and cauliflower with the rest of the oil, season them with a pinch of salt and roast for 20 to 25 minutes, turning once, until browned and crisp at the edges.
Warm the pita in a dry pan or the toaster.
Pile the seitan, mushrooms and cauliflower on a plate with the garlic sauce, tomato, parsley and the drained pickled carrot, and eat with the warm pita.
tip: Double the tofu garlic sauce, it keeps 4 days in the fridge and is good on the falafel too.
ingredients: sliced; sold as vitamin D mushrooms. Plain white mushrooms work, with less vitamin D

name: Baked chickpea and fava falafel in pita with roasted cauliflower and tahini sauce
inspiredBy: Lebanese and Egyptian falafel and ta'ameya, made with chickpeas and fava and baked instead of fried
about: Green, herby chickpea and fava falafel baked until crisp outside and fluffy inside, with warm pita, tahini sauce, a fresh tomato, cucumber and carrot salad and a side of roasted cauliflower. It has all the flavour of the street-stall version with a lot less oil. The chickpeas and fava beans bring **protein, iron and zinc**, and the cauliflower adds choline and vitamin C.
steps: The night before, cover the dried chickpeas and fava beans with plenty of cold water and soak for 12 hours. Drain well and, if you used whole fava beans, slip off the skins. Split, peeled fava beans skip this step.

Heat the oven to 220 C. Pulse the soaked chickpeas and fava beans (double the amount for two portions) in a food processor with the onion, garlic, parsley, cumin, coriander and most of the salt until it looks like coarse couscous, not paste. Rest for 15 minutes so the beans bind.

Shape the mixture into 12 small patties (6 per portion). Toss the cauliflower florets with a third of the canola oil and a pinch of salt and spread them on a big tray. Put a second tray in the oven to preheat, then brush it with the remaining oil, set the falafel on it and brush the tops too.
Bake both trays for 25 minutes, turning the falafel once, until the falafel are deep golden and the cauliflower is browned at the edges.
Whisk the tahini with the lemon juice and enough cold water to make a pourable sauce.

Dice the tomato and cucumber and toss with the grated carrot. Warm the pita, open it and tuck in a few falafel with some salad and tahini sauce. Eat the rest of the falafel, salad and cauliflower on the plate with the remaining sauce. Pack the second portion and the sauce for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: The beans must be soaked from dry. Canned ones turn to mush and the falafel fall apart. Leftover falafel are not good cold: reheat them for 8 minutes at 200 C and pack the tahini sauce separately.
ingredients: dried fava beans, peeled if you can find them, soaked overnight

name: Adas bi hamod, lemony lentil and chard soup with toasted pita
inspiredBy: Lebanese adas bi hamod, the lentil soup with chard and lemon
about: A thick Lebanese lentil soup with silky chard, garlic and plenty of lemon, topped with crisp toasted pita and a swirl of olive oil. It is bright, sour and deeply comforting, and a Lenten favourite. The lentils bring **protein, iron and folate**, and the chard adds vitamins A and K.
steps: Rinse the lentils. Warm the canola oil in a big pot and cook the chopped onion for 6 to 8 minutes, until soft and golden. Add the garlic, cumin and coriander and stir for 30 seconds.
Add the lentils and plenty of water, enough to cover them by about 5 cm. Bring to a boil, then simmer for 25 to 30 minutes, until the lentils are completely soft and falling apart.
Slice the chard stems thin and chop the leaves. Add the stems and cook for 5 minutes, then add the leaves for 3 minutes more, until silky.

Mash some of the soup against the side of the pot with a spoon, or give it a few pulses with a stick blender, so it is thick but still has texture. Add the salt and the lemon juice. It should taste distinctly sour.
Tear the pita into pieces and toast in a dry pan until golden and crisp, about 4 minutes.
Ladle the soup into bowls and top with the pita, the parsley, a drizzle of the olive oil and a pinch of Aleppo pepper. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the pita in a separate bag.
tip: Thin the leftovers with a splash of water when you reheat them. The soup thickens overnight.

name: Lenten chard and mushroom pie with tofu "feta"
inspiredBy: Greek hortopita and manitaropita, the Lenten (nistisimi) pies made with oil and no dairy
about: Crisp layers of oil-brushed phyllo around a lemony filling of chard, mushrooms, dill and herby crumbled tofu. It is the kind of fasting-season pie Greek families bake with no cheese or egg. The tofu brings **calcium and protein**, and the vitamin D mushrooms add **vitamin D** and niacin.
steps: Heat the oven to 190 C. Chop the chard, stems and all, and cook it in a dry pot over medium heat for 5 to 6 minutes, until wilted. Tip it into a colander, cool for a few minutes, then squeeze out as much water as you can.

Cook the chopped onion and mushrooms in the olive oil for 8 minutes, until soft and the liquid has cooked off. Crumble the tofu into a big bowl with the lemon juice, oregano and most of the salt and let it stand while the chard drains.
Mix the chard, onion and mushrooms into the tofu with the dill, parsley, nutmeg, pepper and the rest of the salt. Taste, it should be bright and well seasoned.
Brush a baking dish with some of the canola oil. Lay in half the phyllo sheets, brushing each one lightly with oil, then spread the filling over.
Cover with the remaining phyllo, again brushing each sheet. Tuck in the edges, brush the top generously, and score the top layers into squares with a sharp knife.
Bake for 35 to 40 minutes, until deep golden and crisp. Rest for 10 minutes before cutting. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Thaw frozen phyllo in the fridge overnight, so move the box from the freezer on Friday night. Keep the sheets under a damp towel while you work so they do not dry out and crack. Short on sheets? Skip the bottom layer and scrunch all the phyllo loosely over the filling, brushing as you go. Leftovers crisp up in a hot oven.
ingredients: finely chopped; sold as vitamin D mushrooms. Plain white mushrooms work, with less vitamin D

name: Sicilian caponata with white beans and chickpeas
inspiredBy: Sicilian caponata with a Levantine pomegranate molasses twist, served warm over white beans as a main
about: A sweet-sharp Sicilian eggplant stew with celery, olives, capers and toasted almonds, spooned warm over creamy white beans and chickpeas. It is Sicily's answer to ratatouille, with a bit of agrodolce bite. The beans and almonds bring **protein and calcium**, and the eggplant adds fibre.
steps: Toss the eggplant cubes with the canola oil and a pinch of salt, spread them on a tray and cover with foil. Roast at 220 C for 10 minutes, then take off the foil and roast 15 minutes more, until browned and soft. Toast the almonds in a dry pan for 3 minutes and chop.
Meanwhile, warm the olive oil in a wide pan and cook the onion, celery and pepper for 8 minutes, until soft.
Add the crushed tomato, olives and capers and simmer for 10 minutes.
Stir in the roasted eggplant, the vinegar and the pomegranate molasses and simmer for 5 minutes, until glossy. It should taste sweet and sharp at once.
